conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 18, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Adding Braggtown and Merrick-Moore to the Longtime Homeowner Grant Program (Item 26)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 2-5 on DeDreana Freeman's amendment to immediately include Braggtown and Merrick-Moore in the city's tax-relief pilot alongside Walltown before unanimously approving Walltown alone.
conflicts.side_a_position: Immediately expand the city's Longtime Homeowner Grant criteria to add Braggtown and Merrick-Moore for the 2019-2020 tax years.
side_a_arguments: Legacy Black homeowners in Braggtown and Merrick-Moore are facing urgent tax-bill spikes and gentrification displacement, and the countywide program only begins with 2021 taxes.
If Council can allocate $79,000 for its own raises, it should extend equivalent relief to long-time homeowners fighting to stay housed.
conflicts.side_b_position: Restrict the city pilot to Walltown based on documented city affordable housing investments while pressing Durham County to expand the countywide relief program to 60% AMI.
side_b_arguments: City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg advised that granting neighborhood tax relief where the city had not made qualifying affordable housing investments creates serious North Carolina constitutional emoluments risk.
A countywide program administered with Durham County at 60% AMI is legally sound and covers all underserved neighborhoods equitably without a patchwork city carve-out.
conflicts.resolution: Amendment Failed 2-5; original Walltown & 2020 tax-year motion subsequently Passed 7-0

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Sept. 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 1051 Olive Branch Road Annexation, Suburban Growth in Southeast Durham, and Post-Planning Commission Revisions
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 on annexing and rezoning 1051 Olive Branch Road for 284 units after the developer revised environmental and cemetery proffers following a June 21 continuance and an April 1-11 Planning Commission denial recommendation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation and rezoning because post-continuance commitments substantially improved environmental protection, resolved gravesite family outreach, and added needed housing supply.
side_a_arguments: Majority members noted that post-June revisions secured 13 of 13 descendant family consents alongside an archaeological study, raised distributed tree save to 24% and open space to 35%, and eliminated three vehicular stream crossings.
Supporters cited Durham's housing supply shortage and contiguous alignment with the previously approved adjacent 1101 Olive Branch Road project.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the suburban annexation and rezoning due to sprawling Southeast Durham growth, cumulative neighborhood impacts, and repeated developer bypassing of the Planning Commission.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (01:00:16) and DeDreana Freeman (01:04:45) maintained their opposition to continued far-flung suburban annexations in the Olive Branch corridor and criticized the cumulative infrastructure and community-cost burden.
Members across Council also raised frustration that developers wait until City Council hearings—bypassing the Planning Commission—to introduce major design concessions.
conflicts.resolution: Council approved annexation and rezoning 5-2 (Freeman and Reece nay) and subsequently approved the statutory Consistency Statement 7-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Feb 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Scorecard Rating vs. Paired Weighting Methodology for Ranking Council Budget Requests (Item 20)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 in a straw vote over whether to rank 11 FY2021-22 Council budget requests totaling over $2 million using a multi-criteria scorecard rubric or a forced pairwise-comparison method.
conflicts.side_a_position: Use the Scorecard Rating rubric to evaluate Council budget requests against racial equity and strategic goals.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, and Mark-Anthony Middleton argued scorecard ratings explicitly weigh equity, community impact, and alignment with strategic priorities without flattening complex tradeoffs into binary choices.
conflicts.side_b_position: Use the Paired Weighting tool to force clear relative prioritization among competing requests.
side_b_arguments: Steve Schewel and Charlie Reece contended paired comparisons reveal true priorities more cleanly rather than producing clustered high scores on a subjective rubric.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-2 by straw poll for the Scorecard Rating method; Council also gave unanimous thumbs-up (04:01:42) for an internal City staff review team to score all 11 requests alongside Council scores.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Public Incentive for Ideal Sandwich Shop LLC Without Guaranteed Living Wage and Additional Community Outreach (Item 24)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-3 over whether to approve a $102,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant for Ideal Sandwich Shop LLC in Old East Durham given its $11/hour base starting wage, 2:1 public match ratio, and limited neighborhood resident outreach.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $102,000 incentive now to revitalize a blighted Angier Avenue corner, expand affordable fresh food access, and give a small restaurant startup room to scale up to a living wage.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton and Pierce Freelon argued small neighborhood startups cannot afford $15+/hour on day one without pricing out low-income residents, comparing Ideal's trajectory to local restaurants like Monuts and Copa.

Mayor Steve Schewel noted Council had just unanimously approved Checkers (whose fast-food wages fall below $15.68/hour) and argued keeping $5 sandwiches affordable alongside a $15.68 starting wage is economically unviable at launch.
Javiera Caballero highlighted small-business generosity to Durham schools and the feasibility of scaling wages over 3–4 years.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose or delay the $102,000 public subsidy due to sub-living-wage jobs, the high 2:1 public match ratio, gentrification risks, and unverified resident engagement.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Charlie Reece argued public tax dollars during a pandemic fiscal crunch should not subsidize $11/hour jobs below Durham's ~$15.68/hour living wage.

DeDreana Freeman flagged the steep 2:1 public match (compared to Checkers' 9:1), the omission of community support letters from the packet, and gentrification pressures along the Angier-Driver corridor, requesting a one-cycle delay.
Reece noted the referenced support letters came from adjacent business owners with commercial interests rather than neighborhood residents.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 4-3 on roll call at 02:11:28 (Schewel, Caballero, Freelon, Middleton Aye; Johnson, Freeman, Reece Nay) after Middleton declined Freelon's proposed friendly amendment to delay.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 19, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Petitioned Street Paving and Utility Extensions vs. Full Cost-Recovery Policy (Items 20 and 21, including Linden Terrace)
conflicts.summary: Council split 3-4 on whether to accept certificates of sufficiency for two resident-initiated infrastructure petitions for curb, gutter, paving, water, and sewer improvements while awaiting January staff cost-recovery proposals.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the petitions now to advance long-awaited basic street, water, and fire-hydrant infrastructure for residents.
side_a_arguments: Residents whose land was historically annexed into the city have faced longstanding infrastructure inequities.
Applying a uniform 'fairness' rule going forward ignores past history and leaves existing residents without city water or fire hydrants to fight fires.
conflicts.side_b_position: Decline the petitions under the current framework and establish a full cost-recovery, equity-prioritized citywide policy.
side_b_arguments: Accepting the certificate of sufficiency legally obligates the city to build the improvements at whatever future cost applies rather than under full cost recovery.
Capital prioritization should rely on a racial-equity-informed system that no petitioner can jump ahead of, pending January staff options.
conflicts.resolution: Both motions to accept the certificates of sufficiency failed 3-4 (at 03:10:43 and 03:14:50), ending both petitions while Council awaited staff's January cost-recovery policy presentation.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Courtyards at Doc Nichols Annexation & Rezoning — Low-Density Suburban Growth vs. Accessible Housing & Solar Proffers (Item 16)
conflicts.summary: With Charlie Reece absent, City Council deadlocked 3-3 on Epcon Communities' 133-unit accessible housing proposal in Southeast Durham, defeating the project.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 75-acre annexation and rezoning based on accessible aging-in-place housing, environmental proffers, and $120,000 affordable housing contribution.
side_a_arguments: Provided Durham's first-ever solar conduit residential proffer, 33% tree preservation, and $120,000 dedicated to the city's affordable housing fund.

Middleton and Freelon noted the single-story zero-step courtyard model serves seniors and disability needs in an underserved area, and rejected applying the un-adopted draft Southeast Focus Area Plan against a compliant application.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning as incompatible low-density greenfield sprawl with watershed/stream crossing impacts and luxury price points.
side_b_arguments: At 1.8 units/acre and $500,000-$550,000 home prices, the suburban layout conflicts with smart-growth transit/infrastructure efficiency and the emerging Southeast planning vision.
The Planning Commission recommended denial unanimously (0-12), citing environmental impacts of the stream crossing, buffer encroachment, and neighborhood road safety concerns.
conflicts.resolution: Failed 3-3 on tie vote

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 1, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Latta Park Rezoning — Commercial Expansion, Latta Road Traffic & Eno Watershed Impacts vs. On-Site Affordable Townhomes & Intersection Fixes
conflicts.summary: Latta Park split the Council 6-1 after residents and conservation advocates argued that adding 55,000 sq ft of retail and 200 townhomes at Guess and Latta Roads violated Comprehensive Plan commercial siting, threatened Eno River water quality, and overloaded two-lane Latta Road, while the six-member majority praised unprecedented proffers including 10 60%-AMI townhomes and dual turn lanes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the mixed-use CG(D)/PDR 9.906 rezoning as a needed supply of moderate/affordable townhomes and northern Durham neighborhood retail.
side_a_arguments: Developer proffered over 50 commitments including 10 permanently affordable townhomes at 60% AMI ($1.25M subsidy), 40kW solar, a 1.3-acre park, and 100-year residential stormwater detention.

Dual left-turn lanes improve peak morning Guess/Latta intersection level-of-service from D to C where no NCDOT upgrades are funded, and rejection leaves RS-20 $500k+ McMansions as the by-right alternative.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose commercial and high-density rezoning due to traffic bottlenecks on un-widenable Latta Road, stormwater/Eno watershed risks, and lack of transit walkability.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman voted No after extensive opposition testimony citing level-of-service D egress on Latta Road, right-in/right-out U-turns on Guess Road, and Easley Elementary traffic hazards.
Opponents including Megan Gray and Eno River Association ED Jessica Sheffield noted nearby vacant commercial space, no bus service, and impervious surface runoff above West Point on the Eno.
conflicts.resolution: Council adopted both the Latta Park zoning ordinance and consistency statement by 6-1 roll-call votes, with DeDreana Freeman in dissent.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 1, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Sufficiency of Griffin Place Community Benefits, Affordable Housing Proffer, and Product Integration
conflicts.summary: Council paused the 462-unit Griffin Place annexation and rezoning in eastern Durham because members found initial housing-fund payments, perimeter buffers, and segregated single-family/townhome layouts insufficient relative to the project's scale and state-road congestion.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold the public hearing open until January 3, 2022 to extract stronger affordable housing contributions, better industrial/residential buffering, block-length limits, and improved traffic clarity.
side_a_arguments: Even after raising the affordable housing fund proffer from $150 to $500/unit during the hearing, Council noted the ~$115M project needed stronger design commitments, less rigid product segregation, and better buffering adjacent to Scannell industrial land.
State roads around Cheek and Ferrell Roads lack funded DOT widening, raising urgency around community benefits.
conflicts.side_b_position: Recognize already-proffered traffic signals, 100-year ponds, and Glenn Elementary pedestrian crossings while negotiating additional terms.
side_b_arguments: Applicant argued residential zoning cut trips vs. current industrial zoning and committed to three traffic signals and a $34,000 DPS school contribution.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 7-0 to continue the Griffin Place public hearing open until January 3, 2022.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 18, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: City Council Salary Adjustments During Pandemic Budget Cycle (Item 24)
conflicts.summary: Six Council members voted to raise Council salaries to Durham's $35,200 livable-wage floor starting January 1, 2022 to open officeholding to working-class residents, while DeDreana Freeman dissented over optics and equity toward city employees whose step raises had been paused.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adjust Council member salaries to the city's full-time minimum livable wage ($35,200) and Mayor's salary to $40,536 effective January 1, 2022.
side_a_arguments: Council service requires full-time commitment and dozens of board obligations; sub-living stipends exclude working-class residents and low-wealth candidates.

Outgoing members (including Freelon and Schewel) argued it is an institutional equity reform comparable to recent adjustments in Charlotte and Raleigh, and the City Attorney advised Council cannot bind future budget cycles without passing it now.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose raising Council salaries at this time and prioritize restoring skipped pay steps for municipal workers and resident COVID relief.
side_b_arguments: City staff missed step raises during the pandemic and Council should focus budget dollars on city employees and residents facing hardship first.
Raising post-election stipends alone does not overcome structural fundraising and campaign barriers that prevent working-class candidates from running.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 6-1

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 23, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: City Council Salary Adjustments and Pandemic Budget Priorities (Item 3)
conflicts.summary: A Council majority endorsed raising Council stipends to Durham's livable-wage floor ($35,200 Council / ~$42,000 Mayor) to make officeholding accessible to working-class residents, while DeDreana Freeman opposed moving ahead while employee pay steps had been skipped and Charlie Reece remained torn over spending $78,000.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance an ordinance aligning Council salaries with Durham's full-time minimum livable wage, subject to a public hearing.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon, Jillian Johnson, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Steve Schewel argued sub-living stipends lock working people out of devoting full-time hours to Council service.
Both Charlotte and Raleigh have adopted comparable compensation updates, and City Attorney/Budget staff confirmed Council cannot defer binding a future budget year.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose or question advancing Council raises during pandemic hardship when staff pay steps were skipped and residents need direct relief.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman argued Council should focus first on restoring skipped employee step raises and doubted stipends would overcome campaign cost barriers.
Charlie Reece questioned whether $78,000 was the best pandemic budget choice while Jacqueline Wagstaff urged taxpayer control rather than moving from a part-time stipend model.
conflicts.resolution: Consensus thumbs-up to schedule a public hearing before taking a formal vote

conflicts.meeting_title: Regular Durham City Council Meeting Aug 16, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Courtyards at Southpoint 2 Buffer Protections, ATT Connectivity, and Residential Accountability (Item 18)
conflicts.summary: Residents along Herndon Road and Fenwick Parkway objected to density, stormwater runoff, traffic, and loss of trees along the American Tobacco Trail, prompting Council to press Epcon Southpoint LLC into binding mid-hearing proffers before voting unanimously.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve only with binding written proffers guaranteeing American Tobacco Trail connections, undisturbed buffer trees, traffic calming, and affordable housing support.
side_a_arguments: Neighbors Karen Francola, Dr. Eugene Granger, Barbara Taylor, Bansari Patel, and Trisha Smarr raised flooding, buffer clearing, and Herndon/Fenwick traffic concerns.

Council members pushed Epcon Southpoint LLC to add concrete written commitments for two ATT trail tie-ins, an undisturbed 20-ft ATT buffer outside tie-in corridors, Phase 2 traffic calming, and a $40,000 affordable housing contribution.
conflicts.side_b_position: Initial developer submission relied on standard UDO compliance and a single trail tie-in without Phase 2 traffic-calming or undisturbed-buffer commitments.
side_b_arguments: Applicant attorneys initially defended standard site-plan review for stormwater and buffer management before agreeing to expand written commitments during the hearing.
conflicts.resolution: Epcon Southpoint LLC committed to the added proffers on the record (01:56:10), resolving Council concerns and yielding unanimous 7-0 approval.

conflicts.meeting_title: Regular Durham City Council Meeting Aug 2, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Parcel K Voluntary Annexation and Growth Management in Southeast Durham (Item 27)
conflicts.summary: Council split 6-1 on annexing Parcel K for an 837-unit residential development, weighing urgent housing supply and rare mandatory affordable housing commitments against resident objections to annexation, traffic on Leesville Road, and outward suburban expansion.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation and development to expand housing supply, secure 20-year deed-restricted affordable units and 100-year stormwater protections, and avoid pushing growth into neighboring counties.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson argued Durham faces a severe housing shortage, cannot curb traffic by halting housing (needing transit investments instead), and cannot divert city infrastructure bonds from historically marginalized neighborhoods to state-maintained Leesville Road.

Charlie Reece noted it was the first private project in five years offering dedicated affordable housing and strong stormwater protections, while Javiera Caballero and Planning Director Sara Young noted the site sits inside the fill-in area west of Kemp Road.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject the voluntary annexation of outer Southeast Durham land over neighborhood opposition.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman praised the project's commitments if annexed, but voted No on the annexation itself because residents had organized to protect their home area from city expansion.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation passed 6-1 (Freeman Nay); Council then voted 7-0 to adopt the PDR 5.949 zoning and consistency statement.

conflicts.meeting_title: Regular Durham City Council Meeting Aug 2, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Appointment of Rodrigo Dorfman to the Durham Cultural Advisory Board (Pulled Item 3)
conflicts.summary: Council divided sharply over whether to seat Cultural Advisory Board nominee Rodrigo Dorfman despite community outcry over a 2019 email criticizing two Black women's comprehension and speech.
conflicts.side_a_position: Withhold or reject Dorfman's appointment until he performs reparative work and accountability for racist/coded remarks toward Black women.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued Dorfman's 2019 email invoked hurtful racist tropes about Black women's intellect ('you could tell by the way they spoke') and remained a distraction absent genuine reconciliation.

DeDreana Freeman proposed holding or re-advertising the seat because unrepentant harm disrespects community leadership, and Pierce Freelon suggested Human Relations Commission mediation while taking Black women's testimony seriously.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support Dorfman's appointment based on CAB's recommendation and avoid magnifying a 2019 political/interpersonal dispute or applying selective standards.
side_b_arguments: Jillian Johnson argued the 2019 email stemmed from a polarizing election conflict involving specific individuals rather than all Black women, noted Dorfman resigned from People's Alliance/Nuestra Gente, and warned against turning private disputes into public trials.

Javiera Caballero cited an uneven double standard where critics attacking her citizenship or making xenophobic/anti-Semitic remarks faced no consequences, while Mayor Steve Schewel and Charlie Reece supported Dorfman on the merits while agreeing to pause until Thursday to review the email.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 7-0 to confirm the five uncontested CAB nominees and defer Dorfman's nomination to the August 5 work session; Dorfman subsequently withdrew his application prior to August 5.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 1051 Olive Branch Road Environmental Protections, Grave Relocation, and Suburban Housing Supply (Item 43)
conflicts.summary: Council held a prolonged debate over Pulte Home Company LLC's 284-unit annexation at 1051 Olive Branch Road, pitting housing-supply concerns against East Durham Open Space Plan incompatibility, mass grading, peripheral tree save, and relocation of an on-site cemetery, resulting in continuance to September 7.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue the hearing to seek stronger tree preservation, environmental mitigation, and cemetery/community commitments without immediately killing needed housing stock.
side_a_arguments: Javiera Caballero (02:49:21) and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson (03:08:56) stressed Durham's worsening housing shortage while agreeing existing open questions justified a continuance.

Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:13:19) argued $230k-$300k housing expands supply for working-class firefighters, teachers, and officers while still expressing concern over the gravesite and the negligible 21%-to-22% tree-save increase.

Mayor Steve Schewel (03:04:54) backed increasing supply in Southeast Durham but warned he would vote no immediately given the 'not compatible with East Durham Open Space Plan' staff finding and environmental sensitivity.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose or demand deep substantive redesigns addressing far-flung Southeast Durham sprawl, cost-burden spillover, climate/mass-grading harm, and cemetery removal.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (02:57:53) questioned whether townhouses in far-east Durham near Morrisville actually curb gentrification in Braggtown or Walltown and argued annexation conferred no net benefit to Durham.

DeDreana Freeman (02:23:07, 03:10:27) highlighted cumulative impacts across nine area rezonings, carbon footprint without transit, nearby cost-burdened neighborhoods, and distress over moving a historic cemetery—noting she only supported a continuance if meaningful tree-save and stream-crossing changes returned.
conflicts.resolution: With applicant Tim Sivers' agreement (03:23:52), Council left the public hearing open and continued Item 43 to September 7, 2021.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Duke School $10M Tax-Exempt Revenue Bond Host-Approval Resolution (Item 45)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to pass the federal TEFRA resolution for private Duke School's revenue bonds, with Javiera Caballero voting Nay and Mark-Anthony Middleton raising equity concerns about private tuition and public-service reliance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the routine ministerial TEFRA resolution because the City of Durham incurs zero debt, financial obligation, or taxpayer liability.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:41:30), Pierce Freelon (03:39:47), DeDreana Freeman (03:42:27), and Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:42:00) agreed that federal tax-law pass-through approval carries no city financial risk, though Middleton pressed Duke School officials on $20k-$23k tuition, lack of free/reduced lunch or busing, and reliance on city police/fire.
conflicts.side_b_position: Decline to lend City host-jurisdiction TEFRA approval to a private school revenue bond issuance.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero cast the sole Nay vote on roll call (03:43:18) without stating floor remarks.
conflicts.resolution: TEFRA resolution passed 6-1.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 'We Are The Ones' Violence Prevention Funding Amount, Fund Source, and Scope (Mini-Grants vs. Mutual Aid/Centers)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over how much extra money to allocate from fund balance—versus ARPA—and whether funding should be restricted strictly to mini-grants.
conflicts.side_a_position: Provide an extra $187,600 from fund balance to bring 'We Are The Ones' mini-grants to $250,000 total immediately in FY22.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Charlie Reece, and Mark-Anthony Middleton supported reaching $250,000 immediately to empower grassroots violence-prevention mini-grants rather than deferring to uncertain ARPA scoring.

Restricting the $250,000 allocation to mini-grants addressed concerns from Budget Director Bertha Johnson and Javiera Caballero regarding ARPA procurement and unvetted mutual-aid or center line items.
conflicts.side_b_position: Limit extra one-time fund-balance dollars to $100,000 rather than $187,600 and scrutinize program design before committing $250,000.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel favored adding $100,000 rather than $187,600 to reach $250,000 and cast the sole Nay vote when the $187,600 mini-grant motion was called.
conflicts.resolution: Council passed the $187,600 mini-grant allocation 6-1, with Steve Schewel dissenting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council May 3, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Expedited PDR 8.00 Rezoning Process, Renter Notification, and Stream-Buffer Envelope for CASA Affordable Housing
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over whether to approve CASA's expedited rezoning for 20 deeply affordable units despite concerns regarding minimal renter notification, an alternate building envelope conditioned on a future Board of Adjustment stream-buffer variance, and process equity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the expedited PDR 8.00 rezoning to secure NCHFA financing for urgently needed <=30% AMI affordable housing.
side_a_arguments: The project delivers 20 units for households at or below 30% AMI, which is the hardest tier of affordable housing to build and already holds City funding commitments.
May approval is required to meet the North Carolina Housing Finance Agency's June board deadline.
Council is not granting a stream-buffer variance; the Board of Adjustment retains sole authority over any variance for the alternate building envelope.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the expedited rezoning due to inadequate renter notice, stream-buffer concerns, and unequal expedited process standards.
side_b_arguments: Bare-minimum legal notice went to property owners rather than long-term neighboring renters, leaving residents like Ms. Batson uninformed.
The conditional building envelope raises concerns about infringing on the Falls/Jordan stream buffer and potential flooding or sinking impacts.
Expediting this rezoning bypasses full community engagement and creates inequity compared to other local organizations that are not granted expedited timelines.
conflicts.resolution: Rezoning ordinance passed 6-1, followed by a 7-0 vote adopting the consistency statement.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council March 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 4523 Hope Valley Road — Downstream Stormwater Erosion Concerns
conflicts.summary: Council split 6-1 on whether to delay Navion's congregate-living expansion at 4523 Hope Valley Road for an on-site Stormwater Services inspection following neighbor testimony of gully erosion.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning now based on staff/engineering review, required annual BMP inspections, and upgraded single-room congregate living capacity.
side_a_arguments: Steve Schewel and Charlie Reece noted the property was already largely developed, stormwater site-plan engineering controls and annual BMP inspections apply at permitting, and single-room congregate units improve care standards.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer the vote until Stormwater Services physically inspects erosion conditions reported behind the facility.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman credited neighboring HOA president Alisa Peterson's erosion testimony and asked for on-site verification by Stormwater Services prior to rezoning approval.
conflicts.resolution: Both the rezoning and consistency motions passed 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting Nay.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council March 1, 2021
conflicts.issue: Phillips Valley (2000 Fletcher's Chapel Road) Annexation and Mass Grading Boundaries
conflicts.summary: Council split 6-1 on annexing and translating zoning for the 17-acre, 33-lot Phillips Valley conservation subdivision after DeDreana Freeman questioned where mass grading would occur versus preserved buffers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and Rural Residential conservation subdivision.
side_a_arguments: Majority members accepted the 33-lot conservation design preserving 50% open space and stream buffers under existing Rural Residential density without increasing zoning intensity.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose annexing and extending City utilities to the peripheral eastern subdivision.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman pressed the applicant at 01:18:33 on where mass grading versus conservation buffers would occur and cast the lone Nay vote on annexation and zoning translation.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation/UEA and zoning translation passed 6-1; all seven members then voted 7-0 for the statutory consistency statement.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat Feb 12, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Timing of Property Tax Rate Increase for the $95 Million Affordable Housing Bond (FY2022 vs. FY2023)
conflicts.summary: Council divided at the Budget Retreat over whether to start levying the affordable housing bond debt-service tax in FY2022 (1.38 cents, or $31.64/year for the average homeowner) or defer it one more year to FY2023 (1.50 cents, or $34.39/year).
conflicts.side_a_position: Initiate the 1.38-cent property tax increase in FY2022 as scheduled after the 2020 pandemic pause.
side_a_arguments: Steve Schewel (04:04:47) and Mark-Anthony Middleton (04:00:28, 04:10:57) argued voters already approved the bond knowing taxes would rise and warning that another delay erodes voter trust ahead of a possible green infrastructure bond.
Pierce Freelon (04:08:56) noted the annual household difference between 1.38 and 1.50 cents was less than $3 while funding affordable housing values.
Javiera Caballero (04:09:30, 04:17:41) warned that waiting would still force tax increases two years in a row once employee pay raises are funded in FY2022.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer the housing-bond tax increase until FY2023 (at 1.50 cents) since debt will not be issued until FY2023.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:59:18, 04:13:36) noted Finance Director David Boyd confirmed waiting changes only 0.12 cents and affects zero housing projects or Community Development schedules in FY22.
DeDreana Freeman (04:06:16) cited residents' COVID-19 financial strain and tax fears as reasons to hold off one year.
Jillian Johnson (04:02:29) initially favored deferring until FY23 to preserve taxpayer capacity for employee pay raises, before agreeing at 04:21:17 to join majority staff guidance.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; after Jillian Johnson signaled willingness to align with the majority (04:21:17), Mayor Schewel polled thumbs-up and noted a majority supported directing staff to model the 1.38-cent housing bond increase in the FY2022 draft budget.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb 1, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Voluntary Annexation and Low-Density Extension at 4316 Trenton Road Near Leigh Farm Park (Item 17)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 6-1 to annex 8.25 acres at 4316 Trenton Road for seven large single-family homes, with Charlie Reece dissenting over wetland sensitivity and encroaching on contiguous public conservation land.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation and RS-20 zoning as appropriate low-density residential development next to existing city neighborhood and protected land.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel (00:49:03) noted the proposed seven-home layout represented low-density development suitable along the wet edge of Army Corps land and adjacent to existing Trenton subdivision homes.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny annexation of the wet, trail-crossed forested parcel bordered on nearly all sides by federal Army Corps land, County land, and Leigh Farm Park.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (00:43:36) reported walking the property and argued that adding seven large expensive homes near Piedmont Wildlife Center and wet trail corridors did not justify bringing the parcel into the city.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and UEA passed 6-1 (Reece Nay); companion RS-20 zoning then passed 7-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb 1, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 2720 Fawcett Avenue Annexation: Legacy Black Community Opposition & Cheek Road Safety vs. Proffers Over By-Right Development (Item 18)
conflicts.summary: Council deliberated over whether to approve a 320-unit PDR annexation with an offsite Merrick-Moore Elementary sidewalk, $40,000 Dedicated Housing Fund proffer, and $20,550 DPS proffer, or deny it in solidarity with Merrick-Moore residents over Cheek Road safety, flooding, and historical disinvestment.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize Merrick-Moore residents' opposition, legacy Black neighborhood equity, flooding concerns, and unwalkable Cheek Road traffic safety—voting No even if by-right development proceeds.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman (03:19:20) and Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:05:47, 03:40:50) emphasized 50 years of redlining and infrastructure neglect in Merrick-Moore and insisted elected leaders heed the legacy community rather than impose unwanted density.
Pierce Freelon (03:23:45) credited community leaders like Bonita Green and noted by-right conservation rules at least preserve 50% tree canopy and reduce traffic.
Mayor Steve Schewel (03:43:20) distinguished unwalkable Cheek Road from Olive Branch Road and concluded extra traffic posed unacceptable safety risks.
conflicts.side_b_position: Note that denying rezoning cannot stop a 202-unit by-right county subdivision while forfeiting negotiated sidewalk, affordable housing, and school proffers.
side_b_arguments: Jillian Johnson (03:11:12) and Javiera Caballero warned that a by-right conservation subdivision would still add traffic without delivering the developer's proffered offsite sidewalk to Merrick-Moore Elementary or housing/DPS contributions, while housing supply remains vital to affordability.
conflicts.resolution: Despite voicing different frameworks during deliberation, all seven Council members—including Johnson and Caballero—voted Nay, defeating the annexation 0-7.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan 21, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Partial Municipal Subsidy vs. 100% Property-Owner Cost Recovery in the Infrastructure Petition Process (Item 16)
conflicts.summary: Council debated Option 1 (100% full cost recovery) versus Option 2 (partial subsidy: 100% street paving, 75% water/sewer, and $35/foot Durham Walks sidewalks) for property-owner petitions, balancing equitable city investment in unserved city neighborhoods against wealthy petitioners cutting ahead of CIP priorities.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt Option 2 partial subsidies restricted strictly to properties inside Durham city limits, alongside true full-cost accounting.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Pierce Freelon, and Charlie Reece argued eliminating subsidies altogether would hurt lower-income in-city homeowners on legacy unimproved streets or septic systems while suburban county utility extensions should bear 100% cost.
conflicts.side_b_position: Adopt Option 1 (100% full cost recovery across the board) to prevent petitioned projects from diverting scarce public CIP funds.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel argued any city subsidy lets property owners who can afford upfront assessments jump ahead of the City's equitable street-paving and utility priority lists.
conflicts.resolution: Option 2 (inside city limits) prevailed 6-1 by straw vote, and Council voted 6-0-1 (Charlie Reece abstaining) to base assessments on full construction-plus-engineering/inspection/easement costs before advancing Item 16 to the February 1 Consent Agenda.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 19, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Scale and Pacing of Bull City United (Cure Violence) Expansion: Four Tracts Immediately vs. Two Tracts First
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over whether to fund immediate expansion of Durham's Cure Violence violence-interruption program (Bull City United) across all four new census tracts (~$950,000-$1,000,000) or phase in two tracts (~$350,000) first.
conflicts.side_a_position: Fund immediate expansion across all four census tracts to meet urgent gun-violence levels citywide.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, and Charlie Reece argued surging shooting victims demand investing fully in community-based violence interruption across all four high-need tracts right away.
Javiera Caballero expressed fiscal reservations about pandemic budget constraints (01:07:23) but joined the Aye majority.
conflicts.side_b_position: Begin by funding two additional tracts (~$350,000) to verify program fidelity and preserve budget capacity amid pandemic uncertainty.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel (01:18:31) argued expanding to two tracts first (or pairing with County cost-sharing on a third) would protect multi-year budget stability and allow evaluation of Cure Violence model fidelity before scaling further.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to fund full 4-tract expansion passed 6-1 by roll call (Mayor Schewel cast the sole Nay).

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Jan 15, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Selection of City Manager Executive Search Firm and Assessment Center Methodology
conflicts.summary: Council members initially split in deliberation and an informal straw poll over whether to select Developmental Associates' assessment-center model or The Mercer Group's traditional interview-based national search approach before converging unanimously on Developmental Associates.
conflicts.side_a_position: Select Developmental Associates for its competency-based virtual assessment center, bias-mitigating rubric, diversity placement record, and fit for modern Durham.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued that assessment centers test real-world competencies beyond interviews and that Durham needed a contemporary rubric rather than repeating the 12-year-old Mercer process used to hire Tom Bonfield.

Mayor Steve Schewel cited Durham's national profile to attract candidates regardless of firm and praised Developmental Associates' record placing African-American leaders as well as Durham's Police Chief, Fire Chief, and Deputy City Manager.
conflicts.side_b_position: Initially leaned toward or felt torn about The Mercer Group due to national reach and concern that Developmental Associates' external assessors excluded internal staff and council from early screening.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero favored Mercer on national reach and expressed reticence that Developmental Associates' assessment center delegated candidate evaluation to external assessors rather than internal city staff and council.
DeDreana Freeman noted that while Developmental Associates scored higher in her initial ranking, Ellis Hankins's presentation made Mercer compelling for Durham's needs, leaving her torn.
conflicts.resolution: After Jim O'Donnell clarified at 02:11:27 that internal interview panels (including Tom Bonfield and deputy city managers) had participated in prior Developmental Associates assessment centers, and an initial 5-0-2 straw poll at 02:12:40, both Caballero and Freeman agreed to move forward with Developmental Associates for a 7-0 unanimous informal recommendation (formal contract placed on the January 21 work session agenda).

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: State-Required Local Incentives for Large Corporations Under JDIG (Items 25 and 26)
conflicts.summary: During public hearings on incentives for The Clorox Company ($75,000) and Nuvotronics, Inc. ($150,000), Council Member Charlie Reece challenged the premise of awarding public subsidies to multi-billion-dollar corporations while staff and the Mayor noted state law mandated local matching funds.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $75,000 Clorox and $150,000 Nuvotronics incentives because state JDIG rules require local participation and the projects yield strong ROI, workforce partnerships, and diversity commitments.
side_a_arguments: OEWD Director Andre Pettigrew, Adria Graham Scott, and Durham County's Andrew Miracle confirmed Tier 3 counties like Durham must contribute qualifying local matches for JDIG awards, with Clorox projected to return over $156,000 in city tax revenue within five years.
Staff emphasized both deals are performance-based, exceed living-wage and health-insurance standards, and include workforce pipelines with Durham Public Schools, Durham Tech, NCCU, and NCWorks.
conflicts.side_b_position: Condemn JDIG local-match mandates as a corporate 'race to the bottom' that forces cities to subsidize multi-billion-dollar firms that do not financially need local funds, while reluctantly voting Aye so projects do not leave Durham.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece cited Clorox's $25.27 billion market capitalization and Cubic Corporation's ~$2 billion market cap (Nuvotronics' parent), arguing neither company needs $75,000 or $150,000 from Durham taxpayers.
Reece called on state or federal action to end inter-state corporate incentive competition while voting Aye solely because state law conditioned the JDIG deals on Durham's match.
conflicts.resolution: Both incentives passed 7-0 on roll call (Item 25 at 02:42:49; Item 26 at 02:53:07), with Mayor Schewel also advising staff to include full wage and benefit verification publicly in future packets rather than only in closed session.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Sept 21, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Guardrails, Scope, and Community Access in UDO Text Amendment TC2000003 (Development Agreements)
conflicts.summary: While Council adopted TC2000003 unanimously 7-0, members and public speakers clashed over whether statutory development agreements lacked sufficient public-access guardrails or represented an essential local tool for affordable housing.
conflicts.side_a_position: The draft text amendment risks creating a separate, developer-favored process where complex 40-page contracts are negotiated before public notice and not limited solely to affordable housing.
side_a_arguments: The Planning Commission recommended denial 4-10, warning of expedited hearing risks, insufficient early neighborhood engagement, and unrestricted non-housing uses.
Residents in rapidly gentrifying neighborhoods like Walltown and Braggtown face barriers reviewing 40-page legal contracts late in the process.
conflicts.side_b_position: Development agreements already exist under state law, and TC2000003 adds stronger local guardrails while unlocking affordable housing tools unavailable through standard zoning.
side_b_arguments: Durham's affordable housing density bonus has gone unused, whereas development agreements enable projects like Laurel Street's Farrington Road mixed-income development.
TC2000003 exceeds state law by requiring neighborhood meetings, Planning Commission review with three-cycle continuances, and zero weakening of environmental protections.
conflicts.resolution: Following the inclusion of Planning Commission continuance protections in revised Attachment C, Council voted 7-0 to adopt both the consistency statement and ordinance at 04:41:00.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 18, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Item 26 Amendment: Expand Longtime Homeowner Grant Program to Include Braggtown and Merrick-Moore Neighborhoods
conflicts.summary: DeDreana Freeman moved at 01:32:31 to revise Longtime Homeowner Grant criteria to add Braggtown and Merrick-Moore alongside Walltown; Mayor Schewel recognized a second from an unnamed member at 01:32:48. After City Attorney Rehberg cautioned against state constitutional emoluments risks without prior city housing investments in those neighborhoods, the amendment failed 2-5.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-5)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-5)

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 9, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: City Funding of Weekly COVID-19 Testing (Item 25 CVS Health Contract) vs. Vaccine Mandate or Employee-Paid Testing
conflicts.summary: Council divided sharply over City Manager Wanda Page's proposed $69,700/week CVS Health contract to fund weekly testing for unvaccinated employees out of the self-insured Health Insurance Fund, ultimately pulling the item before a formal vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Do not spend taxpayer or shared employee Health Insurance Fund dollars to subsidize ongoing weekly testing for unvaccinated staff; move toward a vaccine mandate or higher health premiums/employee-paid testing.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel (01:14:19, 02:02:35) argued that paying nearly $70,000/week unfairly shifts costs onto taxpayers and vaccinated employees, urging either a vaccine mandate or requiring unvaccinated workers to pay for testing or higher premiums.
Charlie Reece (via email read at 02:08:53) opposed subsidizing weekly testing and favored a vaccine mandate with medical/religious exemptions and higher premiums for unvaccinated staff.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain a measured transition toward vaccination while addressing UE150 labor concerns, work-hours testing access, attrition risks, and EBO/diversity standards before imposing punitive penalties or mandates.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (01:19:41, 02:10:48), Jillian Johnson (01:47:01, 02:05:02), Javiera Caballero (01:28:16, 02:05:48), and Pierce Freelon (01:34:38, 02:06:55) questioned attrition impacts (with HR staff Anna Davis citing 3% at Houston Methodist and 2% at UVA), testing on work hours, UE150 union proposals, and delay options to examine premium recoupment or vaccine mandates.
Donald Hughes (01:43:41) urged Council not to waive Equal Business Opportunity diversity goals on the testing contract.
conflicts.resolution: By consensus (02:14:26-02:19:43), Item 25 was held off the regular meeting agenda, and City Manager Wanda Page agreed to cancel the October 18 testing start and return with data and revised options for a vaccine mandate or premium adjustments.

conflicts.meeting_title: Regular Durham City Council Meeting Aug 16, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Junction & Ferrell Road 222-Acre Industrial Annexation Timing and Neighborhood Impacts (Item 19)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-1 on annexing 222 acres for speculative light-industrial warehousing along Junction and Ferrell Roads, balancing urgent industrial land supply against premature infrastructure and community-equity concerns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve annexation to unlock a premier industrial site ranked 14/14 in Durham's Industrial Land Study and generate tax base and industrial jobs.
side_a_arguments: Majority members noted the scarcity of ready industrial land in Durham and highlighted regional economic-development support from NCRR and the Durham Chamber of Commerce.
County Industrial Light zoning already existed by right, so city annexation ensured municipal utility service, tax revenue, and direct zoning translation.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose premature 222-acre annexation without an identified end-user, committed infrastructure readiness, or protection for long-time nearby homeowners facing tax pressure.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman (03:06:23) opposed annexing 222 acres without confirmed tenants or full infrastructure and argued that industrial growth without parallel tax-relief tools burdens longtime neighboring residents.
Neighbors Bonita Green and Jason Bazdula raised local traffic, quality-of-life, and impact concerns.
conflicts.resolution: Annexation and UEA passed 5-1 with DeDreana Freeman dissenting (Charlie Reece absent), followed by approval of direct translational zoning.

conflicts.meeting_title: Regular Durham City Council Work Session July 22, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Demographic Accountability and Immediate Approval of the $100,000 Made in Durham Contract (Item 22)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-1 to approve the $100,000 Made in Durham contract under suspended rules, with DeDreana Freeman dissenting over missing participant demographic reporting.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the budgeted $100,000 Made in Durham contract immediately to meet the fiscal-year funding deadline while requesting follow-up information on private funders and program history.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton, Pierce Freelon, and Mayor Steve Schewel praised Made in Durham's youth workforce mission as an upstream public-safety and economic investment already budgeted by Council.
Administration noted suspending the rules was necessary because the funds came from the closing fiscal year.
conflicts.side_b_position: Withhold approval until the contract explicitly includes reporting on who is served by Made in Durham.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman reiterated prior concerns over who Made in Durham serves and stated she could not support the contract without seeing language requiring that data to come back to Council.
conflicts.resolution: Contract passed 5-1; City Manager Wanda Page committed to providing written historical and funding background on Made in Durham.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Longtime Homeowner Grant Program Expansion: Citywide vs. Targeted Equity and Staff Capacity
conflicts.summary: Following Charlie Reece's proposal to hold applications open and rapidly craft a temporary citywide homeowner tax-relief program ahead of the joint City-County program, Council debated equity targeting, included neighborhoods (Braggtown, Merrick-Moore, Walltown), and Community Development staffing capacity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Create a temporary citywide property-tax relief program for the 2020-21 gap year to ensure all burdened longtime low-income homeowners qualify legally and equitably until the joint County program improves.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (04:11:36, 04:18:09, 04:32:16) argued citywide investments city-wide justify legal defensibility whereas ad-hoc neighborhood additions face legal hurdles cited by Assistant City Attorney Krista Kucera, offering to sunset the city program once the County raises AMI limits and benefit caps.
DeDreana Freeman (04:16:52, 04:27:11, 04:50:24) prioritized immediate gap-year relief so Braggtown, Merrick-Moore, and Walltown residents are not left out of 2019-2020 tax cycles.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the 2019 cycle under current parameters through August 31 and avoid a rushed citywide expansion without staff capacity, cost modeling, and equity targeting.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (04:23:20, 04:41:41, 04:51:47) argued against blanket 'equality' floodgates in affluent areas in favor of targeted 'equity' investments (sidewalks, safety, targeted relief) in historically disinvested neighborhoods, citing Reginald Johnson's staffing constraints.

Jillian Johnson (04:28:51, 04:35:56), Pierce Freelon (04:45:52), and Steve Schewel (04:37:30, 04:48:50) respected staff capacity warnings (vacancies from retirement and medical leave) and supported letting the current program finish through Aug. 31 while directing staff to return in early August with a scoping and resource plan-to-make-a-plan.
conflicts.resolution: Council reached consensus thumbs-up (04:53:00-04:53:17) allowing staff to extend current applications administratively to August 31 and bring an assessment/scoping timeline for gap-year options to the first August work session.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 7, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Rollingdale II Townhome Rezoning (25 to 33 Units) Near Jordan Lake Watershed (Item 41)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-1 to override the Planning Commission's 8-4 denial recommendation and approve eight additional townhomes (33 total) at 602–606 W. NC-54 Hwy, with DeDreana Freeman dissenting over watershed, stormwater, and affordability concerns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the 33-unit townhome rezoning with enhanced proffers (45-ft height cap, 100-year stormwater detention, and $33,000 affordable housing contribution) to add badly needed housing supply and keep units in the low-$300,000 range.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Mayor Steve Schewel argued Durham faces an acute housing shortage (more realtors than homes for sale) and adding eight units while preserving more open space and buffers benefits the city.

Pierce Freelon noted infrastructure costs spread over 33 units keep prices around $315k–$350k rather than over $400k, and Mark-Anthony Middleton welcomed the amended $33,000 affordable housing and height proffers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning request in alignment with the Planning Commission's 8-4 vote and neighboring residents' watershed and compatibility objections.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman cited the site's proximity to the Jordan Lake watershed, prior clear-cutting/mass-grading, stormwater and flooding concerns raised by residents, and the fact that $320k–$340k townhomes are not affordable for marginalized residents, noting she was honoring Tom Miller's Planning Commission advice.
conflicts.resolution: Both the rezoning/FLUM ordinance and the consistency statement passed 5-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting Nay.

conflicts.meeting_title: Day Three - City Council Budget Retreat Feb 25, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Green and Equitable Infrastructure Financing Mechanism and 2021 vs. 2022 Bond Timing
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed over whether to pursue an aggressive near-term bond/funding push in 2021 for green and equitable infrastructure or pause to complete deeper racial equity vetting and public engagement toward a 2022 bond or incremental CIP.
conflicts.side_a_position: Urge immediate momentum on bond or capital action in 2021 rather than delaying badly needed equitable sidewalk, transit, and climate investments.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman and Jillian Johnson pressed for timely action on infrastructure backlog and equitable neighborhood investments rather than deferring momentum.
conflicts.side_b_position: Caution that a November 2021 bond timeline lacks sufficient racial equity evaluation and community runway, favoring a 2022 bond, incremental CIP capacity, or narrowing priorities first.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece, and Steve Schewel warned that pandemic pressures, tax-rate capacity, and the May statutory bond deadline left too little time for rigorous racial equity analysis and authentic public co-design before November 2021.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved by thumbs-up consensus to have Council members first complete a category weighting and prioritization exercise so staff could return a refined $50M scenario at the April work session.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Scale of Bull City United Expansion (2 Census Tracts vs. 4 Census Tracts)
conflicts.summary: Council divided over whether to adopt the City Manager's recommendation to expand Bull City United to two additional census tracts (7 FTEs) now and reassess during budget season, or commit immediately to all four high-shooting census tracts (18 FTEs, under $1 million).
conflicts.side_a_position: Expand Bull City United immediately to all four additional census tracts (18 FTEs) as an urgent investment to curb record gun violence.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece, and DeDreana Freeman argued that under $1 million is modest relative to a ~$70 million police budget and essential to save lives across all four impacted communities.

Middleton and Interim City Manager Wanda Page noted that under the county interlocal agreement, actual costs would phase in gradually as Durham County hires and onboards staff rather than requiring an immediate lump-sum payout.
conflicts.side_b_position: Fund the staff-recommended two-tract expansion now and evaluate the remaining two tracts (~$600,000 extra) during the FY 2021–22 budget cycle.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel warned of a severe projected recurring budget shortfall and argued council should preserve room in the regular budget cycle to fund employee raises and avoid layoffs.
Javiera Caballero voiced deep anxiety over the upcoming budget deficit while indicating she would support either two or four tracts and defer to the council majority.
conflicts.resolution: Item 6 was placed on the January 19, 2021 General Business Agenda so a council majority could move for the four-tract expansion.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Nov 16, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Doc Nichols Road Townhome Annexation: Montague Street Stub Traffic vs. Housing Supply and Predictable Rules
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-2 over whether to approve a townhome annexation and rezoning connecting to Montague Street in Fennel Farms or reject it to compel the developer to fund off-site NCDOT/traffic mitigations.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Doc Nichols Road townhome annexation and rezoning because street stubs are intended to connect, the project supplies relatively attainable townhomes, and by-right development would lack proffers.
side_a_arguments: Existing street stubs in newly built subdivisions like Fennel Farms are explicitly designed to be extended into adjacent developments.
The townhomes offer more attainable pricing than surrounding single-family homes and generate modest additional trips compared to by-right development.
Refusing projects under existing rules risks capricious decision-making driven by neighborhood opposition while traffic calming can still be explored.
conflicts.side_b_position: Vote no to send the developer back to the drawing board to finance an alternative NCDOT connection or pursue a one-way traffic hardship solution for Montague Street.
side_b_arguments: Neighbors on Montague Street raised serious pedestrian and senior safety concerns from cut-through traffic.
The developer had not priced or engineered an alternative NCDOT road connection or one-way street arrangement, which only a no vote would force them to pursue.
conflicts.resolution: All three motions (annexation and utility extension, consistency statement, and UDO amendment) passed 4-2, with DeDreana Freeman excused absent.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 10, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Proposed Six-Month Free Pilot of ShotSpotter Acoustic Gunshot Detection System
conflicts.summary: Council split sharply over whether to accept a no-cost six-month ShotSpotter pilot in three square miles of Durham, pitting members advocating immediate data and deterrence against daily neighborhood gunfire against members opposing increased armed police deployments and acoustic surveillance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Test ShotSpotter for six months at zero financial obligation to collect local data and address unreported gunfire traumatizing Black and Brown children.
side_a_arguments: Over 80% of gunfire goes unreported to 911 because residents feel resigned or fear retaliation, leaving children hiding in bathtubs and families traumatized.
A free, no-obligation six-month experiment lets Durham test accuracy and efficacy locally without committing funds, and root-cause alternatives have not yet received major budget funding.
conflicts.side_b_position: Decline ShotSpotter because independent evidence shows high false-positive rates and the system funnels more armed police officers and surveillance into communities of color rather than advancing non-police safety solutions.
side_b_arguments: Charlotte police officers reported confirming gunfire on only 1 in 41 ShotSpotter alerts, creating false-positive responses that strain police resources and heighten community tension.
Technology tied to cameras or drones expands surveillance and undermines Durham's shift toward unarmed crisis response, violence interrupters, and the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force.
conflicts.resolution: No council member offered a motion to proceed; Mayor Schewel closed the discussion at 03:58:43 and clarified at 05:16:37 that any future action would only occur if City Administration formally brought forward a recommendation.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council Aug 31, 2020 (with captions)
conflicts.issue: Ward 3 City Council Vacancy Selection (Pierce Freelon vs. Anita Daniels Keith)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-2 in selecting Vernetta Alston's successor for Ward 3, with four members backing Pierce Freelon's vision and advocacy and two supporting Anita Daniels Keith amid concerns about process transparency and perceived predetermination.
conflicts.side_a_position: Appoint Pierce Freelon to fill the Ward 3 vacancy.
side_a_arguments: Freelon brings deep Ward 3 roots, youth mentorship, arts leadership, and clear alignment on racial equity, police reform, and housing justice.
His hopeful, unapologetic advocacy and past citywide campaign experience equip him to serve effectively until voters decide in the next election.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support Anita Daniels Keith as a custodial steward of the seat and raise concern that the outcome felt predetermined.
side_b_arguments: Daniels Keith's temperament, mental health/social service leadership, and community rootedness best represent a custodial stewardship role until voters weigh in.
Community correspondence (including from the Durham Committee) raised concerns that the appointment felt predetermined toward Freelon despite strong alternative finalists.
conflicts.resolution: Pierce Freelon was elected 4-2 on the first ballot at 00:27:54; Council declined to make the vote unanimous, though Javiera Caballero urged all members to welcome and support Freelon as a colleague.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 21, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Preserving Wheels Fun Park Roller Skating Rink vs. Full Aquatics Site Redevelopment (Item 18)
conflicts.summary: Council members split over how the Ratio States NC aquatics study at Wheels Fun Park should treat the existing indoor roller skating rink, with three members drawing a hard red line to preserve the rink while two others urged waiting for broad community survey input.
conflicts.side_a_position: Explicitly rule out demolishing the roller skating rink and prioritize preserving an affordable Black and community skating institution alongside aquatics improvements.
side_a_arguments: Wheels' roller skating rink is a uniquely important, beloved recreation institution for Durham families and youth of color that should not be put on the chopping block.
Community advocates, including speaker Ideal Ortiz, warned against sacrificing the only local indoor roller rink without clear guarantees.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid prejudging design scenarios before conducting an open community survey on both public aquatics needs and the rink.
side_b_arguments: Durham faces a severe shortage of public swimming pool capacity, and early engineering/community feedback should evaluate all site configurations openly.
Restricting consultant study options prematurely could limit viable ways to meet citywide aquatics equity goals.
conflicts.resolution: Informational / Placed on Consent Agenda (staff instructed to convey Council's feedback on preserving skating alongside robust public engagement)

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Durham County Transit Plan Priorities: Bus Service Equity, Commuter Rail Costs, and City Governance Seat (Item 23)
conflicts.summary: Council and transit staff examined diverging priorities between overall survey respondents favoring commuter rail and POC/daily riders prioritizing late-night/Sunday bus service, alongside City governance representation and light-rail accountability.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize immediate frequency, late-night/weekend reliability, and a full City voting seat on the Staff Working Group alongside pursuing regional rail without over-promising.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson emphasized that transit-dependent riders and POC respondents ranked evening/Sunday bus improvements far higher than commuter rail.

Steve Schewel argued Durham owns the GoDurham bus system and contributes substantial property taxes, making a voting City seat on the Staff Working Group essential, while Mark-Anthony Middleton called for transparent accounting of past light-rail expenditures.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain focus on dual local-and-regional investments including Option C (commuter rail) connectivity, especially near permanently subsidized downtown affordable housing.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero argued Durham will fail unless it delivers both better local bus service and a regional transit system (Options A and C combined).

Schewel also noted Option C nearly doubles 45-minute job accessibility from subsidized downtown housing at 519 E. Main St., Willard St., and DHA sites, whereas Oxford Manor remains an accessibility outlier under all plans.
conflicts.resolution: Informational / Staff directed to bring recommended final transit plan and revised interlocal governance agreement in January 2022

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 10, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Timing, Tiering, and Public Input for City Council Living-Wage Compensation Increases
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to raise Council salaries to a ~$35,000 living wage starting in 2022 or defer any raise until after public engagement and the 2021 election.
conflicts.side_a_position: Move forward promptly toward a ~$35,000 living-wage base in 2022 so working-class candidates and sitting members without independent wealth can afford to serve.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon and Javiera Caballero argued that low part-time stipends exclude lower-income residents from running or remaining on Council and urged an earlier 2022 effective date rather than waiting until 2024.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not enact unvetted mid-budget raises or tiered salaries before the municipal election; defer to public input and a post-election November vote.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece, Steve Schewel, and Mark-Anthony Middleton opposed voting themselves a mid-budget raise without prior public budget engagement, and Middleton also objected to tiered salary levels.
conflicts.resolution: By consensus (03:10:40-03:14:51), Council set aside roughly $80,000 in 'appropriations not authorized' in the FY22 budget to preserve funding capacity for a November 2021 vote after public engagement.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session April 8, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Green and Equitable Infrastructure Funding Mechanism and Bond Timing
conflicts.summary: Council members split over whether to move forward immediately with a $50 million GO bond or 1-cent FY22 CIP tax increase, or defer a bond referendum until 2022 pending equity review, federal stimulus clarity, and full FY22 budget trade-offs.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prefer incremental pay-as-you-go CIP steps or delaying a $50 million bond referendum until 2022 to allow racial equity vetting, public engagement, and clarity on federal infrastructure legislation and FY22 tax rates.
side_a_arguments: Rushing a November 2021 bond vote before the May 3 statutory deadline leaves insufficient time for equitable community engagement and racial equity analysis.
Staff and Council do not yet know the full FY22 property tax rate impact alongside operating needs or how upcoming federal infrastructure stimulus could offset local borrowing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Favor advancing a bond or keeping near-term dedicated funding moving forward rather than stalling equitable infrastructure investments or burdening taxpayers solely through FY22 operating property taxes.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman argued against raising property taxes through immediate CIP increases during COVID-19 recovery, preferring bond financing if infrastructure spending proceeds.
Jillian Johnson favored maintaining momentum on equitable climate and sidewalk investments and keeping both a 2021 bond or dedicated CIP penny on the table.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved by consensus at 02:05:41 without a vote to carry the financing decision to the next work session ahead of the May 3 bond deadline.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council March 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Olive Branch Reserve Annexation — Southeast Durham Moratorium, Wildlife Corridor, and Grave Relocation
conflicts.summary: Council members split over Southeast Durham development pacing, whether to weigh piecemeal annexations against an unpassed moratorium, wildlife corridor impacts of a 300-foot stormwater pond, and unverified family consent to relocate six May family graves.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question piecemeal Southeast Durham annexations pending the Southeast Focus Area Plan and scrutinize auto-dependent suburban sprawl, stormwater encroachment, and unconfirmed descendant consent for grave relocation.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman urged pausing major Southeast Durham rezonings ahead of the focus area plan and protecting existing infrastructure capacity.
Charlie Reece opposed auto-dependent single-family suburban annexation patterns.

Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned the applicant's genealogist and legal framing claiming descendants supported relocating the Wylie Jackson May graves to Maplewood Cemetery without direct documentation.
conflicts.side_b_position: Caution against ad hoc denials equivalent to an un-enacted moratorium while exploring whether wildlife corridor, infrastructure, and descendant-consultation conditions can be resolved.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton also warned against treating individual cases as a de facto moratorium without formal policy adoption.
Steve Schewel and Jillian Johnson weighed regional housing supply needs alongside demands for stronger wildlife corridor protection and direct descendant outreach.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved by consensus at 03:02:20 to continue the public hearing to May 3, 2021 so applicants and staff could verify descendant wishes and address wildlife corridor/infrastructure questions.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session, February 18, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: County DSS vs. Nonprofit Administration of the $8 Million Federal Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP)
conflicts.summary: Council members challenged Durham County DSS's proposed role as sole administrator of roughly $8 million in joint ERAP funds, pointing to prior bottlenecks under CDBG-CV and NC HOPE and debating whether the City should split funds or contract directly with Legal Aid and community nonprofits.
conflicts.side_a_position: Administer the joint City-County ERAP pool through a single Durham County DSS portal to consolidate intake, federal reporting, and compliance.
side_a_arguments: County DSS Director Ben Rose and Janine Gordon argued that combining funds under one portal avoids duplicating application reviews and noted DSS had already issued ~$3 million locally through HOPE and cleared earlier backlogs.
Community Development Director Reginald Johnson noted the City lacked standalone rental-assistance software and staffing capacity to launch a separate parallel program quickly.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reform intake immediately or carve out/contract ERAP outreach, navigation, and distribution through Legal Aid and trusted nonprofits to address DSS distrust and delays.
side_b_arguments: Jillian Johnson (01:12:41) warned that the proposed April ILA lacked concrete processing metrics, software commitments, and guaranteed funding for nonprofit outreach partners.
Javiera Caballero raised fears that undocumented and immigrant residents distrust government DSS portals and face documentation barriers without formal leases or pay stubs.
DeDreana Freeman, Charlie Reece, and Steve Schewel questioned why CDBG-CV funds stalled for months and pressed staff on direct Legal Aid or multi-agency subcontracts before Monday's meeting.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Item 22 was placed on the March 1 General Business Agenda so County and City staff could answer questions about intake software, documentation flexibility, and nonprofit navigation contracts.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Rosewalk II Traffic & Intersection Safety vs. Central Infill Multifamily Housing
conflicts.summary: Neighbors of Trinity Park and Northgate Park argued that Rosewalk II's 310 apartments would exacerbate crashes at N. Duke St and W. Club Blvd and cut-through speeding while sidestepping a Traffic Impact Analysis under the 149-trip cap, whereas council members prioritized centrally located rental supply once additional proffers were added.
conflicts.side_a_position: Delay or require signal/geometric fixes and fuller neighborhood traffic mitigation before approving 310 apartments.
side_a_arguments: Residents reported repeated severe collisions and bus-passenger hazards at W. Club Blvd and N. Duke St.
Neighbors criticized capping trips below 149 to avoid a TIA and argued the driveway should be offset from Woodland Dr.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the 310-unit RU-M(D) rezoning based on central infill location, 35% lower projected rents than downtown, and new traffic/school proffers.
side_b_arguments: Lower land cost (~80% below downtown) and surface parking allow relatively moderate rents near Duke University and I-85.
Applicant committed $30,000 toward a neighborhood traffic circle and $20,500 for DPS students.
conflicts.resolution: Following the applicant's additional traffic-circle and school proffers and transportation staff review, Council unanimously passed the rezoning 7-0 while noting ongoing coordination with NCDOT.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Racial & Economic Equity of Special Assessments for Basic Water and Road Paving on Ardmore Drive
conflicts.summary: While voting unanimously to approve residents' $1.8M self-assessed petition so Ardmore Drive families receive clean water and fire protection immediately, council members criticized a city system that forces longtime Black working-class homeowners to pay steep assessments to skip a multi-year unpaved-road queue.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the resident petition now to end well contamination while condemning special assessments for basic municipal infrastructure.
side_a_arguments: Forcing residents annexed decades ago with bacteria-contaminated wells and no hydrants to pay ~$1.8M across 13-14 properties to jump ahead 4-5 years reflects systemic inequity.
Council urged reforming how Durham funds unpaved roads and water extensions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Note the statutory structure under which petitioned 100%-assessed improvements accelerate capital queue priority under existing policy.
side_b_arguments: Staff and Mayor Schewel noted the $1.8M estimate (~$1.2M paving, ~$600k water lines/laterals) relies on petitioner signatures to advance 4-5 years ahead of standard city-funded scheduling.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 7-0 on all three Ardmore Drive assessment motions so residents could receive water, fire service, and paving, while calling for future funding reforms.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Scope of Tenants' Bill of Rights Under State Preemption vs. Municipal Enforcement Resources
conflicts.summary: During the Item 9 Tenants' Bill of Rights discussion, Bull City Tenants United organizers and some council members pushed to adopt strong local anti-rent-collection and inspection ordinances modeled on Charlotte's code, while the City Attorney warned of NC state statutory preemption and council members debated how far Durham could push legal boundaries without risking invalidation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Push legal boundaries—mirroring Charlotte's minimum-housing rent prohibition and expanding after-hours inspections, translation, Ban-the-Box, and enforcement funding.
side_a_arguments: Tenants live in dangerous slum conditions and face landlords who ignore repairs or send maintenance staff as biased interpreters.
