Charlotte's provision provides practical leverage for tenants seeking treble damages or warranty-of-habitability relief even without direct city prosecution.
conflicts.side_b_position: Focus on legally defensible city investments—free inspection access, language translation, eviction legal aid, and non-discrimination ordinances—while respecting NC statutory preemption.
side_b_arguments: North Carolina preemption and NCGS 42-44 prohibit cities from authorizing unilateral tenant rent withholding or escrow outside court orders, and Charlotte does not enforce its clause.
Municipal funding for legal defense and expanded code enforcement delivers immediate tangible tenant relief.
conflicts.resolution: Council directed the City Manager to assess staffing/funding for inspection access, interpretation, and landlord registration (items 1, 2, 4, 13), directed the City Attorney to review non-discrimination/Ban-the-Box/SOI options (items 3, 6, 11), and tasked DeDreana Freeman with drafting a symbolic resolution (item 8) for January 2022.

conflicts.meeting_title: FY22 Budget Council Follow-Up Meeting June 10, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Proposal to Increase City Council Member Salaries to Full-Time Pay
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed over the urgency, timing, and optics of raising City Council compensation to full-time levels ahead of the FY22 budget adoption.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance a full-time Council salary structure—potentially phased in across staggered 2023/2025 election cycles—so lower-income and working-class residents are not priced out of serving.
side_a_arguments: Pierce Freelon argued Council pay is an equity barrier preventing eligible working residents from running and wanted to set the wheels in motion sooner rather than waiting until 2027.
Javiera Caballero proposed a staggered approach (2023 for at-large seats, 2025/2027) and noted comparable cities like Wilmington/New Hanover and Charlotte pay significantly more.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer or oppose immediate Council raises, prioritizing city staff base pay and ensuring any Council raise only takes effect after all sitting members face voters.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman stated she would much rather direct scarce recurring dollars to city staff base pay than to Council salaries.

Mark-Anthony Middleton cited incumbency advantage and preferred any raise take effect no earlier than 2023 after a full election cycle; Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and staff noted legal uncertainty over staggered pay and that two members had stepped away during the vote readiness check.
conflicts.resolution: No vote was taken; the proposal was referred to a future work session pending legal guidance from the City Attorney's Office.

conflicts.meeting_title: FY22 Budget Council Follow-Up Meeting June 10, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Citywide Expansion vs. County-Led Implementation of Longtime Homeowner Tax Relief
conflicts.summary: While all members wanted stronger property tax relief for longtime low-income homeowners, Council weighed whether to keep running a separate citywide program immediately or rely on the County's $1.25M DSS-administered grant while pressing BOCC to raise the 30% AMI ceiling.
conflicts.side_a_position: Partner through the County's DSS-administered tax grant program (sending a formal resolution urging BOCC to raise eligibility to 60% AMI) rather than rushing an unvetted standalone citywide expansion.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel and Charlie Reece noted state constitutional limits require a clear public-purpose legal nexus (making DSS welfare administration safer than direct city checks) and urged focusing immediate advocacy on raising the County pilot from 30% to 60% AMI.
Jillian Johnson suggested reviewing the current city pilot's results after summer break while keeping pressure on the County to scale up.
conflicts.side_b_position: Move proactively on citywide or neighborhood-expanded tax relief and ensure residents experiencing hardship have immediate local access without restrictive caps.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman argued gentrification affects residents across Durham and expressed concern about delaying relief or limiting caps below $1,000–$1,400.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Mayor Pro Tem Johnson agreed to coordinate with Mayor Schewel on transmitting a resolution to BOCC urging a 60% AMI threshold ahead of the County's June 14 budget vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Day Four- City Council Budget Retreat Feb 26, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 911 Alternative Response Architecture — Independent Unarmed Response vs. Police Co-Responder Menu
conflicts.summary: Council members diverged over whether Durham's 911 alternative response pilot should prioritize non-police independent community health responders or retain police/CIT co-response within a broader triage menu.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize piloting unarmed, independent clinician and community health response without armed police accompaniment unless requested as backup, alongside traffic and alarm-call civilianization.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, and Charlie Reece pushed to design a non-police crisis response track—exploring partnerships with Lincoln Community Health Center—so armed officers do not automatically accompany behavioral health clinicians.
Members also urged removing routine traffic enforcement and false burglar alarm calls from armed DPD first response.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support 911 dispatch diversion while preserving a multi-tiered toolkit including CIT-trained officers and co-responders for unpredictable or potentially volatile scenes.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton endorsed civilian triage at the 911 call center while arguing that dynamic emergency calls require keeping CIT co-responder capability available alongside non-police pilots.
conflicts.resolution: Staff recorded all pilot parameters—testing both independent non-police and co-response pathways, NLP dispatch coding, and caller willingness surveys—for development without a formal vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Day Four- City Council Budget Retreat Feb 26, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: FY22 Property Tax Rate Ceiling, Low-Income Homeowner Relief, and Council Request Funding Parity
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to signal an informal two-cent property tax increase limit in the FY22 Budget Guidelines and questioned unequal recurring versus one-time treatment of community partnership requests.
conflicts.side_a_position: Aim to constrain any total FY22 property tax increase below two cents while retaining formal guideline flexibility.
side_a_arguments: Steve Schewel and Charlie Reece advocated keeping the combined property tax impact below two cents during pandemic economic recovery.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid premature two-cent ceilings if higher investments fund low-income homeowner relief and ensure equitable recurring funding across Black and Latino community initiatives.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman stated she would support up to a five-cent tax rate increase if paired with dedicated low-income homeowner tax relief, and objected to placing El Centro Hispano in recurring baseline funding while treating We Are The Ones ambassadors as temporary one-time funds.
conflicts.resolution: Council gave informal thumbs-up consensus to keep general fund and debt service tax guidelines open while aiming under two cents for formal guidelines review on March 18 and April 5.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Dec 7, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Including Local Charter Amendments in the 2021 Long Session Legislative Agenda
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to formally include two proposed local charter amendments—council vacancy filling flexibility and Raleigh-style grant-making flexibility—in the 2021 Legislative Agenda presented to the General Assembly.
conflicts.side_a_position: Questioned taking charter amendments to the current state legislature due to risk of inviting General Assembly interference with Durham's charter and doubts over whether the grant amendment overcomes constitutional hurdles.
side_a_arguments: Opening Durham's charter before the current composition of the North Carolina General Assembly could invite unwanted modifications.
The grant charter language may still be constrained by the state constitution's exclusive emoluments and public-purpose clauses.
conflicts.side_b_position: Include both charter amendments in the agenda so the Durham delegation can vet their viability during the December 9 consultation.
side_b_arguments: Constituents and civic groups asked for expanded democratic options on council vacancies and municipal agility to distribute COVID-style relief grants.
Durham's charter is already a creature of the state and the city routinely takes principled positions without self-censoring.
Placing the items on the agenda allows candid feedback from the Durham delegation before any bill is filed.
conflicts.resolution: Accepting that the December 9 delegation meeting would vet what was legislatively movable, Charlie Reece joined Mark-Anthony Middleton in moving/seconding the full agenda, which passed unanimously 7-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 19, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Item 20 — Accept Certificate of Sufficiency for Petitioned Curb, Gutter, Paving, Water, and Sewer Improvements
conflicts.summary: After Robert Joiner confirmed accepting the certificate of sufficiency obligates the city to complete improvements at future cost, Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded acceptance. The motion failed 3-4, halting subsequent preliminary and final improvement resolutions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-4)

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Oct 19, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Item 21 — Accept Certificate of Sufficiency for Curb, Gutter, Paving, Water and Sewer Laterals on Linden Terrace
conflicts.summary: With no public speakers at the hearing, DeDreana Freeman moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded accepting the certificate of sufficiency for Linden Terrace. conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-4)

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 24, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Evaluating Pending Southeastern Durham Annexations Amid Infrastructure Deficits
conflicts.summary: Following the SEARLS/Searles Basin briefing showing 3,700+ proposed residential units alongside strained two-lane state roads and limited transit, Council members diverged on whether to hold back pending suburban annexations or avoid changing expectations mid-review.
conflicts.side_a_position: Scrutinize or pause approvals of dense car-dependent developments in southeastern Durham until transit, road, and small-area planning gaps are addressed.
side_a_arguments: Approving thousands more residential units along unmodernized two-lane roads without transit locks in unsustainable growth before comprehensive planning catches up.
Council must avoid repeatedly approving incremental developments that strain infrastructure and fail to match urban infill priorities.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not impose an uncodified de facto moratorium on compliant projects; instead codify any policy shifts in the UDO or Comprehensive Plan.
side_b_arguments: Changing rules mid-game after developers pay fees and follow existing plans risks appearing capricious and harms city credibility.
Adjoining Wake County growth shows that rejecting city-utility projects can push development onto large-lot septic systems in clay soils, worsening environmental risk.
conflicts.resolution: Informational work-session discussion; staff was asked to brief absent members Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman ahead of the October 5 public hearings on continued cases.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual City Council Meeting Sept 8, 2020 (with captions)
conflicts.issue: Politicizing Pro Forma Conduit Bond Approvals vs. Consistent Racial Equity Standards in City Contracting (Trinity School TEFRA Bond)
conflicts.summary: Council debated consistency between denying Excelsior Classical Academy's charter bond and approving Trinity School's TEFRA conduit bond, as well as whether Council can reject city contracts based on vendor workforce demographics.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve Trinity School as a pro forma vote, while calling out inconsistency with the Excelsior denial and challenging Council to deny contracts to vendors lacking Black or Latino employees.
side_a_arguments: Neither bond created city financial exposure, yet Excelsior served low-income Black students with transportation, free lunch, and EC services while Trinity is a wealthy private school without them.
If equity standards are applied to pro forma votes, Council must apply them to companies seeking millions in city contracts.
conflicts.side_b_position: Charter schools now have a separate state DPI borrowing mechanism unlike private schools, and NC procurement law limits Council from rejecting goods/construction bids based on workforce data.
side_b_arguments: State law allows discretion on service contracts but restricts rejecting low-bid goods or building contracts over workforce statistics.
The City Attorney should provide a written legal memo clarifying Council's statutory limits.
conflicts.resolution: Council passed the Trinity School TEFRA resolution 6-1 (Javiera Caballero Nay) at 00:34:35, with staff and the City Attorney expected to report back on contracting discretion.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual City Council Meeting Sept 8, 2020 (with captions)
conflicts.issue: Police Department Taser Replacement Program vs. Work Session Review of Eliminating Tasers
conflicts.summary: Council split over whether to replace 212 inoperable police Tasers immediately or delay the contract for a work-session policy debate on removing Tasers from DPD's toolkit.
conflicts.side_a_position: Delay the purchase for a work session reviewing the Durham Beyond Policing memo and whether officers should carry Tasers.
side_a_arguments: Independent studies cited by Durham Beyond Policing argue Tasers fail to reduce overall use of force or improve safety.
Approving a five-year, 250-unit Taser contract requires deliberating whether that spending aligns with Council's public safety priorities.
conflicts.side_b_position: While Tasers remain authorized equipment, officers must not be left with 212 broken devices, and delayed policy objections should be clearly specified for staff research.
side_b_arguments: Officers deployed Tasers only 10 times in 2019 and rely on working less-lethal options in the field.
Council members requesting further research should send clear written questions to the City Manager and copy all colleagues.
conflicts.resolution: Mayor Schewel officially referred Item 8 back to administration at 02:21:19 without a vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Regular Durham City Council Work Session Aug. 19, 2021
conflicts.issue: Scope and Timing of Expanding the City's Longtime Homeowner Grant Program
conflicts.summary: During Item 7, Council members diverged in emphasis over whether staff had been directed to produce a citywide rollout plan or merely options, and how to balance immediate neighborhood expansion against lobbying Durham County to expand the joint 30% AMI grant.
conflicts.side_a_position: Clarify that Council asked for framework options rather than a finalized citywide mandate, and prioritize pressing Durham County to expand the joint City-County grant from 30% to 60% AMI while targeting city-invested neighborhoods in the interim.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton noted his recollection of the prior charge was to provide options and a framework rather than a directive to implement citywide immediately.

Mayor Steve Schewel and staff highlighted that $500,000 in City funds and $750,000 in County funds were already budgeted for the joint countywide 30% AMI tax grant, making expansion to 60% AMI with the County alongside broader neighborhood targeting the highest-leverage path.
conflicts.side_b_position: Move faster to deliver city grant relief in the current year rather than waiting until FY22 or relying on the County's separate deferral/grant timelines.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman voiced concern that the current discussion meant no expanded relief would reach homeowners this year or before the 2022 fiscal year, and underscored that the County's earlier deferral program creates eventual repayment liability unlike the City's grant.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; staff continued cross-departmental work over the next three months to return with refined options alongside joint City-County program implementation.

conflicts.meeting_title: Regular Durham City Council Work Session Aug. 5, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Timing of Tenants' Bill of Rights Resolution Relative to Legal Review
conflicts.summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman sought to introduce a Tenants' Bill of Rights resolution at the next work session prior to finalizing ARPA housing priorities, while Mayor Steve Schewel and Council Member Charlie Reece pushed to wait for City Attorney vetting of local authority versus state preemption.
conflicts.side_a_position: Bring forward a general resolution supporting a Tenants' Bill of Rights within two weeks while developing enforceable local ordinances on a parallel legal track.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman argued community groups had already agreed on core guardrails and that adopting a resolution promptly would align housing priorities ahead of ARPA funding decisions without waiting on ordinance drafting.
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay the resolution until the City Attorney advises which provisions Durham can legally enforce versus which require General Assembly or federal advocacy, and weigh staff budget capacity.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel cautioned that a symbolic resolution without attorney vetting would be unclear and unproductive.

Charlie Reece noted the proposal implicated significant city staff time and budget investments not included in the newly adopted budget and required distinguishing local powers from state/federal advocacy.
conflicts.resolution: Freeman agreed to bring the Tenants' Bill of Rights item back in one month after meetings with the City Attorney's Office.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council June 21, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Premise and Efficacy of Municipal Corporate Incentives (Item 46 CARsgen Therapeutics)
conflicts.summary: While Council approved the $256,000 CARsgen Therapeutics incentive, members clashed philosophically over the 'but-for' constitutional fiction behind local corporate cash incentives versus net tax-revenue math.
conflicts.side_a_position: Vote Aye only under deep protest because municipal bidding wars force Durham into logically flawed cash giveaways to multi-billion-dollar firms.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:55:54, 04:00:19) argued a newly Hong Kong-listed company valued over $2B clearly did not need $256,000 from Durham 'but for' the grant to locate here, urging federal/state reform while voting yes to avoid losing jobs to competing states.
Jillian Johnson (03:57:50) concurred with Reece's protest.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support economic development incentives as pragmatic capital-leveraging investments yielding positive net property-tax returns and local jobs.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:58:10, 04:01:57) rejected characterizing incentives as morally questionable, noted finance projections showed tax revenues exceeding the $256,000 payout within three years, and urged coupling incentives with vocational training for Durham residents without college degrees (echoing Donald Hughes).
conflicts.resolution: Council approved the $256,000 incentive agreement.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Durham Housing Authority 24/7 Security Cameras vs. ShotSpotter Gunshot Detection Surveillance
conflicts.summary: During discussion of pulled Item 15 (ILA with DHA for security cameras and lighting funded via Participatory Budgeting), council members clashed over privacy, community consent, and hypocrisy in rejecting ShotSpotter acoustic sensors while installing always-on surveillance cameras in public housing.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approving 24/7 cameras in Black and brown public housing complexes while rejecting ShotSpotter sensors is inconsistent, and ShotSpotter merits reconsideration or a free trial.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued 24/7 cameras capture innocent daily life constantly, whereas ShotSpotter sensors stay dormant until gunfire triggers them to dispatch help to shooting locations.

Middleton contended that participatory budgeting demographics (citing 60% white voter figures) and community pleas against gun violence contradict anti-ShotSpotter surveillance critiques; DeDreana Freeman stated she was open to considering a free ShotSpotter trial.
conflicts.side_b_position: Security cameras requested by public housing residents differ fundamentally from ShotSpotter because cameras do not automatically dispatch armed police to loud noises.
side_b_arguments: Pierce Freelon reported that residents he canvassed at Oxford Manor specifically asked for working security cameras while expressing apprehension about ShotSpotter.

Freelon argued ShotSpotter automatically dispatches armed police to loud noises—citing Charlotte data where only a small fraction of alerts yielded gunfire evidence—creating distinct escalation risks compared to passive camera footage.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Item 15 remained on the January 19 consent agenda while members continued debating gun-violence technology options.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Work Session Dec 22, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Scope and Legal Caution in City Contractor Workforce Diversity Procurement Policy
conflicts.summary: During the Finance and City Attorney presentation on contractor workforce diversity, Council members diverged over whether Durham should focus on legally defensible RFP scoring questionnaires or aggressively test statutory limits across all purchase, construction, and repair contracts to advance equity and inclusion.
conflicts.side_a_position: Push beyond narrow diversity snapshots and legal risk avoidance by questioning all contractors—including construction, repair, and purchase bidders—and tying procurement to broader equity initiatives.
side_a_arguments: Focusing only on diversity rather than equity and inclusion perpetuates historical inequities in city spending.
The city should investigate hiring practices across all contract categories and push statutory authority rather than smoothing over issues to avoid lawsuits.
Workforce diversity efforts should be integrated with the Shared Economic Prosperity Plan and Built to Last rather than run on a separate finance track.
conflicts.side_b_position: Advance a legally defensible workforce diversity questionnaire usable as an RFP scoring criterion without losing sight of existing legal constraints.
side_b_arguments: Systematizing workforce diversity as an actual scoring factor in RFPs is a historic first for Durham within state legal constraints.
Progress made through the EBOP ordinance and legally defensible RFP scoring should not be lost while pursuing broader goals.
conflicts.resolution: Informational work session briefing; no formal vote was taken on the procurement policy.

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual City Council Meeting - October 1, 2020 (with captions)
conflicts.issue: Formal RFP Process vs. Expedited Search Firm Selection for City Manager Recruitment
conflicts.summary: Council members differed on whether to issue a competitive RFP to hire an executive search firm for the City Manager search given holiday delays into early 2021.
conflicts.side_a_position: Skip or shorten the RFP process to avoid delaying the search until February 2021.
side_a_arguments: Combining a formal RFP with the holiday season would push the start of the active candidate search to February 2021.
Budget and retreat timelines make starting expeditiously desirable.
conflicts.side_b_position: Conduct a full RFP process despite the extra 1–2 months to maximize search firm options.
side_b_arguments: An open RFP surfaces strong firms and ideas that strict upfront narrowing might miss, similar to the 505 West Chapel Hill Street RFP.
Strong confidence in Interim City Manager Wanda Page mitigates the risk of a 60-day schedule difference.
conflicts.resolution: At 00:30:00–00:30:33, Mayor Schewel yielded to his colleagues' arguments and agreed to move forward with an RFP while asking staff to tighten timelines where feasible.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 24, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Duke Energy Franchise Agreement Term Length (7 Years vs. 10 Years)
conflicts.summary: Council members and staff debated whether to shorten the proposed 10-year Duke Energy electric franchise term to 7 years (as recommended by the Environmental Affairs Board) to maintain flexibility amid rapid renewable energy and regulatory changes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Favor a shorter 7-year term to avoid locking the City into outdated terms as clean energy technology and state policy evolve.
side_a_arguments: Rapid technological, regulatory, and legislative shifts in electricity generation and resale make a shorter term prudent.
The Environmental Affairs Board recommended no more than 7 years to keep leverage aligned with community climate goals.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain the 10-year franchise term because right-of-way rules are standard while clean-energy goals live in the flexible MOU.
side_b_arguments: Under NC law and utilities commission jurisdiction, the franchise only governs right-of-way poles and wires, whereas the Clean Energy MOU is a living, biennial work-plan document.
Seven years versus 10 years is arbitrary without an identified missed opportunity, and 10 years is already shorter than prior 15- to 20-year franchises.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the work session; Steve Schewel indicated he preferred 7 years but could live with 10 years while directing staff to finalize EAB-suggested edits to the MOU before the October 5 vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept 10, 2020 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Local Minority-Owned Business Contracting vs. Intergovernmental Exemption in Texas A&M Transportation Institute (TTI) Transit Contract
conflicts.summary: During review of pulled Item 11 (a $100,000 intergovernmental contract with Texas A&M Transportation Institute), Council members debated whether to pause and restart procurement to include local Black- and minority-owned storytelling firms or proceed to meet urgent GoDurham transit funding deadlines.
conflicts.side_a_position: Consider restarting the procurement or splitting off the ~20% communications/storytelling scope so local minority-owned businesses can compete under an equity lens.
side_a_arguments: Intergovernmental contracts bypass Equal Business Opportunity Program compliance, and roughly $20,000 for visual storytelling could support qualified local Triangle firms.
Community advocates including the Transit Equity Campaign urged restarting the process to align with Durham's racial equity standards.
conflicts.side_b_position: Proceed with the TTI contract while adding GoDurham rider stakeholder language and TTI workforce demographics, because TTI's combined transit-data integration and communications skill set is urgently needed for County Transit Plan advocacy.
side_b_arguments: Restarting procurement or adding a subcontractor would significantly delay data needed to position GoDurham for Durham County Transit Plan funds.
Staff checked NC State and NCCU first without finding comparable transit-data integration capacity and committed to contracting with local M/WBE firms on larger upcoming transit projects.
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to revise Exhibit A to explicitly name GoDurham riders in communities of color and low-wealth neighborhoods as key stakeholders and attach TTI workforce demographic data ahead of the September 21 consent vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 23, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: GoDurham Bus Operator Assaults and Unintended Consequences of Fare-Free Transit
conflicts.summary: Following GoDurham operator testimony on assaults and gunfire threats, members and public speakers differed sharply on whether fare-free transit contributed to onboard disorder.
conflicts.side_a_position: Affirm free transit while noting that zero-fare policy increased individuals riding with nowhere to go, creating more opportunities for conflict.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson emphasized fare-free buses remain a fabulous policy choice that must continue, while noting one unintended consequence reported in driver meetings was more people hanging out on buses.
Drivers cited mask-mandate enforcement conflicts alongside loss of prior private security at Durham Station.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject linking zero-fare transit access to criminal violence or assaults against drivers.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton stressed that fare price points do not deter violence and warned against any narrative stigmatizing low-income Black and brown transit riders.
Speaker Donald Hughes called linking free bus expansion to driver assaults 'appalling' and unsupported by data.
conflicts.resolution: Informational / Staff directed to pursue bus barriers, DPD coordination, and de-escalation training

conflicts.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham Planning Commission & City Council Meeting 9/14/21 at 4 p.m. (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: Interim Legal Weight and Binding Language of Draft Southeast Focus Area Policies
conflicts.summary: Council members, Planning Commissioners, and legal/planning staff differed over how forcefully the unadopted Southeast Focus Area draft recommendations should be worded and applied to pending rezonings before formal Comprehensive Plan adoption in late 2022.
conflicts.side_a_position: Treat draft policies cautiously as non-binding advisory guidance and avoid legally unenforceable 'shall' mandates or density caps that risk court reversal.
side_a_arguments: Charlie Reece (00:27:38, 01:11:48) cautioned against promising residents binding affordability AMI limits, traffic rules, or tree-preservation mandates that North Carolina law and existing UDO/Comprehensive Plan standards cannot sustain on judicial review.

Planning Director Sara Young (00:31:28) and Deputy City Attorney Don O'Toole (01:13:45) explained that the draft recommendations are not yet adopted policy and therefore carry limited legal weight compared to adopted plans and UDO rules.
conflicts.side_b_position: Apply the draft Southeast Focus Area map and 24 policies as strong interim guidance and strengthen policy language from 'should' toward enforceable expectations.
side_b_arguments: Planning Commissioners Baker, Durkin, and Amendolia argued that advisory 'should' phrasing invites developers to ignore community feedback and urged clearer commitments around density, affordability, and tree protection.

Mayor Steve Schewel (01:17:07) stated he would not take the draft recommendations with 'a grain of salt' and would treat them as significant interim guidance reflecting extensive Planning Commission and staff work.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; staff committed to refining the 24 draft policies for future public review and Comprehensive Plan integration while legal counsel advised keeping interim project reviews grounded in adopted ordinances.

conflicts.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Sept. 9, 2021 (Live Stream)
conflicts.issue: 911 Alternate Routing Termination and Call-Center Response Adequacy
conflicts.summary: Following staff's presentation showing 28 FTE vacancies and sub-target 911 answer speeds in July 2021, council members criticized terminating Raleigh mutual-aid backup routing and questioned emergency response safety.
conflicts.side_a_position: Management decisions ending mutual-aid overflow routing to Raleigh and acute dispatcher shortages are compromising urgent resident safety and require immediate corrective remedies.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton (04:15:40, 04:28:33) criticized the ending of mutual-aid routing with Raleigh and questioned whether residents in critical danger are waiting unacceptably long.

DeDreana Freeman (04:23:09) cited a four-minute wait during a Main Street shooting call she experienced and proposed a resolution classifying 911 telecommunicators as First Responders to bolster pay and retention.
conflicts.side_b_position: Raleigh's center faced parallel staffing/routing constraints, and Durham is addressing record July call volume (27,009 calls) through active hiring classes and compensation steps.
side_b_arguments: Director Randy Beaman and Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson explained operational factors behind the mutual-aid pause, noted a hiring pipeline underway, and cautioned that August metrics would likely mirror July's backlog.
conflicts.resolution: Informational report; no formal vote was taken while staff continued recruitment and Council flagged First Responder classification for potential follow-up.

conflicts.issue: On-Street Parking Loss vs. Curbside Activation in Permanent Outdoor Seating Ordinance (Item 7)
conflicts.summary: Public comment and Council staff Q&A highlighted tension between downtown street-dining permits using metered parking spaces and off-corridor neighborhood businesses facing spill-over parking deficits.
conflicts.side_a_position: Make outdoor dining permanent citywide up to 50% of interior capacity while charging meter fees for occupied spaces and conducting curbside management review.
side_a_arguments: Outdoor dining kept locally owned downtown restaurants alive during COVID-19 and activates public streets.
Requiring restaurants to pay the meter rate avoids subsidizing parking loss, and the ordinance expands availability citywide alongside design templates.
conflicts.side_b_position: Address severe parking deficits in Central Park / Old North Durham and avoid effectively subsidizing downtown corridor businesses that convert public spaces.
side_b_arguments: Accordion Club owner Scott Ritchie testified that Geer Street businesses already suffer from overflow event parking deficits and lack sidewalks/street space to benefit equally from street-cafe permits.
Sidewalk cafes adjacent to businesses are reasonable, whereas claiming on-street parking spaces reduces affordable evening parking supply.

conflicts.side_b_position: Reallocate 60 vacant police officer positions to unarmed responders and community safety programs rather than policing or ShotSpotter.
side_b_arguments: Public hearing speakers (including organizers with Durham for All and Durham Beyond Policing) argued surveys of residents of color favored investing in non-police unarmed responders over vacant police slots.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 18, 2021 at 1 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Opening the final work session chaired by retiring Mayor Steve Schewel, council members, City Manager Wanda Page, City Attorney Kim Rehberg, and City Clerk Diana Schreiber delivered farewell tributes before Council approved six unanimous 7-0 motions. Under suspended rules requested by the administration to expedite eviction prevention, Council approved two Emergency Rental Assistance (ERA2) contracts with Legal Aid of North Carolina and Benevate Inc. (Neighborly Software), while speakers raised concerns about landlords refusing ERA funds and Zoom chat deactivation. Council also reviewed pulled items—including Durham Athletic Park's 9th amendment, the $416,350 Built2Last Innovations Lab MOU, and $4M in standby storm-debris contracts—and received the Affordable Housing Implementation Committee's inaugural 6-month report and the FY2022 Q1 Financial Report highlighting fare-free transit and parking revenue shortfalls.

agenda_items.title: Farewell Tributes to Retiring Mayor Steve Schewel and Hillside High Shout-Out
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Colleagues Charlie Reece, Jillian Johnson, Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, and Javiera Caballero—followed by City Manager Wanda Page, City Attorney Kim Rehberg, and City Clerk Diana Schreiber—paid tribute to Mayor Steve Schewel at his final work session. Middleton also recognized Hillside High School students and theater director Wendell Tabb's 'State of Urgency' production.

agenda_items.title: Priority Item Adjustments and Immediate Approval of ERA2 Rental Assistance Contracts (Legal Aid & Benevate)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page requested suspending rules for immediate action on Items 4 and 5 and noted minor updates to Items 13 and 18, which Council approved 7-0. After public comment including Jacqueline Wagstaff questioning Zoom chat removal and landlord refusals of ERA funds, Council suspended the rules and unanimously approved Item 4 (Legal Aid NC eviction defense/ERA2 grant contract) and Item 5 (Benevate/Neighborly Software ERA2 SaaS contract) 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Items: Durham Athletic Park, Built2Last Innovations Lab MOU, and FEMA Debris Contracts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Schewel and Reece discussed long-term community stewardship and turf/event options for Durham Athletic Park (Item 10) following Durham Central Park's letter. Middleton and Stella Adams questioned startup governance and funding structure on the $416,350 Built2Last Innovations Lab MOU (Item 13) with Deputy City Manager Keith Chadwell, while Johnson and Schewel examined FEMA standby thresholds and minority/women employment on DRC Emergency Services ($3M, Item 15) and Tetra Tech ($1M, Item 16).

agenda_items.title: Affordable Housing Implementation Committee Inaugural 6-Month Report (Forever Home Durham)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and committee co-chairs Tiffany Elder and Diane Catotti presented the committee's first semi-annual report tracking Forever Home Durham bond investments amid 25% annual home-price escalation (median ~$397k) and 20% pandemic rent hikes. Presentations highlighted Willard Street (82 units), Laurel Oaks (34 preserved units), UMCNC's $130M MWBE capacity target, and how pre-July 2019 baseline rules count projects.

agenda_items.title: FY2022 Q1 Financial Report and Settling the December 6 Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance/Budget staff including Christina Riordan presented the FY2022 Q1 financial report, detailing a $2.7M Transit Fund shortfall under fare-free service and a $2.5M fund balance draw in the Parking Fund ahead of upcoming rate/fee discussions. Council then voted 7-0 to settle the December 6 agenda (Consent 1-3, 6-16; GBA Public Hearings 18-19) before Mayor Schewel struck the gavel for his final adjournment.

votes.discussion_detail: Under suspended rules, Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Jillian Johnson seconded authorizing the Legal Aid of North Carolina Emergency Rental Assistance (ERA2) contract and grant ordinance. Passed 7-0 by voice vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Returning to City Hall chambers for Durham's first hybrid regular meeting, Council proclaimed David Price Day and Veterans Day, recognized 911 dispatcher Dwayne McIntyre, and hosted nearly 90 minutes of community tributes honoring retiring Council Member Pierce Freelon and Mayor Steve Schewel. Council unanimously passed the Consent Agenda 7-0 (including five Crane/Elizabeth/Eva/Gurley/Marne affordable-housing land conveyances) and adopted UDO Text Amendment TC2104 (tenant notification and permit updates) 7-0. After an extended public hearing over traffic, signalization, and school capacity, Council approved the 310-apartment Rosewalk II rezoning at West Club Blvd and North Duke St 7-0 after applicants proffered $30,000 for a traffic circle and $20,500 for DPS students, and then unanimously voted 7-0 across three motions to order $1.8M in petitioned Ardmore Drive ribbon paving and water/sewer lines while criticizing special-assessment inequity.

agenda_items.title: David Price Day, Veterans Day, 911 Dispatcher Tribute, and Farewells to Freelon & Schewel
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In Durham's first hybrid in-person meeting since the pandemic, Council presented proclamations for Congressman David Price Day and Veterans Day and honored 911 dispatcher Dwayne McIntyre. Former officials, state legislators, county commissioners, and community leaders—including Bill Bell, Brenda Howerton, Wendy Jacobs, and Mike Woodard—delivered lengthy farewell tributes honoring Pierce Freelon and Mayor Steve Schewel.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Boards/Commissions, FY23 Budget Schedule, Affordable Housing Conveyances, and Infrastructure Contracts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Clerk Diana Schreiber removed Item 2 (Cultural Advisory Board nominee moved out of Durham) and Jacqueline Wagstaff withdrew her pull of Item 9 (Tenants' Bill of Rights discussion). Council voted 7-0 to approve Consent Items 1, 3-5, and 7-15, including five parcel conveyances for affordable housing, the HR&A 505 W Chapel Hill St advisory contract, and fleet/stormwater contracts.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment TC2104 — Updates for Applications, Permits, and Tenant Notifications
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Michael Stock presented TC2104, expanding public-hearing mail notifications to renters and site occupants (not only property owners), clarifying right-of-way sign posting, and codifying street-renaming, closing, and annexation procedures (recommended 13-0 by Planning Commission). Council praised the renter-notice reform and adopted both the ordinance and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Rosewalk II (W. Club Blvd & N. Duke St, 7.865 Acres, RU-M(D) for 310 Apartments)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dan Jewell and developer Bob Chapman proposed rezoning 10 parcels at West Club Blvd and North Duke St to RU-M(D) for up to 310 apartments and an existing church while staying under 149 peak-hour trips to avoid a TIA. Nearby residents Mimi Kessler, Virginia Bowman, Mary Kopac, Joe Deem, and John Paces-Wiles warned of dangerous intersection conditions and cut-through traffic on Woodland and Ruffin Streets, while proponents Tiffany Elder and Dan Bach cited central rental supply. After applicants added proffers of $30,000 for a traffic circle and $20,500 ($500 x 41 students) for DPS, Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Ardmore Drive Petitioned Improvements — Ribbon Paving, Water Main, and Water/Sewer Laterals ($1.8M)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works presenter Robert Joiner outlined the ~$1.8M special assessment (~$1.2M paving, ~$600k water/sewer) across 13-14 Ardmore Drive parcels, moving residents 4-5 years up the unpaved road queue compared to last year's denied petition. Residents Isaac Woods Sr. and Jr. pleaded for safe drinking water and fire hydrants after decades of contaminated wells; Middleton, Freelon, and Freeman condemned forcing Black working-class neighborhoods to pay assessments for basic services before voting 7-0 across all three statutory motions.

votes.item_title: Item 18 — Adopt UDO Text Amendment Ordinance TC2104 (Updates for Applications, Permits, and Tenant Notice)
votes.discussion_detail: Following Michael Stock's staff report and questions from Javiera Caballero on expanding the 600-foot notice radius, Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded adopting TC2104. Passed 7-0 via chamber electronic voting.

votes.item_title: Item 18 — Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for UDO Text Amendment TC2104
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement for TC2104. Passed 7-0 via chamber electronic voting.

votes.item_title: Item 19 — Adopt Zoning Map Change Ordinance and FLUM Amendment for Rosewalk II (RU-M(D), Up to 310 Apartments)
votes.discussion_detail: After the applicant added proffers of $30,000 for a traffic circle at Woodland/Englewood or Ruffin/Knox and $20,500 ($500 per 41 students) for DPS, DeDreana Freeman moved and Pierce Freelon seconded approving the Rosewalk II rezoning and FLUM change. Passed 7-0 via chamber electronic voting.

votes.item_title: Item 19 — Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Consistency Statement for Rosewalk II
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for Rosewalk II. Passed 7-0 via chamber electronic voting.

votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded accepting the petition Certificate of Sufficiency for Ardmore Drive ribbon paving and water/sewer main and laterals. Passed 7-0 via chamber electronic voting.

votes.item_title: Item 20 — Adopt Preliminary Assessment Resolution for Ardmore Drive Improvements
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Pierce Freelon seconded adopting the Preliminary Resolution for Ardmore Drive improvements. Passed 7-0 via chamber electronic voting.

votes.item_title: Item 20 — Adopt Final Resolution Ordering Ardmore Drive Ribbon Paving and Water/Sewer Improvements
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Javiera Caballero seconded adopting the Final Resolution ordering the $1.8M assessed improvements on Ardmore Drive. Passed 7-0 via chamber electronic voting.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Rosewalk II Traffic & Intersection Safety vs. Central Infill Multifamily Housing
disagreements.summary: Neighbors of Trinity Park and Northgate Park argued that Rosewalk II's 310 apartments would exacerbate crashes at N. Duke St and W. Club Blvd and cut-through speeding while sidestepping a Traffic Impact Analysis under the 149-trip cap, whereas council members prioritized centrally located rental supply once additional proffers were added.
disagreements.side_a_position: Delay or require signal/geometric fixes and fuller neighborhood traffic mitigation before approving 310 apartments.
side_a_arguments: Residents reported repeated severe collisions and bus-passenger hazards at W. Club Blvd and N. Duke St.
Neighbors criticized capping trips below 149 to avoid a TIA and argued the driveway should be offset from Woodland Dr.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the 310-unit RU-M(D) rezoning based on central infill location, 35% lower projected rents than downtown, and new traffic/school proffers.
side_b_arguments: Lower land cost (~80% below downtown) and surface parking allow relatively moderate rents near Duke University and I-85.
Applicant committed $30,000 toward a neighborhood traffic circle and $20,500 for DPS students.
disagreements.resolution: Following the applicant's additional traffic-circle and school proffers and transportation staff review, Council unanimously passed the rezoning 7-0 while noting ongoing coordination with NCDOT.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Racial & Economic Equity of Special Assessments for Basic Water and Road Paving on Ardmore Drive
disagreements.summary: While voting unanimously to approve residents' $1.8M self-assessed petition so Ardmore Drive families receive clean water and fire protection immediately, council members criticized a city system that forces longtime Black working-class homeowners to pay steep assessments to skip a multi-year unpaved-road queue.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the resident petition now to end well contamination while condemning special assessments for basic municipal infrastructure.
side_a_arguments: Forcing residents annexed decades ago with bacteria-contaminated wells and no hydrants to pay ~$1.8M across 13-14 properties to jump ahead 4-5 years reflects systemic inequity.
Council urged reforming how Durham funds unpaved roads and water extensions.
disagreements.side_b_position: Note the statutory structure under which petitioned 100%-assessed improvements accelerate capital queue priority under existing policy.
side_b_arguments: Staff and Mayor Schewel noted the $1.8M estimate (~$1.2M paving, ~$600k water lines/laterals) relies on petitioner signatures to advance 4-5 years ahead of standard city-funded scheduling.
disagreements.resolution: Council voted 7-0 on all three Ardmore Drive assessment motions so residents could receive water, fire service, and paving, while calling for future funding reforms.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson presiding in the absence of Charlie Reece and Javiera Caballero (and Mayor Steve Schewel arriving mid-session), Council congratulated newly elected Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Council Member Leonardo Williams and unanimously passed 4-0 priority-item motions updating Ardmore Drive notice dates, entering closed session on two litigation matters, and adjusting board appointments. Council reviewed the FY23 budget schedule and the 505 W Chapel Hill St HR&A contract before conducting a lengthy work-session debate with Bull City Tenants United over their 13-point Tenants' Bill of Rights, directing the City Manager and City Attorney to return with enforceable options on housing inspections, language access, right-to-counsel, Ban-the-Box, and source-of-income protections. Council also received an Equitable Pedestrian Infrastructure briefing shifting sidewalk prioritization toward racial equity and the 2021 Employee Engagement Survey showing sharp morale declines in public safety, before voting 5-0 to set the November 15 agenda and end Zoom chat.

agenda_items.title: Election Congratulations, Priority Items (Ardmore Dr & Appointments), and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Presiding Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson noted excused absences for Charlie Reece and Javiera Caballero and delayed arrival for Mayor Steve Schewel, as members congratulated Mayor-elect Elaine O'Neal, Council Member-elect Leonardo Williams, and re-elected incumbents. Council passed three 4-0 votes accepting Item 20's updated Ardmore Drive notice dates, holding a closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) for Estate of Brooklyn Maynard (Kelly) and Tony Scott Jr./Sr. litigation, and accepting Clerk priority items 6-7.

agenda_items.title: FY23 Budget Schedule and 505 W Chapel Hill Street HR&A Advisors Contract
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On Item 8, Budget Director John Allore walked through the FY23 budget development timeline and confirmed no major structural changes. On Item 12, Stacy Poston and Deputy Manager Keith Chadwell explained why the $198k HR&A Advisors contract for redeveloping 505 W Chapel Hill St skips redoing prior community engagement and unbundles RFQ teams, while resident Stella Adams urged community land trust considerations.

agenda_items.title: Tenants' Bill of Rights Proposals (Bull City Tenants United) and Preemption Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following public remarks from Bull City Tenants United organizers Howie Machtinger, Alex Perlman, Lee Ganz, Emerson Goldstein, and Irene Lawrence—plus Ajax Woolley, Stella Adams, and Jacqueline Wagstaff—Council reviewed 13 tenant protection demands alongside City Attorney Kim Rehberg's legal analysis of NC preemption limits (including NCGS 42-44 and rent-withholding limits vs. Charlotte's ordinance). Council directed the City Manager to evaluate items 1, 2, 4, and 13 (after-hours/non-fee inspections, translation, landlord registry), asked the City Attorney to draft options on items 3, 6, and 11 (Ban-the-Box, source-of-income, non-discrimination), and tasked DeDreana Freeman with drafting a symbolic bill-of-rights resolution for item 8.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Placed on Consent / Staff direction given

agenda_items.title: Equitable Pedestrian Infrastructure and Vision Zero Prioritization Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan, Brian Taylor, and Doug Wright presented an equity-centered overhaul of sidewalk corridor and intersection prioritization toward Durham's $450M (300-mile at $1.5M/mile) sidewalk backlog, showing that 80% of the 2017 Bike+Walk priority intersections fell outside race-equity priority neighborhoods. Council members—joined by Mayor Steve Schewel, who noted upcoming Green and Equitable Infrastructure Bond needs—strongly endorsed applying racial equity scoring and low-cost traffic calming in future CIP requests.

agenda_items.title: 2021 Employee Engagement Survey, Ending Zoom Chat, Appointments, and Set Nov. 15 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant HR Director Timothy Howe and TalentKeepers CEO Christopher Mulligan presented the April-May 2021 survey (72% participation of 2,421 employees), revealing strong gains in direct-supervisor engagement (reaching the 80% goal) and governance/admin units, offset by a 20-point satisfaction drop in Public Safety (41% of respondents) and declining pay satisfaction. Schewel emphasized upcoming off-cycle public-safety pay adjustments and announced Zoom chat would end on November 15; Council heard Clerk appointments and voted 5-0 to set the November 15 agenda before recessing to closed session.

votes.notes: Roll call with four members present at opening.

votes.discussion_detail: Pierce Freelon moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded returning Item 6 (Workforce Development Board appointment) and correcting the DOST nominee's name on Item 7. Passed 4-0 on roll call.

votes.discussion_detail: After Mayor Schewel joined mid-session, DeDreana Freeman moved and Pierce Freelon seconded approving the November 15 docket (Consent Items 1-5 and 7-15; GBA Public Hearings 18-20). Passed 5-0 on roll call (Reece and Caballero absent excused).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov. 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Scope of Tenants' Bill of Rights Under State Preemption vs. Municipal Enforcement Resources
disagreements.summary: During the Item 9 Tenants' Bill of Rights discussion, Bull City Tenants United organizers and some council members pushed to adopt strong local anti-rent-collection and inspection ordinances modeled on Charlotte's code, while the City Attorney warned of NC state statutory preemption and council members debated how far Durham could push legal boundaries without risking invalidation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Push legal boundaries—mirroring Charlotte's minimum-housing rent prohibition and expanding after-hours inspections, translation, Ban-the-Box, and enforcement funding.
side_a_arguments: Tenants live in dangerous slum conditions and face landlords who ignore repairs or send maintenance staff as biased interpreters.
Charlotte's provision provides practical leverage for tenants seeking treble damages or warranty-of-habitability relief even without direct city prosecution.
disagreements.side_b_position: Focus on legally defensible city investments—free inspection access, language translation, eviction legal aid, and non-discrimination ordinances—while respecting NC statutory preemption.
side_b_arguments: North Carolina preemption and NCGS 42-44 prohibit cities from authorizing unilateral tenant rent withholding or escrow outside court orders, and Charlotte does not enforce its clause.
Municipal funding for legal defense and expanded code enforcement delivers immediate tangible tenant relief.
disagreements.resolution: Council directed the City Manager to assess staffing/funding for inspection access, interpretation, and landlord registration (items 1, 2, 4, 13), directed the City Attorney to review non-discrimination/Ban-the-Box/SOI options (items 3, 6, 11), and tasked DeDreana Freeman with drafting a symbolic resolution (item 8) for January 2022.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 1, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: In a nearly six-hour virtual Council meeting on November 1, 2021, Council opened by celebrating Bloomberg Philanthropies funding for Durham's guaranteed income pilot and Mayor Steve Schewel's 10th annual Run with the Mayor before unanimously passing the Consent Agenda 7-0 (including CASA's Bryan Place loan and Lake Michie land acquisition). Following an extensive public hearing on Item 22 (Griffin Place, 462 homes on East Geer St/Ferrell Rd), Council voted 7-0 to continue the hearing open until January 3, 2022 to seek stronger affordable housing and buffer commitments even after the applicant raised its housing fund proffer from $150 to $500 per unit (~$230,000), and then unanimously approved Item 23 (Bethpage Office 2, IL(D) to OI(D)) 7-0. After nearly four hours of emotional neighborhood and Eno River Association testimony on Item 24 (Latta Park at Guess and Latta Roads — up to 55,000 sq ft commercial CG(D) and 200 townhomes PDR 9.906 with 10 affordable units at 60% AMI and 40kW solar), Council passed both the rezoning ordinance and consistency statement 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman casting the lone Nay vote, before approving excused absences for Caballero and Reece.

agenda_items.title: Guaranteed Income Grant, Run with the Mayor, Priority Item 14, and Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council celebrated Bloomberg Philanthropies' guaranteed income award and staff participation in Run with the Mayor, received City Manager Page's Item 14 attachment update (Brady Integrated Security for Water Management), and voted 7-0 to pass Consent Items 1-5, 7-10, and 13-20 (including Bryan Place Apartments loan, Lake Michie land acquisition, and Water Management contracts).

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — Griffin Place (82.84 Acres, PDR 5.578 for 462 Units)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Danny Cultra and applicant Jarod Edens/Fred Shackle proposed annexing and rezoning 82.84 acres on East Geer St and Ferrell Rd for 168 single-family homes and 294 townhomes with three traffic signals, pedestrian crossings to Glenn Elementary, and 100-year stormwater ponds. Seven residents (including Taryn Kavanaugh, Kyle Marion, Robert Von Briesen, Jason Bazdula, Lindsey Dunn, Faith Neary, Shane Price, and Robin Sorrell) opposed road congestion and school overcrowding; although Edens added $34,000 for DPS and raised the affordable-housing fund proffer from $150 to $500/unit (~$230k), Mayor Schewel and council members questioned design commitments, separated product types, and industrial buffering, voting 7-0 to hold the hearing open to January 3, 2022.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Deferred / Continued to Jan. 3, 2022 (Passed 7-0 Roll Call)

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Bethpage Office 2 (5321 & 5421 Chin Page Rd, 24.62 Acres, IL(D) to OI(D))
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Attorney Patrick Byker (representing Tri Properties) and Creekside neighborhood leader Kevin Walls urged rezoning 24.62 acres between FedEx and Creekside homes from Light Industrial to Office & Institutional with a text-only development plan (limiting traffic to 149 peak-hour trips and buffering neighbors against FedEx parking expansion). Despite questions from Schewel, Reece, and Freeman over the text-only format lacking guaranteed office vs. residential uses and administrative site-plan notice, Council approved both the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Latta Park (Guess & Latta Roads, 31 Acres, RS-20 to CG(D) & PDR 9.906)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Alexander Cahill and applicants Jamie Schwedler and Austin Williams (Crossland Southeast) presented Latta Park's proposal for up to 55,000 sq ft of retail/commercial on 10 acres and 200 townhomes (PDR 9.906) on 20 acres—featuring 10 on-site 60%-AMI affordable townhomes ($1.25M subsidy), 40kW solar, a 1.3-acre park, Easley Elementary bike/ped connection, dual left-turn lanes at Latta/Guess, and 100-year stormwater ponds. An organized opposition group led by Megan Gray alongside Eno River Association ED Jessica Sheffield, stormwater speakers, and residents warned of Latta Rd congestion, Eno runoff, and incompatible suburban commercial, while northern Durham proponents supported modern retail, intersection fixes, and townhomes. Council passed the rezoning and consistency statement 6-1, with DeDreana Freeman voting Nay.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 6-1 (two Roll Call votes; Freeman Nay)

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences for Javiera Caballero and Steve Schewel (Nov. 4 Work Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Prior to adjourning at 12:47 AM, Council voted unanimously 7-0 in two separate roll-call votes to grant excused absences from the November 4, 2021 work session for Javiera Caballero and Mayor Steve Schewel.

votes.item_title: Item 22 — Continue Griffin Place Public Hearing Open Until January 3, 2022
votes.discussion_detail: Even after applicant Jarod Edens added $34,000 for DPS and raised the affordable housing fund proffer from $150 to $500 per unit (~$230,000), Charlie Reece moved and Javiera Caballero seconded continuing the Griffin Place public hearing open until January 3, 2022 so the developer could return with stronger buffers, block-length/design commitments, and housing benefits. Passed 7-0 on roll call.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 1, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Latta Park Rezoning — Commercial Expansion, Latta Road Traffic & Eno Watershed Impacts vs. On-Site Affordable Townhomes & Intersection Fixes
disagreements.summary: Latta Park split the Council 6-1 after residents and conservation advocates argued that adding 55,000 sq ft of retail and 200 townhomes at Guess and Latta Roads violated Comprehensive Plan commercial siting, threatened Eno River water quality, and overloaded two-lane Latta Road, while the six-member majority praised unprecedented proffers including 10 60%-AMI townhomes and dual turn lanes.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the mixed-use CG(D)/PDR 9.906 rezoning as a needed supply of moderate/affordable townhomes and northern Durham neighborhood retail.
side_a_arguments: Developer proffered over 50 commitments including 10 permanently affordable townhomes at 60% AMI ($1.25M subsidy), 40kW solar, a 1.3-acre park, and 100-year residential stormwater detention.

Dual left-turn lanes improve peak morning Guess/Latta intersection level-of-service from D to C where no NCDOT upgrades are funded, and rejection leaves RS-20 $500k+ McMansions as the by-right alternative.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose commercial and high-density rezoning due to traffic bottlenecks on un-widenable Latta Road, stormwater/Eno watershed risks, and lack of transit walkability.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman voted No after extensive opposition testimony citing level-of-service D egress on Latta Road, right-in/right-out U-turns on Guess Road, and Easley Elementary traffic hazards.
Opponents including Megan Gray and Eno River Association ED Jessica Sheffield noted nearby vacant commercial space, no bus service, and impervious surface runoff above West Point on the Eno.
disagreements.resolution: Council adopted both the Latta Park zoning ordinance and consistency statement by 6-1 roll-call votes, with DeDreana Freeman in dissent.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting Nov. 1, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Sufficiency of Griffin Place Community Benefits, Affordable Housing Proffer, and Product Integration
disagreements.summary: Council paused the 462-unit Griffin Place annexation and rezoning in eastern Durham because members found initial housing-fund payments, perimeter buffers, and segregated single-family/townhome layouts insufficient relative to the project's scale and state-road congestion.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold the public hearing open until January 3, 2022 to extract stronger affordable housing contributions, better industrial/residential buffering, block-length limits, and improved traffic clarity.
side_a_arguments: Even after raising the affordable housing fund proffer from $150 to $500/unit during the hearing, Council noted the ~$115M project needed stronger design commitments, less rigid product segregation, and better buffering adjacent to Scannell industrial land.
State roads around Cheek and Ferrell Roads lack funded DOT widening, raising urgency around community benefits.
disagreements.side_b_position: Recognize already-proffered traffic signals, 100-year ponds, and Glenn Elementary pedestrian crossings while negotiating additional terms.
side_b_arguments: Applicant argued residential zoning cut trips vs. current industrial zoning and committed to three traffic signals and a $34,000 DPS school contribution.
disagreements.resolution: Council voted 7-0 to continue the Griffin Place public hearing open until January 3, 2022.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 21, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: The October 21, 2021 Work Session was largely procedural and informational, with seven unanimous Council votes accepting City Manager and City Clerk priority items, suspending the rules to pass two urgent Water Management facility IT/AV contracts (ePlus Technology and Contact Systems), and setting the November 1 Regular Meeting agenda. During pulled items, Council examined cost overruns and CDBG 1.5 expenditure-test risks on Reinvestment Partners' 2816 Ross Road rehabilitation (Item 10), and heard public testimony from GoDurham operators Tamika Walker and Kurt Mitchell pressing for stronger bus safety shields and reduced late-night service. Council members clashed over the Ratio States aquatics study at Wheels Fun Park (Item 18), with Charlie Reece, DeDreana Freeman, and Pierce Freelon opposing any option that would eliminate the roller skating rink while Steve Schewel and Javiera Caballero favored gathering broad public survey data on aquatics needs. Council also received presentations on Durham's Source Water Risk and Response Plan, a proposed $300,000 Cultural Master Plan, and the Clerk's timeline to return to in-person Council meetings on November 15.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Council Announcements, and Acceptance of Manager & Clerk Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order with all seven Council members present and offered brief remarks on upcoming appointments and community updates. City Manager Wanda Page presented priority items including suspending rules to approve two time-sensitive Water Management facility contracts (Items 11 and 12), updating the 2816 Ross Road contract motion (Item 10), and withdrawing speaker Daniel Williams on Item 25. City Clerk Diana Schreiber added a priority discussion on returning Council and boards/commissions to in-person meetings.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 7-0 (two separate votes on Manager and Clerk priority items)

agenda_items.title: ePlus Technology Inc. Network Infrastructure Contract for Department of Water Management
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page requested suspension of the rules due to supply-chain lead times for integral network infrastructure at the new Department of Water Management facility complex. Council unanimously suspended the rules and authorized execution of the contract with ePlus Technology Inc.

agenda_items.title: Contact Systems Inc. Audio-Visual Equipment Contract for Department of Water Management
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page requested rule suspension to lock in procurement pricing and delivery for audio-visual equipment at the Department of Water Management facility complex. After clarifying that Brady Integrated Security (Item 14) had been withdrawn by the department rather than slated for a vote today, Council suspended the rules and approved the Contact Systems contract.

agenda_items.title: Reinvestment Partners Contract Amendment for Rehabilitation of 2816 Ross Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Item 10 to review significant pandemic-driven construction cost increases on Reinvestment Partners' affordable housing rehab at 2816 Ross Road, which staff proposed revising back to the original contract figure after a previous amendment push. Members questioned project timeline delays, contractor oversight, and HUD CDBG 1.5 timeliness-test implications if funds remained unspent.

agenda_items.title: GoDurham Bus Operator Safety Concerns
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GoDurham bus operator Tamika Walker and union leader Kurt Mitchell addressed Council following recent assaults and threats against drivers, urging immediate installation of enclosed operator safety barriers and questioning late-night route hours. City Manager Wanda Page committed that Deputy City Manager Keith Chadwell and Transportation Director Sean Egan would review the concerns and follow up.

agenda_items.title: Durham Parks and Recreation Outdoor Aquatics Study Contract (Wheels Fun Park / Ratio States)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed the contract with Ratio States NC to design aquatic facility plans at the former Wheels Fun Park site alongside public comment from Ideal Ortiz warning against displacing the community roller skating rink. Charlie Reece, DeDreana Freeman, and Pierce Freelon insisted that destroying the skating rink was non-negotiable, while Steve Schewel and Javiera Caballero argued residents should first weigh in through an open survey balancing aquatics needs and skating preservation.

agenda_items.title: Source Water Risk and Response Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Department of Water Management staff presented Durham's Source Water Risk and Response Plan detailing protection of Lake Michie, Little River Reservoir, and surrounding watersheds against contamination spills and drought events. Council praised the long-term utility planning and emergency coordination protocols.

agenda_items.title: Durham Cultural Advisory Board FY23 Cultural Master Plan Funding Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services staff and Cultural Advisory Board representatives presented a $300,000 proposal to commission a comprehensive Cultural Master Plan ahead of FY23 budget deliberations. Council asked questions about equitable artist engagement, consultant scope, and alignment with ongoing Equity and Inclusion efforts.

agenda_items.title: Return to In-Person Meetings Timeline and Committee Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Clerk Diana Schreiber reviewed logistics for transitioning City Council back to in-person meetings on November 15 and allowing boards and commissions to vote to return in January 2022, following up on Council's board appointments (Items 2-6). Members discussed COVID-19 masking, hybrid public comment access, and room safety protocols.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Agenda for November 1, 2021 Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page recommended placing Items 1-10 and 13-20 on the November 1 Consent Agenda and Items 22-24 on the General Business Agenda Public Hearings. Council approved the agenda unanimously and adjourned at 3:43 PM.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted the City Manager's priority additions and revisions, including rule-suspension requests for Items 11 and 12, revised Item 10 motion language for 2816 Ross Road, and removal of speaker Daniel Williams from Item 25.

votes.item_title: Accept City Clerk's Priority Items (Return to In-Person Meetings Discussion)
votes.discussion_detail: Added the City Clerk's priority discussion regarding transitioning City Council and boards/commissions back to in-person meetings.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules to Vote on Item 11 (ePlus Technology Network Contract)
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended Council rules at the work session to take immediate final action on Item 11 due to IT hardware supply-chain urgency.

votes.item_title: Item 11: Purchase Contract with ePlus Technology Inc. for Department of Water Management Network Infrastructure
votes.discussion_detail: Approved purchase contract with ePlus Technology Inc. for network infrastructure at the new Department of Water Management facility complex.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules to Vote on Item 12 (Contact Systems Audio-Visual Contract)
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended Council rules at the work session to vote immediately on Item 12.

votes.item_title: Item 12: Purchase Contract with Contact Systems for Department of Water Management Audio-Visual Equipment
votes.discussion_detail: Approved contract with Contact Systems for audio-visual equipment at the Department of Water Management facility complex.

votes.item_title: Set Agenda for November 1, 2021 Regular City Council Meeting
votes.notes: Auto-captions masked the first three roll-call names under '[Music]' before capturing Freelon, Freeman, Middleton, and Reece voting Aye, and the Clerk/Mayor announced the motion passed unanimously (all 7 members present).
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted City Manager Wanda Page's recommended November 1 Regular Meeting agenda placing Items 1-10 and 13-20 on Consent and Items 22-24 on GBA Public Hearings.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct. 21, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Preserving Wheels Fun Park Roller Skating Rink vs. Full Aquatics Site Redevelopment (Item 18)
disagreements.summary: Council members split over how the Ratio States NC aquatics study at Wheels Fun Park should treat the existing indoor roller skating rink, with three members drawing a hard red line to preserve the rink while two others urged waiting for broad community survey input.
disagreements.side_a_position: Explicitly rule out demolishing the roller skating rink and prioritize preserving an affordable Black and community skating institution alongside aquatics improvements.
side_a_arguments: Wheels' roller skating rink is a uniquely important, beloved recreation institution for Durham families and youth of color that should not be put on the chopping block.
Community advocates, including speaker Ideal Ortiz, warned against sacrificing the only local indoor roller rink without clear guarantees.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid prejudging design scenarios before conducting an open community survey on both public aquatics needs and the rink.
side_b_arguments: Durham faces a severe shortage of public swimming pool capacity, and early engineering/community feedback should evaluate all site configurations openly.
Restricting consultant study options prematurely could limit viable ways to meet citywide aquatics equity goals.
disagreements.resolution: Informational / Placed on Consent Agenda (staff instructed to convey Council's feedback on preserving skating alongside robust public engagement)
