meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council May 17, 2021 at 7 p.m.
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 17, 2021 regular virtual meeting, all seven members of the Durham City Council recognized the Durham Recovery and Renewal Task Force co-chairs and issued proclamations for Period Poverty Awareness Week and Tourette's Syndrome Awareness Day. Following public hearings, Council unanimously passed three 7-0 votes approving a Suburban-to-Urban Tier Comprehensive Plan amendment, RU-5(D) rezoning, and consistency statement, followed by three 7-0 votes authorizing a new five-year Downtown Durham Municipal Service District contract with Downtown Durham, Inc. (up to $1,181,500 in year one). Council also voted 7-0 to adopt revised FY 2022 stormwater rates effective July 1, 2021, raising residential Tier 1, 2, and 3 monthly fees by $0.25, $0.51, and $3.00 respectively.

agenda_items.title: Recovery & Renewal Task Force Recognition, Proclamations, and Vaccine Updates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council honored Durham Recovery and Renewal Task Force co-chairs Matisha Sims and Katie Galbraith, proclaimed Period Poverty Awareness Week with Diaper Bank of NC Executive Director Michelle Old, and proclaimed June 4 as Tourette's Syndrome Awareness Day with Chelsea Phoebeach. During announcements, Javiera Caballero shared walk-in COVID-19 vaccine access for ages 12+ at Wheels and Duke's Karsh Alumni Center, and members noted an Office of Equity and Inclusion FUSE fellowship.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Tier Amendment (Suburban to Urban) and RU-5(D) Zoning Map Change
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Closing the public hearing with support expressed for the proposed development, Council approved three consecutive motions—amending the Comprehensive Plan Tier Map and Future Land Use Map from Suburban to Urban Tier, rezoning the property from RS-20 and RU-5 to RU-5 with a development plan, and adopting the consistency statement—each passing 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Five-Year Contract with Downtown Durham, Inc. for Downtown Durham Municipal Service District
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff member Mr. Nixon and Downtown Durham, Inc. President Nicole Thompson appeared for the public hearing on renewing DDI's management of the Downtown Durham Municipal Service District, with no public speakers signed up. Council unanimously approved three motions authorizing a five-year contract (July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2026), year-one funding up to $1,181,500, and future payments subject to budget authorization.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Ordinance Revising FY 2022 Stormwater Fee Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staffer Paul Wiebke presented the proposed FY 2022 stormwater rate adjustments effective July 1, 2021 ($0.25/month increase to $3.75 for Tier 1, $0.51/month to $7.76 for Tier 2, $3.00/month for Tier 3 residential, and $0.51 per 2,400 sq. ft. impervious surface for non-residential). After DeDreana Freeman praised staff's creative rate structuring and no public speakers appeared, Council unanimously adopted the ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Resolution Amending Comprehensive Plan Tier Map and FLUM (Suburban Tier to Urban Tier)
votes.discussion_detail: Following the closed public hearing, Charlie Reece moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the resolution amending the Comprehensive Plan Tier Map and Future Land Use Map from Suburban Tier to Urban Tier; the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Adopt UDO Ordinance Rezoning Property from RS-20 and RU-5 to RU-5(D)
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the UDO rezoning ordinance taking the property out of RS-20 and RU-5 and establishing RU-5 with a development plan; the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consistency Statement for RU-5(D) Zoning Map Change
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement; the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Item 30 — Authorize Five-Year Contract with Downtown Durham, Inc. (FY22-FY26)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded authorizing the City Manager to execute a five-year contract with Downtown Durham, Inc. (July 1, 2021 to June 30, 2026) to operate the Downtown Durham Municipal Service District; all seven members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Item 30 — Authorize Year-One MSD Payment to Downtown Durham, Inc. (Up to $1,181,500)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded authorizing payment to Downtown Durham, Inc. up to $1,181,500 for the first fiscal year of the MSD contract; the motion passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Item 30 — Authorize Future MSD Payments Subject to Budget Authorization
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Charlie Reece seconded authorizing future MSD contract payments subject to annual City Council budget authorization; all seven members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Revising FY 2022 Stormwater Fee Schedule
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting the ordinance revising the stormwater fee schedule effective July 1, 2021; the motion passed unanimously 7-0.

meetings.title: City Manager Wanda Page's FY 2021 - 2022 Budget Presentation May 17, 2021
meetings.executive_summary: In her inaugural budget address on May 17, 2021, City Manager Wanda Page presented a proposed $524.6 million FY 2021-2022 budget (a 4.38% increase) and a $235.6 million General Fund budget (up 9.8%), utilizing $10.2 million in fund balance alongside a proposed two-cent property tax rate increase to 55.176 cents per $100 of assessed value. Page allocated 1.38 cents of the tax hike to debt service for the $95 million 2019 Affordable Housing Bond ($12.7 million dedicated housing budget, plus $500,000 for a longtime homeowner tax grant), 0.5 cents to green and equitable infrastructure debt service, and 0.12 cents to the General Fund, while proposing a new Community Safety Department to lead non-police crisis prevention and intervention and staff the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force. All seven City Council members warmly praised the proposal ahead of budget work sessions and hearings, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman noted they would continue probing details to ensure equitable staffing and responsiveness to marginalized residents; no votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Wanda Page's FY 2021-2022 Proposed Budget and CIP Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page outlined a $524.6 million total budget ($235.6 million General Fund) funded in part by $10.2 million in fund balance and a proposed two-cent property tax increase (1.38 cents for Affordable Housing Bond debt, 0.5 cents for green and equitable infrastructure, and 0.12 cents for General Fund operations), plus previously discussed water, stormwater, solid waste, and planning fee updates. Key initiatives included creating the Community Safety Department, expanding Forever Home Durham to $12.7 million for FY22 (including Willard Street Apartments and a $500,000 longtime homeowner tax grant for <=30% AMI residents), employee pay increases, and COVID-19 recovery.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Comments on Proposed Budget Priorities
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After confirming registered public speaker Hillary Ensminger was not present in the virtual queue, all seven Council members expressed strong enthusiasm for Page's first budget. Members highlighted full housing bond funding, the Community Safety Department, the language access coordinator, green and equitable infrastructure, the Office on Performance and Innovation, and future transit fare considerations, while Middleton and Freeman emphasized testing the budget's impact on marginalized communities and departmental staffing needs during upcoming work sessions.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting with Congressman David Price (NC 4th District) May 10, 2021
meetings.executive_summary: Durham City Council held a 45-minute special virtual meeting with U.S. Representative David Price (NC-04) and senior staffer Tracy Lovett, moderated by Senior Assistant to the City Manager Karmisha Wallace, to align local priorities with federal appropriations and COVID-19 relief opportunities. City leaders thanked Price for his 34 years of service, light-rail advocacy, CDBG support, and CARES Act rent and utility assistance, while Price highlighted the return of transparent congressional community project funding (earmarks), HUD Section 811 and Choice Neighborhoods grants, and federal Treasury relief monitoring alongside Durham's $95 million affordable housing bond. During Q&A, Council members questioned Price on H.R. 40 reparations legislation, addressing decades of deferred maintenance in public housing communities like McDougald Terrace through federal infrastructure bills, alternative community safety responses, federal voting rights (H.R. 1) amid the Senate filibuster, and immigration and refugee policy; no formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Durham City Priorities Overview and Congressman David Price Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel and Karmisha Wallace welcomed Congressman David Price, thanking him for supporting the American Tobacco Trail, prior light-rail efforts, CDBG funding, and CARES Act rental/utility relief administered with Durham County Social Services. Price outlined opportunities from the return of transparent congressional earmarks, pairing federal housing programs (Section 811, Choice Neighborhoods) with Durham's $95 million affordable housing bond to counter gentrification, and tracking nearly $2 trillion in federal relief.

agenda_items.title: Dialogue on Public Housing Maintenance, Policing Alternatives, Voting Rights, and Immigration
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Congressman Price responded to Council questions regarding his co-sponsorship of H.R. 40 on reparations, efforts to fold public housing deferred-maintenance backlogs (such as McDougald Terrace) into federal infrastructure legislation, and support for flexible alternatives to traditional policing. Jillian Johnson pressed Price on passing federal voting rights legislation (H.R. 1) against state-level voter suppression given the Senate filibuster, and Council also discussed immigration and refugee reforms; Price noted budget reconciliation bypasses the filibuster for relief and infrastructure, whereas voting and immigration bills face the filibuster directly.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council May 3, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Opening the May 3, 2021 virtual meeting with a moment of silence for Jocelyn Chadwell and murder victim A.J. Marsh, Council issued proclamations for Children's Mental Health Awareness, National Drinking Water Week, Better Hearing Month, and the NC Teacher of the Year. During announcements, Mark-Anthony Middleton urged Council to address gun violence urgently and formally take up the question of police funding/defunding to protect staff fairness, civilian police employee morale, and institutional integrity. In a contested public hearing, Council voted 6-1—with Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece in favor, and DeDreana Freeman opposed—to approve CASA's expedited PDR 8.00 rezoning for 20 housing units at or below 30% AMI, after Freeman argued the minimum notice left neighboring renters uninformed, flagged stream-buffer concerns, and objected to bypassing standard process equity. Council then unanimously adopted the statutory consistency statement 7-0.

Marsh, recognized proclamations for Children's Mental Health Awareness, National Drinking Water Week, and Better Hearing Month, and honored the NC Teacher of the Year. Council heard an update on FUSE Fellows before Mark-Anthony Middleton implored the community to confront shootings affecting Durham youth and called on Council to formally address the police defunding issue for reasons of staff fairness, civilian employee morale, and institutional integrity.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council May 3, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Expedited PDR 8.00 Rezoning Process, Renter Notification, and Stream-Buffer Envelope for CASA Affordable Housing
disagreements.summary: Council divided 6-1 over whether to approve CASA's expedited rezoning for 20 deeply affordable units despite concerns regarding minimal renter notification, an alternate building envelope conditioned on a future Board of Adjustment stream-buffer variance, and process equity.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the expedited PDR 8.00 rezoning to secure NCHFA financing for urgently needed <=30% AMI affordable housing.
side_a_arguments: The project delivers 20 units for households at or below 30% AMI, which is the hardest tier of affordable housing to build and already holds City funding commitments.
May approval is required to meet the North Carolina Housing Finance Agency's June board deadline.
Council is not granting a stream-buffer variance; the Board of Adjustment retains sole authority over any variance for the alternate building envelope.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the expedited rezoning due to inadequate renter notice, stream-buffer concerns, and unequal expedited process standards.
side_b_arguments: Bare-minimum legal notice went to property owners rather than long-term neighboring renters, leaving residents like Ms. Batson uninformed.
The conditional building envelope raises concerns about infringing on the Falls/Jordan stream buffer and potential flooding or sinking impacts.
Expediting this rezoning bypasses full community engagement and creates inequity compared to other local organizations that are not granted expedited timelines.
disagreements.resolution: Rezoning ordinance passed 6-1, followed by a 7-0 vote adopting the consistency statement.

Davis and City Manager Wanda Page. Pierce Freelon announced grassroots conversations with Black men and boys alongside the Office on Youth to craft an emergency violence-prevention strategy, and Council spoke out against three anti-transgender bills pending in the North Carolina General Assembly (HB 358, SB 514, and SB 515). meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session April 8, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the April 8, 2021 Work Session, Council voted unanimously 5-0 (with Charlie Reece excused and Pierce Freelon joining later) to excuse Charlie Reece's absence, and later voted 6-0 (with Pierce Freelon signaling aye on video due to a microphone failure) to set the April 19 Regular Meeting agenda. During pulled consent items, members examined racial and gender equity tracking for affordable housing contracts, a Black Maternal Health resolution, R. Kelly Bryant Jr. Bridge signage with NCDOT, Valley Springs Park change orders, and a sole-source DPAC lighting contract. Two major presentations covered a $50 million prioritized Green and Equitable Infrastructure project slate and the five-year 'Forever Home, Durham' Affordable Housing Investment Plan ($160 million total, extended through FY25 due to COVID-19). Council members debated whether to fund the green infrastructure package via a FY22 property tax increase for pay-as-you-go CIP or defer a general obligation bond to 2022, ultimately agreeing without a formal vote to revisit the decision at the next work session before the May 3 bond deadline.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session April 8, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Green and Equitable Infrastructure Funding Mechanism and Bond Timing
disagreements.summary: Council members split over whether to move forward immediately with a $50 million GO bond or 1-cent FY22 CIP tax increase, or defer a bond referendum until 2022 pending equity review, federal stimulus clarity, and full FY22 budget trade-offs.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prefer incremental pay-as-you-go CIP steps or delaying a $50 million bond referendum until 2022 to allow racial equity vetting, public engagement, and clarity on federal infrastructure legislation and FY22 tax rates.
side_a_arguments: Rushing a November 2021 bond vote before the May 3 statutory deadline leaves insufficient time for equitable community engagement and racial equity analysis.
Staff and Council do not yet know the full FY22 property tax rate impact alongside operating needs or how upcoming federal infrastructure stimulus could offset local borrowing.
disagreements.side_b_position: Favor advancing a bond or keeping near-term dedicated funding moving forward rather than stalling equitable infrastructure investments or burdening taxpayers solely through FY22 operating property taxes.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman argued against raising property taxes through immediate CIP increases during COVID-19 recovery, preferring bond financing if infrastructure spending proceeds.
Jillian Johnson favored maintaining momentum on equitable climate and sidewalk investments and keeping both a 2021 bond or dedicated CIP penny on the table.
disagreements.resolution: Resolved by consensus at 02:05:41 without a vote to carry the financing decision to the next work session ahead of the May 3 bond deadline.

Under Item 5 (Budget Development Guidelines), Mayor Schewel highlighted expected American Rescue Plan Act allocations (including ~$50 million for the City and $63 million for the County), and NIS staff presented Item 12 on the Equitable Community Engagement Blueprint detailing over $250,000 paid to community engagement partners.

Members condemned anti-Asian violence following the Atlanta spa shootings, recognized Transit Workers Appreciation Week with GoDurham union leader Stella Adams, congratulated Charlie Reece on the birth of his daughter Darcy, and discussed equitable local hiring for Google's planned ~1,000-job Durham engineering hub.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council March 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: The March 15, 2021 Regular Meeting featured the unanimous 7-0 appointment of Wanda Page as Durham's permanent City Manager alongside ten formal roll-call votes across the Consent Agenda and three major development public hearings. Council unanimously approved the Gillings Tract consolidated annexation and 90-townhome rezoning (6-0 annexation before Pierce Freelon arrived; 7-0 rezoning and consistency) and 920 Sherron Road's 55-townhome annexation and rezoning (6-0 annexation and rezoning while DeDreana Freeman briefly stepped away; 7-0 consistency). A lengthy, contentious hearing on Olive Branch Reserve (~114 acres, up to 350 units, Planning Commission 0-13 against) saw sharp debate over Southeast Durham development moratoriums, wildlife corridor buffers, and unverified family consent to relocate six May family graves, ending by consensus continuation to May 3, 2021. Finally, Council approved the 4523 Hope Valley Road congregate-living rezoning and consistency statement (Item 25) by identical 6-1 split votes, with Ayes from Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece, and Nay from DeDreana Freeman over neighboring stormwater erosion concerns.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Proclamations for Robert D. Teer Jr. and March for Meals, and Consent Agenda (Items 1-20)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the meeting with six Council members initially present (Pierce Freelon joined at 00:38:43) and issued proclamations honoring 22-year RDU Airport Authority member Robert D. Teer Jr. and March for Meals Month. City Attorney Kim Rehberg clarified virtual absence versus abstention voting rules, and Council approved Consent Agenda Items 1-20 unanimously 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation and Rezoning — Gillings Tract (4001 Page Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a public hearing on Lennar's proposal (presented by Nils Gosch) to annex and rezone ~21 acres at 4001 Page Road from Rural Residential (RR) to Planned Density Residential (PDR 4.44) for up to 90 townhomes. Council approved annexation 6-0, and—following Pierce Freelon's arrival at 00:38:43—approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Appointment of Wanda Page as Permanent City Manager and Employment Contract
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel announced the selection of Acting City Manager Wanda Page as permanent City Manager and summarized her employment agreement. Council voted unanimously 7-0 to appoint Page, with every member praising her long tenure and celebrating Durham's all-women trifecta of Council-appointed officials (City Manager, City Attorney, City Clerk).

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — Olive Branch Reserve (1607 Olive Branch Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held an extended public hearing on Olive Branch Reserve, a ~114-acre proposal for up to 350 single-family and townhome units that received a 0-13 negative recommendation from the Planning Commission. Applicants and genealogist Debra Joy discussed plans to relocate six Wylie Jackson May family graves to Maplewood Cemetery, while opponent Stephen Cannell urged a Southeast Durham moratorium; citing unresolved descendant outreach, wildlife corridor impacts, and focus-area concerns, Council continued the hearing by consensus to May 3, 2021.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — 920 Sherron Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council heard Edens Land Corp's proposal (presented by Jared Edens) to annex and rezone 7.67 acres at 920 Sherron Road to PDR 7.171 for up to 55 townhomes with proffers including $3,000 for Durham Public Schools and $8,250 for dedicated affordable housing. With DeDreana Freeman briefly away during the first two votes and returning for the third, Council approved the annexation 6-0, rezoning 6-0, and consistency statement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — 4523 Hope Valley Road (Navion Congregate Living)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tim Seivers presented a rezoning on 3.44 acres at 4523 Hope Valley Road allowing up to 32,000 square feet of single-room congregate senior living expansion, opposed by neighboring HOA president Alisa Peterson citing downstream stormwater erosion. DeDreana Freeman urged postponing for an on-site stormwater inspection and voted Nay, while the other six Council members approved both the rezoning and consistency statement 6-1.

votes.discussion_detail: Formally appointed Wanda Page as permanent City Manager of Durham and approved her employment contract.

votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman remained away from her screen and was not recorded.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council March 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Olive Branch Reserve Annexation — Southeast Durham Moratorium, Wildlife Corridor, and Grave Relocation
disagreements.summary: Council members split over Southeast Durham development pacing, whether to weigh piecemeal annexations against an unpassed moratorium, wildlife corridor impacts of a 300-foot stormwater pond, and unverified family consent to relocate six May family graves.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question piecemeal Southeast Durham annexations pending the Southeast Focus Area Plan and scrutinize auto-dependent suburban sprawl, stormwater encroachment, and unconfirmed descendant consent for grave relocation.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman urged pausing major Southeast Durham rezonings ahead of the focus area plan and protecting existing infrastructure capacity.
Charlie Reece opposed auto-dependent single-family suburban annexation patterns.

Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned the applicant's genealogist and legal framing claiming descendants supported relocating the Wylie Jackson May graves to Maplewood Cemetery without direct documentation.
disagreements.side_b_position: Caution against ad hoc denials equivalent to an un-enacted moratorium while exploring whether wildlife corridor, infrastructure, and descendant-consultation conditions can be resolved.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton also warned against treating individual cases as a de facto moratorium without formal policy adoption.
Steve Schewel and Jillian Johnson weighed regional housing supply needs alongside demands for stronger wildlife corridor protection and direct descendant outreach.
disagreements.resolution: Resolved by consensus at 03:02:20 to continue the public hearing to May 3, 2021 so applicants and staff could verify descendant wishes and address wildlife corridor/infrastructure questions.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council March 15, 2021 at 7 p.m. (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: 4523 Hope Valley Road — Downstream Stormwater Erosion Concerns
disagreements.summary: Council split 6-1 on whether to delay Navion's congregate-living expansion at 4523 Hope Valley Road for an on-site Stormwater Services inspection following neighbor testimony of gully erosion.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning now based on staff/engineering review, required annual BMP inspections, and upgraded single-room congregate living capacity.
side_a_arguments: Steve Schewel and Charlie Reece noted the property was already largely developed, stormwater site-plan engineering controls and annual BMP inspections apply at permitting, and single-room congregate units improve care standards.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer the vote until Stormwater Services physically inspects erosion conditions reported behind the facility.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman credited neighboring HOA president Alisa Peterson's erosion testimony and asked for on-site verification by Stormwater Services prior to rezoning approval.
disagreements.resolution: Both the rezoning and consistency motions passed 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting Nay.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session March 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson at Mayor Steve Schewel's request, the March 4, 2021 Work Session featured four unanimous 7-0 procedural votes accepting City Manager and City Attorney priority items, setting the March 15 Regular Meeting agenda, and entering closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) for City Manager personnel deliberations. Pulled consent items examined expanding Bull City United with Durham County ($930,000, Item 5), traffic signal contracts (Item 8), Equal Business Opportunity Ordinance extension (Item 12), and a contentious $250,000 purchase of 814 Carroll Street (appraised at $168,000) after late discovery of a public sewer easement blocked developer plans. Two major presentations detailed the Durham Beltline Trail 65% design contract ($966,000 with John R. McAdams Co., highlighting a $4.5M-$6M transportation-phase funding gap) and Durham's 123-page procurement policy alongside MWBE/EBOP equity hurdles under North Carolina's lowest-responsive-responsible-bidder statute.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, In-Person Transition Remark, and Manager/Attorney Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order with all seven Council members present, briefly discussed planning for an eventual return to in-person meetings, and handed presiding duties to Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson. Council voted 7-0 to accept City Manager priority updates (adding Item 15 presentation and revised Items 23-25 attachments) and 7-0 to add a City Attorney closed-session item under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6).

agenda_items.title: Bull City United ILA (Item 5), Traffic Signals (Item 8), and EBOP Extension (Item 12)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Item 5 (interlocal agreement with Durham County allocating $930,000 to expand Bull City United gun violence interruption), Item 8 (city-owned traffic signals contract), and Item 12 (extension of the Equal Business Opportunity Ordinance). DeDreana Freeman questioned reliance on 2016 disparity study data for EBOP and urged timely updated disparity metrics.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Acquisition of 814 Carroll Street for $250,000
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff from Water Management (Don Greeley), General Services (David Fleischer), and Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson explained why the City negotiated $250,000 for a vacant lot at 814 Carroll Street appraised at $168,000 after late municipal notice of an 8-foot sewer line clearance invalidated building plans following $45,000 in developer hard costs. Charlie Reece objected to effectively compensating a developer for lost speculative profit and losing a duplex, while Jillian Johnson noted City notice errors contributed to the dispute.

agenda_items.title: Human Relations Commission 2020 Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Human Relations Commission Chair John Rooks experienced audio failure during his scheduled presentation of the 2020 Annual Report. Council accepted the written report on the Consent Agenda and invited Rooks to resubmit remarks or appear at a future session.

agenda_items.title: Durham Beltline Trail 65% Design Contract Presentation (John R. McAdams Co.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Millicent 'Nia' Rogers presented Item 15, a $966,000 contract with John R. McAdams Co. (plus $85,000 with Perkins & Will for engagement) to advance the Durham Beltline Trail to 65% design. Staff noted the core transportation corridor costs $9.5M-$11M ($29.6M full master plan) against $5.5M currently available, leaving a $4.5M-$6M funding gap.

agenda_items.title: City Procurement Policy and MWBE / EBOP Participation Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director David Boyd and Equity & Inclusion Director Deborah Giles walked Council through Durham's 123-page procurement policy, state lowest-responsive-responsible-bidder rules, and MWBE participation tracking. Mayor Schewel pressed for public HUB/subcontractor utilization dashboards, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman pushed for deeper vendor-pool data and stronger equity interventions within legal bounds.

agenda_items.title: PB Steering Committee Nomination, Set March 15 Regular Agenda, and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council nominated Constance Wright to fill the 10th at-large seat on the Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee. Council then voted 7-0 to set the March 15 Regular Meeting agenda (Consent Items 1-20, Public Hearings 22-25) and 7-0 to enter closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6).

disagreements.issue: 814 Carroll Street Over-Appraisal Purchase ($250,000 vs. $168,000 Appraisal)

disagreements.side_a_position: Criticize compensating a private developer above appraised market value for lost opportunity/profit after demolition of an existing duplex.

disagreements.side_b_position: Acknowledge municipal notice error created partial City culpability and justify acquiring the parcel to permanently clear the sewer corridor.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council March 1, 2021
meetings.executive_summary: This recording of the March 1, 2021 Regular City Council meeting begins earlier than the live stream, capturing nine roll-call votes starting with a unanimous 7-0 approval of Consent Agenda Items 1-18 excluding pulled Item 11. Council then voted 7-0 twice to adopt the Durham County DSS Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP) ILA and commit up to $8,414,809 in U.S. Treasury funds (Item 22), voted 7-0 twice to grant a Major Special Use Permit and Site Plan at 5002 Guardian Drive (Item 19), and voted 7-0 on pulled Item 11 authorizing up to $9 million in housing bonds for J.J. Henderson Seniors New Construction after DeDreana Freeman pressed DHA CEO Anthony Scott on Section 3 and MWBE participation. On Item 20 (Phillips Valley consolidated annexation at 2000 Fletcher's Chapel Road), Council passed both the annexation/UEA and zoning translation by 6-1 split votes—with Ayes from Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece, and Nay from DeDreana Freeman—while unanimously 7-0 adopting the consistency statement. Council also heard public testimony during the second FY2021-22 Annual Action Plan public hearing (Item 21).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-18 excluding Item 11)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman pulled Item 11 (J.J. Henderson Seniors affordable housing bonds) for separate discussion after the public hearings. Council then approved Consent Agenda Items 1-18 (excluding Item 11) unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP) ILA and $8,414,809 U.S. Treasury Funding
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson, Karen Lado, and Durham County DSS Director Ben Rose presented the joint Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP) funded by $8.41 million in City Treasury funds alongside $9.77 million in County funds for rent and utility arrears. Council voted 7-0 to approve the County ILA and 7-0 to commit up to $8,414,809.

agenda_items.title: Quasi-Judicial Hearing — 5002 Guardian Drive Major Special Use Permit (M1800001) & Major Site Plan (D1700380)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In a quasi-judicial hearing, Planning staff Eliza Monroe and applicant representatives Farazad Saeed and engineer Mr. Creidle requested a 70-foot reduction of a 100-foot major transportation corridor buffer for commercial office development at 5002 Guardian Drive. Council voted unanimously 7-0 to grant Major SUP M1800001 and 7-0 to approve Major Site Plan D1700380.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation — Phillips Valley (2000 Fletcher's Chapel Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jared Edens presented a 17-acre, 33-lot Rural Residential conservation subdivision at 2000 Fletcher's Chapel Road preserving 50% open space and stream buffers. DeDreana Freeman questioned where mass grading versus conservation buffers would occur and cast the lone Nay vote on annexation and zoning translation (both passed 6-1), while all seven members approved the consistency statement 7-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (6-1 Annexation; 6-1 Zoning; 7-0 Consistency; Nay on Motions 1-2: DeDreana Freeman)

agenda_items.title: FY2021-22 Annual Action Plan Second Needs Public Hearing (CDBG / HOME / ESG / HOPWA)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff (Wilma Conyers, Reginald Johnson) and DHA CEO Anthony Scott opened the second Annual Action Plan public hearing. Speakers Cynthia Faison, Constance Wright, Stella Adams, and Ms. Azikpe urged dedicated investment in Black heritage neighborhoods (Braggtown, Merrick-Moore, Walltown, Southside), stronger tenant rights/eviction prevention, and Section 3/MWBE enforcement.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item — J.J. Henderson Seniors New Construction Affordable Housing Revenue Bonds ($9,000,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman pulled Item 11 to question DHA CEO Anthony Scott on Section 3 hiring, MWBE participation, and contractor pipeline outcomes at the J.J. Henderson Seniors project. Following Scott's assurances on DHA equity goals and workforce reporting, Council approved the $9,000,000 bond issuance resolution 7-0.

votes.discussion_detail: Committed up to $8,414,809 in federal Emergency Rental Assistance funds for Durham residents.

votes.discussion_detail: Approved Major Site Plan D1700380 for commercial office development at 5002 Guardian Drive.

votes.discussion_detail: Adopted annexation ordinance and UEA for 17 acres at 2000 Fletcher's Chapel Road; DeDreana Freeman voted Nay.

votes.discussion_detail: Translated zoning from County Rural Residential to City Rural Residential for the 33-lot conservation subdivision; DeDreana Freeman voted Nay.

votes.discussion_detail: Adopted statutory consistency statement for the Phillips Valley RR zoning translation.

meetings.title: Day Four- City Council Budget Retreat Feb 26, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Day Four of the City Council Budget Retreat on February 26, 2021 was an informational and consensus-building session with no formal roll-call votes. Office of Performance & Innovation staff and RTI International researchers presented foundational analysis of Durham's 911 Calls for Service and Alternative First Response models (laying the groundwork for HEART), reporting that only ~20% of 911 calls were crime-related and that ~2% initial mental-health CAD call codes severely undercounted behavioral crisis calls. Council members debated alternative response architecture—with Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, and Charlie Reece urging independent unarmed clinician response (such as partnering with Lincoln Community Health Center) while Mark-Anthony Middleton advocated keeping a full menu including CIT co-responders. Budget Director Bertha Johnson then reviewed draft FY2021-22 Budget Development Guidelines (53.17-cent base rate plus 1.38-cent housing bond allocation, tiered equity bonuses, up to 3.6% water/sewer adjustments, and $603,000 in Council priority requests), prompting debate over holding total tax increases under two cents versus funding low-income homeowner relief and program parity.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Day Four Framing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called Day Four of the virtual budget retreat to order with all seven Council members present, joined by Budget Director Bertha Johnson and Acting City Manager Wanda Page to preview 911 alternative response findings and FY2021-22 Budget Guidelines.

agenda_items.title: 911 Calls for Service Analysis and Alternative First Response Pilot Proposals (RTI / OPI)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OPI staff (Monica Toplar, Shannon Delaney) and RTI researchers (Dr. Kevin Strom, Dr. Brian Aagaard, Dr. Renee Mitchell) presented Durham 911 call analytics showing ~20% of calls were crime-related, ~3,000 were animal calls, and >50% of CIT crisis referrals originated under non-mental-health call natures. After reviewing models like CAHOOTS and LAPD CAMP, RTI proposed four pilots including co-response versus independent clinician dispatch, NLP CAD tracking, P2C non-urgent diversion, and caller willingness surveys.

agenda_items.title: Draft FY2021-22 Budget Development Guidelines and Council Requests Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: BMS Director Bertha Johnson and John Allore presented draft FY2021-22 Budget Guidelines reflecting the 53.17-cent general/transit/debt rate plus 1.38 cents dedicated to the housing bond, proposed utility increases (up to 3.6% water/sewer, $0.51/month stormwater), pay raises (up to 2% general, 4% police, 3.5% fire) plus tiered $1,000-$1,500 equity bonuses, and $603,000 in Council budget additions ($212k one-time, $388k recurring). Council gave thumbs-up consensus on compensation structure and flexible tax guidelines while targeting an overall increase under two cents.

agenda_items.title: FY2021-22 Budget Calendar Review and Retreat Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff reviewed key budget milestones including March 3 public engagement, the March 18 work session and April 5 guidelines adoption, the May City Manager budget presentation, May 27-28 budget work sessions, and June 15 budget adoption.

disagreements.meeting_title: Day Four- City Council Budget Retreat Feb 26, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: 911 Alternative Response Architecture — Independent Unarmed Response vs. Police Co-Responder Menu
disagreements.summary: Council members diverged over whether Durham's 911 alternative response pilot should prioritize non-police independent community health responders or retain police/CIT co-response within a broader triage menu.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prioritize piloting unarmed, independent clinician and community health response without armed police accompaniment unless requested as backup, alongside traffic and alarm-call civilianization.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, and Charlie Reece pushed to design a non-police crisis response track—exploring partnerships with Lincoln Community Health Center—so armed officers do not automatically accompany behavioral health clinicians.
Members also urged removing routine traffic enforcement and false burglar alarm calls from armed DPD first response.
disagreements.side_b_position: Support 911 dispatch diversion while preserving a multi-tiered toolkit including CIT-trained officers and co-responders for unpredictable or potentially volatile scenes.
side_b_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton endorsed civilian triage at the 911 call center while arguing that dynamic emergency calls require keeping CIT co-responder capability available alongside non-police pilots.
disagreements.resolution: Staff recorded all pilot parameters—testing both independent non-police and co-response pathways, NLP dispatch coding, and caller willingness surveys—for development without a formal vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Day Four- City Council Budget Retreat Feb 26, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: FY22 Property Tax Rate Ceiling, Low-Income Homeowner Relief, and Council Request Funding Parity
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to signal an informal two-cent property tax increase limit in the FY22 Budget Guidelines and questioned unequal recurring versus one-time treatment of community partnership requests.
disagreements.side_a_position: Aim to constrain any total FY22 property tax increase below two cents while retaining formal guideline flexibility.
side_a_arguments: Steve Schewel and Charlie Reece advocated keeping the combined property tax impact below two cents during pandemic economic recovery.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid premature two-cent ceilings if higher investments fund low-income homeowner relief and ensure equitable recurring funding across Black and Latino community initiatives.
side_b_arguments: DeDreana Freeman stated she would support up to a five-cent tax rate increase if paired with dedicated low-income homeowner tax relief, and objected to placing El Centro Hispano in recurring baseline funding while treating We Are The Ones ambassadors as temporary one-time funds.
disagreements.resolution: Council gave informal thumbs-up consensus to keep general fund and debt service tax guidelines open while aiming under two cents for formal guidelines review on March 18 and April 5.

meetings.title: Day Three - City Council Budget Retreat Feb 25, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Day Three of the City Council Budget Retreat on February 25, 2021 opened with a moment of silence for former Transportation Director Mark Ahrendsen and proceeded through three major planning sessions using informal thumbs-up consensus without formal roll-call votes. Human Resources staff (Regina Youngblood and JJ Scott) presented three compensation scenarios addressing pay lags (9% police, 8% fire, 3-5% general open range) and fire-recruit living-wage gaps, with Council backing Scenario 2 base raises (2% general, 4% police, 3.5% fire) plus raised minimum tiered one-time equity bonuses ($1,000+ floor) without property tax hikes for salaries. Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson and Finance Director David Boyd then presented a $224.4 million Green and Equitable Infrastructure menu comparing a 1-cent GO bond (~$50M upfront) versus a 1-cent CIP (~$100M over 10 years), sparking debate between DeDreana Freeman and Jillian Johnson urging near-term action and Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece, and Steve Schewel seeking stronger racial equity vetting and community runway ahead of any bond. Finally, Council ranked 11 member budget requests totaling over $2 million, reaching consensus behind DEAR, the Immigrant Legal Defense Fund, We Are The Ones Ambassadors, El Centro support, and modest board/commission stipends and grants while deferring Council pay changes to take effect January 2024.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Moment of Silence for Mark Ahrendsen
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called Day Three of the virtual budget retreat to order with all seven Council members present and led a moment of silence honoring former Transportation Director Mark Ahrendsen. Budget Director Bertha Johnson and Acting City Manager Wanda Page introduced compensation, infrastructure, and Council budget-request sessions.

agenda_items.title: Employee Compensation, Market Pay Lags, and Tiered Equity Bonus Scenarios
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Regina Youngblood and JJ Scott reviewed market competitiveness data showing pay lags of 9% for Police, 8% for Fire, and 3-5% for general employees alongside fire-recruit living-wage adjustments, presenting three cost scenarios up to ~$6.7 million. Council signaled consensus support for Scenario 2 base adjustments (2% general, 4% police, 3.5% fire) paired with raising the lowest-tier one-time equity bonus floor to $1,000 without raising property taxes to fund salaries.

agenda_items.title: Green and Equitable Infrastructure $224.4M Menu and CIP vs. GO Bond Financing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson and Finance Director David Boyd presented a $224.4 million menu spanning sidewalks ($78.4M across categories), trails ($61.1M), building efficiency ($18.5M), recycling/composting ($13.8M), renewables ($13.5M), transit access ($10M), bike lanes ($7.7M), fleet electrification ($7.2M), dirt streets ($5.6M), energy resilience ($5M), green spaces ($2.8M), and pedestrian safety ($2.6M), comparing a 1-cent GO bond (~$50M upfront) to a 1-cent CIP (~$100M over 10 years). After debating timing and equity review, Council gave thumbs-up consensus to score and weight project categories first.

agenda_items.title: Scorecard Prioritization of $2M+ in City Council FY2021-22 Budget Requests
agenda_items.discussion_summary: BMS staff presented 11 Council budget proposals totaling over $2 million. Council reached informal consensus to advance the top four priorities—Driver's License Restoration/DEAR, Immigrant Legal Defense Fund, We Are The Ones Ambassadors ($62,400 initial 1/3 city share), and El Centro support—plus scaled board/commission stipends ($50k) and grants ($25k), while Javiera Caballero withdrew the Language Access Coordinator item to a staff request and Council pay equity increases were deferred to take effect January 2024 post-2023 election.

disagreements.meeting_title: Day Three - City Council Budget Retreat Feb 25, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Green and Equitable Infrastructure Financing Mechanism and 2021 vs. 2022 Bond Timing
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over whether to pursue an aggressive near-term bond/funding push in 2021 for green and equitable infrastructure or pause to complete deeper racial equity vetting and public engagement toward a 2022 bond or incremental CIP.
disagreements.side_a_position: Urge immediate momentum on bond or capital action in 2021 rather than delaying badly needed equitable sidewalk, transit, and climate investments.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman and Jillian Johnson pressed for timely action on infrastructure backlog and equitable neighborhood investments rather than deferring momentum.
disagreements.side_b_position: Caution that a November 2021 bond timeline lacks sufficient racial equity evaluation and community runway, favoring a 2022 bond, incremental CIP capacity, or narrowing priorities first.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece, and Steve Schewel warned that pandemic pressures, tax-rate capacity, and the May statutory bond deadline left too little time for rigorous racial equity analysis and authentic public co-design before November 2021.
disagreements.resolution: Resolved by thumbs-up consensus to have Council members first complete a category weighting and prioritization exercise so staff could return a refined $50M scenario at the April work session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session, February 18, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 18, 2021 City Council Work Session, Council approved three unanimous 7-0 roll-call votes: accepting City Manager priority items, accepting a City Clerk priority item on boards and commissions attendance, and settling the March 1 Regular Meeting agenda (including nominating Tammy E. Hall for the RDU Airport Authority). The meeting centered on an extended deliberation over Item 22, an Interlocal Agreement with Durham County to jointly administer roughly $8 million in federal Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP) funds, where Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Charlie Reece, and Mayor Steve Schewel pressed Durham County DSS Director Ben Rose and City Community Development staff on past CDBG-CV and NC HOPE bottlenecks, lack of intake software, and partnering with Legal Aid and community nonprofits rather than relying solely on County DSS (held for Monday's General Business Agenda with no vote). Council also scrutinized Durham Housing Authority's JJ Henderson new-construction bond request and RAD relocation plans (Item 11), reviewed the FY2021 Second Quarter Financial Report showing stronger-than-expected revenue and $600,000 in Solid Waste COVID-19 overtime overruns (Item 16), and informally directed the Clerk to maintain pandemic attendance leniency while engaging chairs before removing inactive board appointees.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Manager Priority Items (5, 19, 22), Item 19 Legal Update, and Clerk Priority Item
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the work session to order with all seven Council members answering roll call. Council unanimously voted 7-0 to accept City Manager Wanda Page's priority items (budget request Item 5, updated 5002 Guardian Drive attachments for Item 19, and Emergency Rental Assistance ILA Item 22) and 7-0 to accept a City Clerk priority item on boards and commissions attendance, while Deputy City Attorney Don O'Toole advised that Item 19's quasi-judicial Major Special Use Permit cannot proceed remotely without opposition consent.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 7-0 (Manager Priority Items); Passed 7-0 (Clerk Priority Item)

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Pulled Items Summary and Item 8 Board of Adjustment 2020 Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed Consent Items 1-18, Public Hearings 19-21, and Supplemental Item 22, pulling Items 8, 11, 16, and 22 for work-session discussion. On Item 8, staff explained that Board of Adjustment quasi-judicial appeals—including a long-pending flea market case—remained delayed pending safe resumption of in-person evidentiary hearings.

agenda_items.title: Tax-Exempt Bond Financing for Durham Housing Authority JJ Henderson New Construction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented a request supporting tax-exempt bonds for Durham Housing Authority's 80-unit JJ Henderson new construction project, including 20 public housing Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) units. Public speaker Ajax Woolley and Council members Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, and DeDreana Freeman pressed DHA Executive Director Anthony Scott on RAD relocation tracking and resident protections for nine existing JJ Henderson families.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Forwarded to Consent Agenda (No separate vote)

agenda_items.title: FY2021 Second Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director David Boyd and Assistant Budget Director John Allore presented the FY2021 Q2 report showing revenues holding better than projected alongside a $600,000 Solid Waste personnel overrun from COVID-19 leave and temporary staffing, plus Parking Fund shortfalls offset by DPAC and Ballpark reserves. Council members questioned Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) permitting timelines, the $12 million Transit Fund federal relief reserve, roughly $31 million in accumulated impact fees, and Exhibit 4 liability claims.

agenda_items.title: Interlocal Agreement with Durham County for Federal Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham County DSS Director Ben Rose, Janine Gordon, and City Community Development staff Reginald Johnson and Karen Lado presented a draft Interlocal Agreement designating the County as administrator for roughly $8 million in joint ERAP funds ($5.49M City allocation and ~$2.6M County allocation). Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Charlie Reece, and Mayor Steve Schewel sharply questioned County DSS capacity and past bottlenecks under CDBG-CV and NC HOPE, urging nonprofit and Legal Aid application navigation ahead of Monday's General Business Agenda consideration.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session, February 18, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: County DSS vs. Nonprofit Administration of the $8 Million Federal Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP)
disagreements.summary: Council members challenged Durham County DSS's proposed role as sole administrator of roughly $8 million in joint ERAP funds, pointing to prior bottlenecks under CDBG-CV and NC HOPE and debating whether the City should split funds or contract directly with Legal Aid and community nonprofits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Administer the joint City-County ERAP pool through a single Durham County DSS portal to consolidate intake, federal reporting, and compliance.
side_a_arguments: County DSS Director Ben Rose and Janine Gordon argued that combining funds under one portal avoids duplicating application reviews and noted DSS had already issued ~$3 million locally through HOPE and cleared earlier backlogs.
Community Development Director Reginald Johnson noted the City lacked standalone rental-assistance software and staffing capacity to launch a separate parallel program quickly.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reform intake immediately or carve out/contract ERAP outreach, navigation, and distribution through Legal Aid and trusted nonprofits to address DSS distrust and delays.
side_b_arguments: Jillian Johnson (01:12:41) warned that the proposed April ILA lacked concrete processing metrics, software commitments, and guaranteed funding for nonprofit outreach partners.
Javiera Caballero raised fears that undocumented and immigrant residents distrust government DSS portals and face documentation barriers without formal leases or pay stubs.
DeDreana Freeman, Charlie Reece, and Steve Schewel questioned why CDBG-CV funds stalled for months and pressed staff on direct Legal Aid or multi-agency subcontracts before Monday's meeting.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Item 22 was placed on the March 1 General Business Agenda so County and City staff could answer questions about intake software, documentation flexibility, and nonprofit navigation contracts.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat Feb 12, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: During Day 2 of the FY2021-22 City Council Budget Retreat on February 12, 2021, Council held no formal roll-call votes but reviewed the Racial Equity Budget Tool, FY2022 financial projections showing a smaller-than-feared $674,000 baseline gap before any employee pay raises ($7 million), 10-year Capital Improvement Program (CIP) equity reprioritization, NC State economist Dr. Michael Walden's regional outlook, and a potential November 2021 green/resilient infrastructure bond. Council divided over whether to start levying a property tax increase for the voter-approved $95 million affordable housing bond in FY2022 (1.38 cents, $31.64/year for the average homeowner) or delay until FY2023 (1.50 cents, $34.39/year): Steve Schewel, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Pierce Freelon, and Javiera Caballero favored moving ahead in FY2022 to keep faith with voters and avoid stacking back-to-back increases, whereas Charlie Reece, DeDreana Freeman, and Jillian Johnson initially preferred waiting one year to reduce pandemic household strain and leave budget room for employee raises. After confirming with Finance Director David Boyd that delaying would not slow Community Development's housing spend, Jillian Johnson yielded to give majority thumbs-up guidance to include the 1.38-cent housing-bond tax rate in the FY2022 draft budget.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Racial Equity Budget Tool, and Virtual Budget Engagement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant Budget Director John Allore convened Day 2 while Mark-Anthony Middleton arrived shortly after an NCLM presentation and COVID-19 vaccination, and Javiera Caballero joined remotely. Budget analysts Aaron Parrish and Tony Thompson reviewed the Racial Equity Budget Tool across 78 departmental requests ($17M) and Allore previewed March 3 Durham CAN budget engagement, winning Council consensus behind Jillian Johnson's proposal for fall joint budget conversations with Durham County and Durham Public Schools.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Thumbs-up consensus on fall joint budget engagement (No formal vote)

agenda_items.title: FY2021-22 Financial Projections and Multi-Year Budget Outlook
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson reported that FY21 property taxes ($108M collected to date) and rebounding sales taxes ($18.5M Q1, ~$2.5M ahead of budget) yielded a smaller-than-expected $674,000 baseline FY22 deficit with fund balance near 24%, but noted that model excludes employee pay adjustments (~$7M / 2 cents), $17M in departmental requests, $2M in Council requests, RTS police pilots, and housing-bond debt service. Council debated how Durham's low fee structure (no solid waste fee) compares to peer cities and asked staff for national property-tax comparisons.

agenda_items.title: 10-Year Capital Improvement Program (CIP) and Affordable Housing Bond Debt Modeling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: John Allore and Finance Director David Boyd walked through the 10-year CIP backed by the 11-cent dedicated capital tax rate, including street paving ($10M funded vs. $20M needed), Long Meadow Pool/Wheels Aquatics, CIP equity scoring, and GIS mapping. Boyd modeled the $95M affordable housing bond tranches ($45M late FY23, $50M FY25), showing a 1.38-cent tax increase if initiated in FY22 versus 1.50 cents if deferred to FY23.

agenda_items.title: Economic Outlook Presentation by NC State Economist Dr. Michael Walden
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Michael Walden forecast accelerating post-vaccine national recovery and highlighted Durham-Chapel Hill's 35th-fastest growth among 380 U.S. metros since 2000. He warned of long-term pressures on gas-tax transportation funding, demographic shifts, and uneven pandemic harm to women and minority-owned small businesses needing local recovery capital.

agenda_items.title: Council Guidance on FY2022 Affordable Housing Bond Tax Rate and Potential Green Infrastructure Bond
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated whether to include a 1.38-cent tax increase in FY22 or delay until FY23 for the $95M affordable housing bond; after extended debate, Jillian Johnson joined Steve Schewel, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Pierce Freelon, and Javiera Caballero in giving thumbs-up majority staff direction for 1.38 cents in the draft FY22 budget. Council then explored a fall 2021 green/resilient infrastructure GO bond for sidewalks, trails, parks, and solar/energy upgrades, with David Boyd clarifying water, sewer, and stormwater rely on enterprise revenue bonds instead, before adjourning at 2:50 PM.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informal majority thumbs-up guidance for 1.38-cent FY22 housing bond tax (No formal vote)

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat Feb 12, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Timing of Property Tax Rate Increase for the $95 Million Affordable Housing Bond (FY2022 vs. FY2023)
disagreements.summary: Council divided at the Budget Retreat over whether to start levying the affordable housing bond debt-service tax in FY2022 (1.38 cents, or $31.64/year for the average homeowner) or defer it one more year to FY2023 (1.50 cents, or $34.39/year).
disagreements.side_a_position: Initiate the 1.38-cent property tax increase in FY2022 as scheduled after the 2020 pandemic pause.
side_a_arguments: Steve Schewel (04:04:47) and Mark-Anthony Middleton (04:00:28, 04:10:57) argued voters already approved the bond knowing taxes would rise and warning that another delay erodes voter trust ahead of a possible green infrastructure bond.
Pierce Freelon (04:08:56) noted the annual household difference between 1.38 and 1.50 cents was less than $3 while funding affordable housing values.
Javiera Caballero (04:09:30, 04:17:41) warned that waiting would still force tax increases two years in a row once employee pay raises are funded in FY2022.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer the housing-bond tax increase until FY2023 (at 1.50 cents) since debt will not be issued until FY2023.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (03:59:18, 04:13:36) noted Finance Director David Boyd confirmed waiting changes only 0.12 cents and affects zero housing projects or Community Development schedules in FY22.
DeDreana Freeman (04:06:16) cited residents' COVID-19 financial strain and tax fears as reasons to hold off one year.
Jillian Johnson (04:02:29) initially favored deferring until FY23 to preserve taxpayer capacity for employee pay raises, before agreeing at 04:21:17 to join majority staff guidance.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; after Jillian Johnson signaled willingness to align with the majority (04:21:17), Mayor Schewel polled thumbs-up and noted a majority supported directing staff to model the 1.38-cent housing bond increase in the FY2022 draft budget.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat Feb 11, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Day 1 of the FY2021-22 City Council Budget Retreat on February 11, 2021 was entirely informational with no formal votes or council split votes. City Manager Wanda Page opened by prioritizing employee compensation in the upcoming budget, followed by ETC Institute's 2020 Resident Satisfaction Survey showing 83% overall quality-of-life satisfaction alongside sharp racial disparities in affordable housing, police relations, and city racial-equity progress. Performance Strategy Manager Sheri Metcalf reported 77% of the FY18-21 Strategic Plan's 95 initiatives were completed or ongoing and outlined a 10-to-15-initiative Gap Strategic Plan pending appointment of a permanent city manager. Staff Goal Teams and Idea Starter leads briefed Council on DEAR expungement clinics, $3 million in small-business recovery lending, Fire and DPD recruitment diversity, urban forestry equity targeting, and the Durham Belt Line trail before adjourning at 1:05 PM.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and City Manager Opening Keynote on Organizational Priorities
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel and Budget Director Bertha Johnson opened Day 1 at 9:02 AM with all seven Council members participating. City Manager Wanda Page highlighted employee dedication during the pandemic, flagged employee pay adjustments as a top FY2022 priority, and welcomed Council comments on maintaining organizational resilience.

agenda_items.title: 2020 Annual Resident Satisfaction Survey Results and Racial Disaggregation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Performance Strategy Manager Sheri Metcalf and ETC Institute's Jason Morado presented results from 637 survey households (+/- 3.8% margin of error): 83% rated Durham an excellent or good place to live, employee customer service scored 33 points above the national benchmark, and affordable housing, street maintenance, schools, and policing led investment priorities. Council members DeDreana Freeman, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece, and Mayor Schewel examined steep racial gaps—including Black residents reporting 32% satisfaction with racial-equity progress vs. 49% of white residents and 43% vs. 57% on police relations—and urged better Spanish/non-English outreach.

agenda_items.title: FY18-21 Strategic Plan Closeout and Interim Gap Strategic Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sheri Metcalf reviewed the FY18-21 Strategic Plan (5 goals, 18 objectives, 95 initiatives—77% completed or ongoing despite COVID-19 disruptions) and proposed a focused one-to-two-year Gap Strategic Plan of 10-15 initiatives aligned with the budget until a permanent City Manager leads the next full multi-year plan.

agenda_items.title: Strategic Plan Goal Team Progress Briefings (Goals 1 through 5)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Departmental Goal Team co-chairs presented highlights on trilingual outreach, DEAR driver's-license restoration, $3M small-business CARES recovery funds, Training to Work, Fire Department diversity hiring (30.4% Black, 8.7% Hispanic in recent academy), DPD Community Engagement Unit at DHA, 85% equity-area urban forestry planting, trails, and Data Academy training. During Goal 2, DeDreana Freeman criticized $15/hour wage 'benefits cliffs,' prompting Equity & Inclusion Director Deborah Giles to cite joint racial-equity and workforce alignment work.

agenda_items.title: Employee Idea Starter Updates and Preview of Subsequent Budget Retreats
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presenters Shannon Delaney, Tanya Daughtridge, and Muriel Williman briefed Council on Sustainable City Hall and the virtual home-composting Idea Starter transition. Bertha Johnson and Wanda Page previewed the remaining February budget retreats and adjourned Day 1 at 1:05 PM.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb 1, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 1, 2021 Regular City Council Meeting, Council cast six formal roll-call votes, highlighted by the unanimous 7-0 adoption of the Consent Agenda (including Item 8's CROWN Act resolution against hair discrimination) and unanimous 7-0 rezoning approvals for 1000 Hazel Street (Item 19) and NCCU's School of Business (Item 20). Two public hearings produced notable votes and debate: on Item 17 (4316 Trenton Road annexation and utility extension for seven homes near Leigh Farm Park), Council approved annexation 6-1—Ayes: Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, and Mark-Anthony Middleton; Nay: Charlie Reece, who walked the forested wetland parcel and opposed annexing it—before approving RS-20 zoning 7-0. On Item 18 (2720 Fawcett Avenue consolidated annexation for 320 units adjacent to the historic Black Merrick-Moore community), over 20 residents led by Bonita Green opposed the project over Cheek Road safety, flooding, and displacement; despite Jillian Johnson and Javiera Caballero warning that a by-right conservation subdivision would omit the developer's proffered offsite sidewalk and housing/school funds, Council voted unanimously 0-7 to deny annexation (Nays: Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece; Ayes: none).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Black History Month Announcements, and Adoption of Consent Agenda (incl. CROWN Act)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson briefly called the meeting to order and took a two-minute recess until Mayor Steve Schewel connected via Zoom, with all seven Council members answering roll call. Announcements from Charlie Reece, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and DeDreana Freeman highlighted Black History Month, sit-in history, and the CROWN Act natural-hair resolution (Item 8), before Council passed Consent Agenda Items 1-3, 5, 7-9, 11-12, and 14-16 unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation, Utility Extension Agreement, and RS-20 Zoning — 4316 Trenton Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Alexander Cahill and applicant Tim Sivers presented an 8.25-acre voluntary annexation and utility extension for seven single-family lots and two open-space parcels near Leigh Farm Park. Charlie Reece opposed annexation after walking the wet, forested parcel bordering federal Army Corps land, casting the lone Nay in a 6-1 annexation vote before joining a 7-0 vote to translate zoning to RS-20.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Annexation & UEA Passed 6-1 (Reece Nay); Zoning RS-20 Passed 7-0

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation and Zoning Map Change — 2720 Fawcett Avenue (Merrick-Moore / Cheek Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a nearly three-hour public hearing in which Planning Commission's 12-0 denial recommendation, Bonita Green, and over 20 residents warned that 320 units would worsen Cheek Road pedestrian hazards, flooding, and gentrification in the legacy Black Merrick-Moore neighborhood, Council weighed developer proffers ($20,550 DPS, $40,000 Dedicated Housing Fund, and offsite sidewalk to Merrick-Moore Elementary). Although Jillian Johnson and Javiera Caballero warned a 202-unit by-right conservation subdivision would eliminate the sidewalk and proffers, Council unanimously voted 0-7 to deny annexation.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Failed 0-7 (All 7 members voted Nay; second zoning motion unnecessary)

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change (Z2000027) — 1000 Hazel Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dan Jewel and applicant Aaron Lubeck presented Z2000027 rezoning roughly one acre at 1000 Hazel Street from Industrial Light (IL) to Residential Urban-5(2) with a text-only development plan for single-family and duplex infill. Council approved the ordinance unanimously 7-0 by roll call.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change (Z1900029) — NCCU School of Business
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Michael Stock and NC Central University representatives Eric Davis and Deirdre McIntyre presented Z1900029 rezoning 19 parcels totaling 4.5 acres from RU-5/RU-5(2) to University and College (UC) with a development plan for the new NCCU School of Business. disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb 1, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Voluntary Annexation and Low-Density Extension at 4316 Trenton Road Near Leigh Farm Park (Item 17)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to annex 8.25 acres at 4316 Trenton Road for seven large single-family homes, with Charlie Reece dissenting over wetland sensitivity and encroaching on contiguous public conservation land.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve annexation and RS-20 zoning as appropriate low-density residential development next to existing city neighborhood and protected land.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel (00:49:03) noted the proposed seven-home layout represented low-density development suitable along the wet edge of Army Corps land and adjacent to existing Trenton subdivision homes.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny annexation of the wet, trail-crossed forested parcel bordered on nearly all sides by federal Army Corps land, County land, and Leigh Farm Park.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece (00:43:36) reported walking the property and argued that adding seven large expensive homes near Piedmont Wildlife Center and wet trail corridors did not justify bringing the parcel into the city.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and UEA passed 6-1 (Reece Nay); companion RS-20 zoning then passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Feb 1, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: 2720 Fawcett Avenue Annexation: Legacy Black Community Opposition & Cheek Road Safety vs. Proffers Over By-Right Development (Item 18)
disagreements.summary: Council deliberated over whether to approve a 320-unit PDR annexation with an offsite Merrick-Moore Elementary sidewalk, $40,000 Dedicated Housing Fund proffer, and $20,550 DPS proffer, or deny it in solidarity with Merrick-Moore residents over Cheek Road safety, flooding, and historical disinvestment.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prioritize Merrick-Moore residents' opposition, legacy Black neighborhood equity, flooding concerns, and unwalkable Cheek Road traffic safety—voting No even if by-right development proceeds.
side_a_arguments: DeDreana Freeman (03:19:20) and Mark-Anthony Middleton (03:05:47, 03:40:50) emphasized 50 years of redlining and infrastructure neglect in Merrick-Moore and insisted elected leaders heed the legacy community rather than impose unwanted density.
Pierce Freelon (03:23:45) credited community leaders like Bonita Green and noted by-right conservation rules at least preserve 50% tree canopy and reduce traffic.
Mayor Steve Schewel (03:43:20) distinguished unwalkable Cheek Road from Olive Branch Road and concluded extra traffic posed unacceptable safety risks.
disagreements.side_b_position: Note that denying rezoning cannot stop a 202-unit by-right county subdivision while forfeiting negotiated sidewalk, affordable housing, and school proffers.
side_b_arguments: Jillian Johnson (03:11:12) and Javiera Caballero warned that a by-right conservation subdivision would still add traffic without delivering the developer's proffered offsite sidewalk to Merrick-Moore Elementary or housing/DPS contributions, while housing supply remains vital to affordability.
disagreements.resolution: Despite voicing different frameworks during deliberation, all seven Council members—including Johnson and Caballero—voted Nay, defeating the annexation 0-7.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan 21, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the January 21, 2021 City Council Work Session, Council approved seven unanimous 7-0 roll-call votes—accepting City Manager and Clerk priority items, suspending rules and approving a $260,000 emergency Snow Hill Road pump-station rental supporting Corning's Operation Warp Speed COVID-19 vaccine vial production (Item 10), suspending rules and issuing the Duke Energy Green Source Advantage 20 MW solar RFP (Item 13), and settling the February 1 agenda. Council divided on two straw votes over Item 16, the City's revised Petition Process for street, water, sewer, and sidewalk assessments: Mayor Pro Tempore Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece backed Option 2's partial subsidies inside city limits (6-1), while Mayor Steve Schewel voted alone for Option 1's 100% full cost recovery to prevent wealthy petitioners from jumping the capital queue. On a companion straw poll defining 'actual cost' to include consultant design, inspection, and easement costs rather than construction alone, Schewel, Johnson, Caballero, Freelon, Freeman, and Middleton voted Aye while Charlie Reece abstained (6-0-1).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Priority Items (10, 13, 14, 16; Clerk Item 6), and Item 10 Emergency Lift Station Rental
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel convened the work session with all seven members present and noted the retirement of Finance Assistant Director Keith Herman. Council voted 7-0 to accept City Manager priority items (10, 13, 14, 16) and Clerk priority Item 6 (delaying Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee appointments two weeks to stagger terms), then voted 7-0 to suspend rules and 7-0 to approve Item 10's $260,000 Xylem Dewatering emergency rental ($219,821 Army reimbursement) supporting Corning COVID-19 vaccine vial manufacturing.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Executive Search Contract Review and Sanctuary Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Charlie Reece opened Item 14 by celebrating Pastor Jose Chicas leaving 3.5 years of church sanctuary following President Biden's deportation moratorium. Mark-Anthony Middleton and DeDreana Freeman requested the City Attorney verify Section 5 contract termination/fee provisions in case Council appoints an internal City Manager candidate.

agenda_items.title: Duke Energy Green Source Advantage 20 MW Municipal Solar RFP
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sustainability staff Paul Cameron, Angela Strickland, and General Services' Wendy Fleener presented a joint 30 MW utility-scale solar procurement (20 MW City, 10 MW County) projected at ~$10.6 million net cost over 20 years (~4 cents/kWh vs. ~10 cents for rooftop solar) to meet 80% renewable goals early. After DeDreana Freeman flagged public-notice trade-offs of expedited action, Council voted 7-0 to suspend rules and 7-0 to authorize issuing the RFP.

agenda_items.title: Petition Process Revisions for Street Paving, Water, Sewer, and Sidewalk Improvements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff Robert Joyner and Marvin Williams presented Option 1 (100% owner full cost recovery) vs. Option 2 (partial subsidy inside city limits: 100% streets, 75% water/sewer, $35/linear-foot Durham Walks sidewalk rate). After extended equity debate over 'line jumping' versus helping legacy city neighborhoods, Council chose Option 2 (limited to inside city limits) 6-1 by straw vote (Schewel Nay) and backed including design/engineering/easement overhead in the full-cost definition 6-0 with Charlie Reece abstaining.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council confirmed nominations for AHIC (Laura Beatty), DOST (Shihira Campbell), Planning Commission (Anthony McCEs), and Chanel Chambers to the Housing Appeals Board after a multi-round straw vote, then voted 7-0 to settle the February 1 Regular Meeting agenda (Consent 1-5, 7-9, 11-12, 14-16; Public Hearings 17-20) and adjourned at 3:19 PM.

votes.notes: Named straw poll (6-1): Schewel was the sole supporter of Option 1 (100% full cost recovery).
votes.discussion_detail: Straw poll selecting Option 2's partial city subsidies—restricted to parcels inside Durham city limits (with outside-city utility extensions paying full cost)—over Option 1's 100% owner-funded model.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan 21, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Partial Municipal Subsidy vs. 100% Property-Owner Cost Recovery in the Infrastructure Petition Process (Item 16)
disagreements.summary: Council debated Option 1 (100% full cost recovery) versus Option 2 (partial subsidy: 100% street paving, 75% water/sewer, and $35/foot Durham Walks sidewalks) for property-owner petitions, balancing equitable city investment in unserved city neighborhoods against wealthy petitioners cutting ahead of CIP priorities.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt Option 2 partial subsidies restricted strictly to properties inside Durham city limits, alongside true full-cost accounting.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Pierce Freelon, and Charlie Reece argued eliminating subsidies altogether would hurt lower-income in-city homeowners on legacy unimproved streets or septic systems while suburban county utility extensions should bear 100% cost.
disagreements.side_b_position: Adopt Option 1 (100% full cost recovery across the board) to prevent petitioned projects from diverting scarce public CIP funds.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel argued any city subsidy lets property owners who can afford upfront assessments jump ahead of the City's equitable street-paving and utility priority lists.
disagreements.resolution: Option 2 (inside city limits) prevailed 6-1 by straw vote, and Council voted 6-0-1 (Charlie Reece abstaining) to base assessments on full construction-plus-engineering/inspection/easement costs before advancing Item 16 to the February 1 Consent Agenda.
