meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 19, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the January 19, 2021 Regular City Council Meeting, Council presented a Key to the City to NC DHHS Secretary Dr. Mandy Cohen, issued MLK and National Day of Racial Healing proclamations, and passed nine unanimous 7-0 roll-call votes—adopting the Consent Agenda (highlighted by Item 5 expanding Durham's Non-Discrimination Ordinance after HB 142's sunset, Item 10 buying six Gillig electric buses, and Item 19 funding Recovery Innovations clinicians) alongside approvals for 1316 Page Road Townhomes (Item 22), NCGS 160D UDO alignment TC200004 (Item 23), The Forest at Duke Z2000012 (Item 24), and Corners at Brier Creek Townhomes South (Item 25). The meeting's lone contested roll-call vote occurred on the General Business Agenda over expanding the Bull City United Cure Violence program: Council voted 6-1 to fund full expansion across four census tracts (~$950,000-$1,000,000) rather than two tracts (~$350,000)—Ayes: Jillian Johnson, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece; Nay: Mayor Steve Schewel, who urged a two-tract expansion first to verify program fidelity and safeguard the pandemic budget.

agenda_items.title: Key to the City for Dr. Mandy Cohen, MLK and Racial Healing Proclamations, and Consent Agenda (incl. Non-Discrimination Ordinance)

Council members celebrated Item 5 expanding Durham's Non-Discrimination Ordinance following HB 142's sunset before unanimously passing Consent Items 1-21 (including six Gillig electric buses, DHA security lighting, and Recovery Innovations mental-health clinicians) 7-0 by roll call.

agenda_items.title: Expansion of Bull City United (Cure Violence) Program to Four Census Tracts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated whether to fund immediate expansion of the Bull City United violence-interruption program to all four recommended census tracts (~$950,000-$1,000,000) or limit initial city expansion to two tracts (~$350,000). disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 19, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Scale and Pacing of Bull City United (Cure Violence) Expansion: Four Tracts Immediately vs. Two Tracts First
disagreements.summary: Council divided 6-1 over whether to fund immediate expansion of Durham's Cure Violence violence-interruption program (Bull City United) across all four new census tracts (~$950,000-$1,000,000) or phase in two tracts (~$350,000) first.
disagreements.side_a_position: Fund immediate expansion across all four census tracts to meet urgent gun-violence levels citywide.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, and Charlie Reece argued surging shooting victims demand investing fully in community-based violence interruption across all four high-need tracts right away.
Javiera Caballero expressed fiscal reservations about pandemic budget constraints (01:07:23) but joined the Aye majority.
disagreements.side_b_position: Begin by funding two additional tracts (~$350,000) to verify program fidelity and preserve budget capacity amid pandemic uncertainty.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel (01:18:31) argued expanding to two tracts first (or pairing with County cost-sharing on a third) would protect multi-year budget stability and allow evaluation of Cure Violence model fidelity before scaling further.
disagreements.resolution: Motion to fund full 4-tract expansion passed 6-1 by roll call (Mayor Schewel cast the sole Nay).

meetings.title: Special Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Jan 15, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel presided over the January 15, 2021 special virtual meeting with all seven council members present to select an executive search firm for Durham's next City Manager from two finalists out of 11 RFP respondents. Developmental Associates (Dr. Steven Strauss, Joe Durham, and Janice Allen Jackson) presented a local, competency-based recruitment process featuring a two-day virtual assessment center, structured NeoGov comparisons, emotional intelligence testing, and executive coaching, while The Mercer Group (Ellis Hankins) emphasized a 14-state national network, candidate phone vetting, a two-tier slate, and an optional management style inventory without an assessment center. During council deliberation, an informal straw poll initially drew five hands for Developmental Associates (Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Pierce Freelon, and Charlie Reece) while Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman held back—with Caballero citing national reach and concerns over external assessors—before staff clarified internal interview panels could participate and Council converged on a unanimous 7-0 informal recommendation for Developmental Associates (formal contract deferred to the January 21 work session). Before adjourning, Mayor Schewel also shared an update from NC DHHS Secretary Mandy Cohen's staff that the state would partner with Durham County and Duke on multiple high-throughput COVID-19 vaccination sites including Southern High School, with 10,000 doses expected the following week.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Search Firm Selection Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the special virtual meeting to order at 2:00 p.m. for the sole purpose of interviewing two finalist search firms for the City Manager recruitment, with all seven seated council members answering roll call. Staff representatives Ms. Youngblood and Jim O'Donnell explained that Council had evaluated 11 proposals to select the top two firms, each allotted 30 minutes to present and 15 minutes for questions.

agenda_items.title: Search Firm Presentation and Q&A: Developmental Associates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Steven Strauss, Joe Durham, and Janice Allen Jackson presented Developmental Associates' Durham-based local government recruitment model, detailing stakeholder job analysis (including former manager Tom Bonfield), targeted diversity outreach via NFBPA and Emerging Local Government Leaders, structured NeoGov applications, video/written screening for up to 15 candidates, a two-day virtual Assessment Center with external and community assessors, emotional intelligence testing for five finalists, and executive coaching. Council Members Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Mayor Steve Schewel questioned the team on city manager placement volume (at least 50 managers/assistant managers), national reach, assessor and applicant diversity (citing five African-American managers placed in North Carolina over two years), and virtual community engagement during COVID-19.

agenda_items.title: Search Firm Presentation and Q&A: The Mercer Group
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Mercer Group Senior Vice President Ellis Hankins (who disclosed his Wake County appointment to the RDU Airport Authority Board and leading the Charlotte City Attorney search that hired Patrick Baker) outlined his firm's 14-state partner network, 6-week advertising window, intensive phone vetting, background checks, two-tier candidate slate in mid-April, optional Teleometrics management style inventory, and $24,500 fee plus up to $5,500 in expenses. Council Members Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Mayor Steve Schewel probed why Mercer omitted an assessment center for city managers, how the firm mitigates bias without standardized competency exercises, leadership team demographics, and how an out-of-state network would conduct authentic local engagement.

agenda_items.title: Council Deliberation and Informal Recommendation for City Manager Search Firm
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council weighed Developmental Associates' competency-based assessment center and track record placing Black leaders and Durham executives (including the Police Chief, Fire Chief, and Deputy City Manager) against The Mercer Group's national reach and council/staff-centered interviews. After an initial informal straw poll showed five members favoring Developmental Associates and Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman undecided, Jim O'Donnell clarified that internal panels including former manager Tom Bonfield and deputy city managers had participated in past assessment centers, prompting Caballero and Freeman to join a unanimous 7-0 informal recommendation for Developmental Associates ahead of formal contract action at the January 21 work session.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Informal 7-0 unanimous recommendation (No formal vote)

agenda_items.title: MLK Jr. Holiday Remarks, Key to the City Announcement, and COVID-19 Vaccination Sites Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a brief tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s birthday, Mayor Steve Schewel announced he would present a Key to the City to NC DHHS Secretary Mandy Cohen on Tuesday night. Schewel also reported on a morning briefing with Secretary Cohen's staff (joined by County Commission Chair Brenda Howerton), noting that instead of a single mass vaccination facility, the state, Durham County, and Duke would operate several high-throughput sites including Southern High School, with 10,000 vaccine doses expected the following week before adjourning at 4:19 p.m.

disagreements.meeting_title: Special Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Jan 15, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Selection of City Manager Executive Search Firm and Assessment Center Methodology
disagreements.summary: Council members initially split in deliberation and an informal straw poll over whether to select Developmental Associates' assessment-center model or The Mercer Group's traditional interview-based national search approach before converging unanimously on Developmental Associates.
disagreements.side_a_position: Select Developmental Associates for its competency-based virtual assessment center, bias-mitigating rubric, diversity placement record, and fit for modern Durham.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued that assessment centers test real-world competencies beyond interviews and that Durham needed a contemporary rubric rather than repeating the 12-year-old Mercer process used to hire Tom Bonfield.

Mayor Steve Schewel cited Durham's national profile to attract candidates regardless of firm and praised Developmental Associates' record placing African-American leaders as well as Durham's Police Chief, Fire Chief, and Deputy City Manager.
disagreements.side_b_position: Initially leaned toward or felt torn about The Mercer Group due to national reach and concern that Developmental Associates' external assessors excluded internal staff and council from early screening.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero favored Mercer on national reach and expressed reticence that Developmental Associates' assessment center delegated candidate evaluation to external assessors rather than internal city staff and council.
DeDreana Freeman noted that while Developmental Associates scored higher in her initial ranking, Ellis Hankins's presentation made Mercer compelling for Durham's needs, leaving her torn.
disagreements.resolution: After Jim O'Donnell clarified at 02:11:27 that internal interview panels (including Tom Bonfield and deputy city managers) had participated in prior Developmental Associates assessment centers, and an initial 5-0-2 straw poll at 02:12:40, both Caballero and Freeman agreed to move forward with Developmental Associates for a 7-0 unanimous informal recommendation (formal contract placed on the January 21 work session agenda).

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the January 7, 2021 Durham City Council work session—held one day after the attack on the U.S. Capitol—Mayor Steve Schewel and all six colleagues opened with reflections on democracy, Georgia's Senate runoff turnout, COVID-19 vaccine expansion to Group 1b, and a new privately funded Guaranteed Income pilot led by Council Members Mark-Anthony Middleton and Pierce Freelon through Mayors for a Guaranteed Income. Council unanimously adopted the City Manager's priority items (7-0) and voted 7-0 twice to suspend the rules and approve an expedited revised utility extension agreement with Corning Incorporated and Durham County (Item 20) to support COVID-19 vaccine vial manufacturing, reimbursed up to $460,380 via an Army Corps of Engineers grant. In pulled consent and presentation discussions, members clashed sharply over 24/7 Durham Housing Authority security cameras versus ShotSpotter gunshot sensors (Item 15), reviewed RTI International's initial Phase 1 analysis of three years of 911 calls for service (Item 21), and debated expanding Bull City United to two versus four census tracts (Item 6), with Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece, and DeDreana Freeman backing immediate four-tract expansion (~$900K+) over Mayor Schewel's budget caution favoring staff's two-tract recommendation. Council also reviewed the draft Non-Discrimination Ordinance (Item 5) following HB 142's sunset and unanimously voted 7-0 to settle the January 19, 2021 council meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Capitol Attack Reflections, Vaccine Update, and Guaranteed Income Pilot Announcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the 1:00 p.m. virtual work session to order with all seven council members present. Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Charlie Reece reflected on the January 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol and Georgia's Senate runoff election, while Reece highlighted Duke Health and UNC Health opening COVID-19 vaccines to Group 1b (ages 75+). Mayor Schewel then announced Durham's pursuit of a privately funded Guaranteed Income pilot (~March timeline) through Mayors for a Guaranteed Income (supported by Jack Dorsey funds), spearheaded by Middleton and Freelon with staff and Duke's Samuel DuBois Cook Center.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items Acceptance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim City Manager Wanda Page presented priority updates, requesting rule suspension for an expedited vote on Item 20 (Corning Phase 2 utility extension for COVID-19 vaccine vial manufacturing, reimbursed up to $460,380 via an Army Corps of Engineers grant) along with updated attachments for Items 5, 6, 10 (six Gillig electric buses), and 20. Council voted 7-0 by roll call to accept the priority items.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review and Expedited Approval of Item 20 (Corning Phase 2 Utility Extension Agreement)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the administrative consent agenda (Items 1–20), during which Jillian Johnson pulled Item 5 (Non-Discrimination Ordinance) and Mark-Anthony Middleton pulled Item 15 (DHA security cameras/lighting ILA) for discussion. Acting on Item 20 immediately due to its federal COVID-19 vaccine supply-chain designation, Council unanimously voted 7-0 to suspend the rules and then voted 7-0 to authorize the City Manager to enter into the revised utility extension agreement with Corning Incorporated and Durham County for water and sanitary sewer service to Corning Phase 2.

agenda_items.title: Item 15: Amendment to Interlocal Agreement with Durham Housing Authority for Security Cameras and Lighting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services staffer Logan Small confirmed that the participatory-budgeting cameras at three DHA complexes operate 24/7 near front entrances and public areas, recording continuously over older footage. Mark-Anthony Middleton sharply criticized the city for funding constant 24/7 video surveillance in Black and brown public housing communities while rejecting ShotSpotter gunshot sensors that activate only on gunfire; Pierce Freelon argued residents requested cameras whereas ShotSpotter automatically triggers armed police responses with high false-positive rates, while DeDreana Freeman expressed openness to a free ShotSpotter trial.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Kept on consent for Jan 19

agenda_items.title: Item 21: 911 First Responder Calls for Service Evaluation Update and Initial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant Budget Director Monica Croskey-Toepfer and RTI International researchers Brian Aagaard and Dr. Renee Mitchell presented Phase 1 findings from three years of Durham Police Department Computer-Aided Dispatch (CAD) data, showing directed patrols and general assistance made up over half of calls, traffic-related calls represented 7.2% of calls (13% of officer time, 99.93% with no arrest), acute mental health calls represented ~1% of calls (2.5% of officer time), and violent crime under 1%. With Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson presiding temporarily for one hour, council members probed mental health versus quality-of-life coding (~7% combined), data visualization, racial/spatial bias mapping, and whether unarmed or co-responder pilots (such as Eugene's CAHOOTS) can safely handle escalating calls ahead of the budget retreat.

agenda_items.title: Item 6: Expansion of Bull City United (Cure Violence Model)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant to the City Manager Karmisha Wallace, Durham County General Manager Joanne Pierce, and Interim City Manager Wanda Page reviewed Cure Violence outcomes (a 1.78% violent crime drop in target census tracts 13.01 and 14.00 from Oct 2013–Sept 2019 compared to a 16.49% citywide rise) and presented three expansion tiers targeting 820 shooting incidents (Oct 2019–Sept 2020): 1 tract, staff-recommended 2 tracts (13.04 and 17.09; 7 FTEs), or 4 tracts (18 FTEs; under $1 million). Despite Mayor Schewel's concern over adding recurring obligations outside the budget cycle amid a severe FY 2021–22 budget shortfall, a five-member majority (Johnson, Freelon, Middleton, Reece, and Freeman, with Javiera Caballero willing to join the majority) signaled support for four-tract expansion phased via actual-expense county ILA billing, placing the item on the Jan 19 General Business Agenda.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Placed on Jan 19 General Business Agenda

agenda_items.title: Item 5: Non-Discrimination Ordinance (NDO) Draft Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Attorney Kim Rehberg and Senior Assistant City Attorney Krista Cucurullo presented the draft Non-Discrimination Ordinance enabled by the December 1, 2020 sunset of HB 142's local moratorium, extending protections in employment and public accommodations to military status, sexual orientation, gender identity, and protected hairstyles (CROWN Act), modernizing disability terminology, and assigning enforcement to Neighborhood Improvement Services and the Human Relations Commission subcommittee with a proposed July 1, 2021 effective date. Council members unanimously endorsed the ordinance and signaled willingness to fund enforcement capacity in the budget while directing Rehberg and Interim City Manager Page to refine placeholder enforcement/effective-date language before placing it back on the Jan 19 consent agenda.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Returned to consent for Jan 19

agenda_items.title: Board/Commission Appointments and Settling the January 19, 2021 Council Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced council nominations/actions for the Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners (Pebble Lucas), re-advertising the Durham Workers Rights Commission, and the Human Relations Commission (Maria Solis-Guzman and Stacey D. White-Knight). Interim City Manager Wanda Page then presented the proposed January 19, 2021 agenda (Consent Items 1–5 and 7–19; General Business Item 6; Public Hearings 22–25), which Council unanimously approved 7-0 before adjourning at 4:36 p.m.

votes.item_title: Acceptance of City Manager's Priority Items
votes.notes: Unanimous roll call vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted Interim City Manager Wanda Page's priority additions and revisions, including requesting rule suspension for Item 20 (Corning Phase 2) and updated attachments for Items 5, 6, 10, and 20.

votes.item_title: Suspend the Rules to Vote on Item 20 (Corning Phase 2 Utility Extension Agreement)
votes.notes: Unanimous roll call vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted to suspend work-session rules to take immediate action on Item 20 because Corning's vial manufacturing facility was designated a critical federal COVID-19 vaccination component.

votes.item_title: Item 20: Revised Utility Extension Agreement with Corning Incorporated and Durham County (Corning Phase 2)
votes.notes: Expedited unanimous vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Authorized the City Manager to enter into a revised utility extension agreement with Corning Incorporated and Durham County to extend water and sanitary sewer service to Corning Phase 2, with Corning reimbursing Durham up to $460,380 via an Army Corps of Engineers grant.

votes.item_title: Settle the January 19, 2021 City Council Meeting Agenda
votes.notes: Clerk roll call omitted 'Freelon' in ASR text (rendering 'Freeman' twice in sequence) between Caballero and Middleton; all seven seated members voted Aye.
votes.discussion_detail: Settled the January 19, 2021 regular council meeting agenda with Consent Items 1–5 and 7–19, General Business Item 6 (Bull City United expansion), and Public Hearings 22–25.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Durham Housing Authority 24/7 Security Cameras vs. ShotSpotter Gunshot Detection Surveillance
disagreements.summary: During discussion of pulled Item 15 (ILA with DHA for security cameras and lighting funded via Participatory Budgeting), council members clashed over privacy, community consent, and hypocrisy in rejecting ShotSpotter acoustic sensors while installing always-on surveillance cameras in public housing.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approving 24/7 cameras in Black and brown public housing complexes while rejecting ShotSpotter sensors is inconsistent, and ShotSpotter merits reconsideration or a free trial.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton argued 24/7 cameras capture innocent daily life constantly, whereas ShotSpotter sensors stay dormant until gunfire triggers them to dispatch help to shooting locations.

Middleton contended that participatory budgeting demographics (citing 60% white voter figures) and community pleas against gun violence contradict anti-ShotSpotter surveillance critiques; DeDreana Freeman stated she was open to considering a free ShotSpotter trial.
disagreements.side_b_position: Security cameras requested by public housing residents differ fundamentally from ShotSpotter because cameras do not automatically dispatch armed police to loud noises.
side_b_arguments: Pierce Freelon reported that residents he canvassed at Oxford Manor specifically asked for working security cameras while expressing apprehension about ShotSpotter.

Freelon argued ShotSpotter automatically dispatches armed police to loud noises—citing Charlotte data where only a small fraction of alerts yielded gunfire evidence—creating distinct escalation risks compared to passive camera footage.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Item 15 remained on the January 19 consent agenda while members continued debating gun-violence technology options.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Jan 7, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Scale of Bull City United Expansion (2 Census Tracts vs. 4 Census Tracts)
disagreements.summary: Council divided over whether to adopt the City Manager's recommendation to expand Bull City United to two additional census tracts (7 FTEs) now and reassess during budget season, or commit immediately to all four high-shooting census tracts (18 FTEs, under $1 million).
disagreements.side_a_position: Expand Bull City United immediately to all four additional census tracts (18 FTEs) as an urgent investment to curb record gun violence.
side_a_arguments: Jillian Johnson, Pierce Freelon, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Charlie Reece, and DeDreana Freeman argued that under $1 million is modest relative to a ~$70 million police budget and essential to save lives across all four impacted communities.

Middleton and Interim City Manager Wanda Page noted that under the county interlocal agreement, actual costs would phase in gradually as Durham County hires and onboards staff rather than requiring an immediate lump-sum payout.
disagreements.side_b_position: Fund the staff-recommended two-tract expansion now and evaluate the remaining two tracts (~$600,000 extra) during the FY 2021–22 budget cycle.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Steve Schewel warned of a severe projected recurring budget shortfall and argued council should preserve room in the regular budget cycle to fund employee raises and avoid layoffs.
Javiera Caballero voiced deep anxiety over the upcoming budget deficit while indicating she would support either two or four tracts and defer to the council majority.
disagreements.resolution: Item 6 was placed on the January 19, 2021 General Business Agenda so a council majority could move for the four-tract expansion.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At the January 4, 2021 virtual Durham City Council meeting, Mayor Steve Schewel proclaimed January 2021 National Mentoring Month and Council unanimously approved the consent agenda (7-0), including bicycle/pedestrian municipal agreements, street and sidewalk contracts, and the Gang Reduction Strategy interlocal agreement. Following the statutory FY 2021–22 HUD Annual Action Plan public hearing (Item 22)—where staff agreed to add an intermediate March public hearing and prioritize community outreach—Council approved three unanimous 7-0 economic development incentives: $140,000 for Bookman Commercial Holdings LLC (Checkers franchise on Fayetteville Street, Item 23), $75,000 for The Clorox Company's Burt's Bees/Better Health expansion (Item 25), and $150,000 for Nuvotronics, Inc.'s 5G manufacturing expansion (Item 26), despite Council Member Charlie Reece's sharp criticism of state-mandated corporate JDIG matches as a 'race to the bottom.' On Item 24, a $102,000 neighborhood revitalization grant for Ideal Sandwich Shop LLC (2108 Angier Avenue), Council split 4-3—with Mayor Steve Schewel, Javiera Caballero, Pierce Freelon, and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting Aye to back the small Old East Durham bodega/sandwich shop startup, and Jillian Johnson, DeDreana Freeman, and Charlie Reece voting Nay over its $11/hour starting wage (below Durham's ~$15.68 living wage), steep 2:1 public match, and neighborhood gentrification and outreach concerns.

agenda_items.title: National Mentoring Month Proclamation, Council Announcements, and Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel read a proclamation designating January 2021 as National Mentoring Month (submitted by DeWarren Langley) and congratulated Mark-Anthony Middleton on his feature in the NC League of Municipalities' Southern Cities magazine. Interim City Manager Wanda Page noted an additional attachment on Item 13 (Gang Reduction Strategy interlocal agreement), and Council voted 7-0 by roll call to approve the consent agenda (Items 1–3, 6, and 8–18, covering board appointments, C-MAC bike/wayfinding agreements, employment training grants, street/sidewalk/sewer contracts, and a Merck utility extension).

agenda_items.title: Item 22: FY 2021–2022 Annual Action Plan Needs Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Wilma Conyers opened the first statutory HUD public hearing covering anticipated FY 2021–22 allocations (~$2M CDBG, ~$1.1M HOME, ~$174K ESG, ~$483K HOPWA). Speakers Larissa Seibel (Durham People's Alliance), Stella Adams, and Marie Faison urged prioritizing eviction prevention, legal aid, direct rental assistance, home repairs, and MWBE/Section 3 contracting, and requested a second interim hearing around March 1 before the April/May draft deadline; Johnson agreed to add an intermediate public hearing and Javiera Caballero requested Spanish interpretation. Separately, Charlie Reece highlighted Pierce Freelon's children's album 'D.A.D.' after three white Grammy nominees withdrew to protest the lack of BIPOC nominees.

agenda_items.title: Item 23: Public Hearing and Economic Development Incentive — Bookman Commercial Holdings LLC ($140,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD staff member Chris Dickey and Director Andre Pettigrew presented a $140,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant (~$1.4M total project, ~9:1 private-to-public leverage) to demolish an underutilized building (the historic Notebook Store site) at 2520 Fayetteville Street and open a Checkers franchise creating 30 jobs near NCCU. Owner Dobbin Bookman (continuing the 70-year McLaughlin/Bookman family legacy) and Stella Adams spoke in support; following questions on employee health benefits, COVID protocols, neighborhood heritage, and formalizing OEWD's project scorecard, Council approved the incentive 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 24: Public Hearing and Economic Development Incentive — Ideal Sandwich Shop LLC ($102,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chris Dickey presented a $102,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant ($335,000 total project, ~2:1 match) for owner Ian Bracken and partner Paul Treika to renovate a blighted 1940s building at 2108 Angier Avenue in Old East Durham into a 930-square-foot sandwich shop and small grocery/bodega offering $5–$6 sandwiches, SNAP acceptance, and a rooftop garden with the Durham Children's Initiative. Council divided sharply over Bracken's $11/hour plus tips starting wage (below Durham's ~$15.68/hour living wage), the 2:1 public match, omitted community support letters, and East Durham gentrification concerns; after Middleton declined Freelon's proposed friendly amendment to delay one cycle, Council approved the grant 4-3 (Schewel, Caballero, Freelon, Middleton Aye; Johnson, Freeman, Reece Nay).

agenda_items.title: Item 25: Public Hearing and Economic Development Incentive — The Clorox Company ($75,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD's Adria Graham Scott, Greater Durham Chamber CEO Geoff Durham, Burt's Bees/Clorox representative Matt Kopac, Brian Fox, and Durham County's Andrew Miracle presented a $75,000 performance-based local incentive matching a state JDIG grant for Clorox's $7.5M investment and 158 new jobs (including ~60 IT roles and a new R&D facility) expected to yield over $156,000 in city tax revenue within five years. After Charlie Reece criticized subsidizing a $25B+ corporation as a state-driven 'race to the bottom'—and staff confirmed the local match was legally required for Tier 3 county JDIG eligibility and included living-wage and health-insurance mandates—Council approved the agreement 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 26: Public Hearing and Economic Development Incentive — Nuvotronics, Inc. ($150,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Adria Graham Scott, Geoff Durham, and Nuvotronics representative Martin Amen presented a $150,000 performance-based local incentive paired with a state JDIG award to expand Nuvotronics' 5G PolyStrata microelectronics manufacturing in Durham, investing $50M and creating 150 jobs. Charlie Reece reiterated his objection to corporate subsidies for a firm acquired by ~$2B Cubic Corporation before casting a reluctant Aye vote, and Council approved the agreement 7-0 before adjourning at 9:59 p.m.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Public Incentive for Ideal Sandwich Shop LLC Without Guaranteed Living Wage and Additional Community Outreach (Item 24)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 over whether to approve a $102,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant for Ideal Sandwich Shop LLC in Old East Durham given its $11/hour base starting wage, 2:1 public match ratio, and limited neighborhood resident outreach.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the $102,000 incentive now to revitalize a blighted Angier Avenue corner, expand affordable fresh food access, and give a small restaurant startup room to scale up to a living wage.
side_a_arguments: Mark-Anthony Middleton and Pierce Freelon argued small neighborhood startups cannot afford $15+/hour on day one without pricing out low-income residents, comparing Ideal's trajectory to local restaurants like Monuts and Copa.

Mayor Steve Schewel noted Council had just unanimously approved Checkers (whose fast-food wages fall below $15.68/hour) and argued keeping $5 sandwiches affordable alongside a $15.68 starting wage is economically unviable at launch.
Javiera Caballero highlighted small-business generosity to Durham schools and the feasibility of scaling wages over 3–4 years.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose or delay the $102,000 public subsidy due to sub-living-wage jobs, the high 2:1 public match ratio, gentrification risks, and unverified resident engagement.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson and Charlie Reece argued public tax dollars during a pandemic fiscal crunch should not subsidize $11/hour jobs below Durham's ~$15.68/hour living wage.

DeDreana Freeman flagged the steep 2:1 public match (compared to Checkers' 9:1), the omission of community support letters from the packet, and gentrification pressures along the Angier-Driver corridor, requesting a one-cycle delay.
Reece noted the referenced support letters came from adjacent business owners with commercial interests rather than neighborhood residents.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 4-3 on roll call at 02:11:28 (Schewel, Caballero, Freelon, Middleton Aye; Johnson, Freeman, Reece Nay) after Middleton declined Freelon's proposed friendly amendment to delay.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Jan 4, 2021 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: State-Required Local Incentives for Large Corporations Under JDIG (Items 25 and 26)
disagreements.summary: During public hearings on incentives for The Clorox Company ($75,000) and Nuvotronics, Inc. ($150,000), Council Member Charlie Reece challenged the premise of awarding public subsidies to multi-billion-dollar corporations while staff and the Mayor noted state law mandated local matching funds.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the $75,000 Clorox and $150,000 Nuvotronics incentives because state JDIG rules require local participation and the projects yield strong ROI, workforce partnerships, and diversity commitments.
side_a_arguments: OEWD Director Andre Pettigrew, Adria Graham Scott, and Durham County's Andrew Miracle confirmed Tier 3 counties like Durham must contribute qualifying local matches for JDIG awards, with Clorox projected to return over $156,000 in city tax revenue within five years.
Staff emphasized both deals are performance-based, exceed living-wage and health-insurance standards, and include workforce pipelines with Durham Public Schools, Durham Tech, NCCU, and NCWorks.
disagreements.side_b_position: Condemn JDIG local-match mandates as a corporate 'race to the bottom' that forces cities to subsidize multi-billion-dollar firms that do not financially need local funds, while reluctantly voting Aye so projects do not leave Durham.
side_b_arguments: Charlie Reece cited Clorox's $25.27 billion market capitalization and Cubic Corporation's ~$2 billion market cap (Nuvotronics' parent), arguing neither company needs $75,000 or $150,000 from Durham taxpayers.
Reece called on state or federal action to end inter-state corporate incentive competition while voting Aye solely because state law conditioned the JDIG deals on Durham's match.
disagreements.resolution: Both incentives passed 7-0 on roll call (Item 25 at 02:42:49; Item 26 at 02:53:07), with Mayor Schewel also advising staff to include full wage and benefit verification publicly in future packets rather than only in closed session.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Work Session Dec 22, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting virtually on December 22, 2020 for its final work session of the year, all seven Durham City Council members unanimously approved 7-0 the City Manager's priority items requesting suspension of the rules to act on a COVID-19 temporary outdoor seating extension and a cold-weather White Flag emergency shelter contract with Open Table Ministry Inc. Council heard a Citizen's Matter from Stella Adams critiquing low Small Local Business Enterprise (SLBE) participation under City Code Section 18-86 and urging stronger supplier diversity for Black-owned and minority/women-owned firms. During a presentation on City Contractor Workforce Diversity, staff and the City Attorney explained legal limits under Equal Business Opportunity Program (EBOP) rules while introducing a workforce diversity questionnaire usable in RFP scoring; DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton urged pushing beyond narrow legalistic diversity checks toward broader equity integration, while Steve Schewel praised incorporating workforce diversity into RFP scoring. Following a tie-breaking appointment vote by Mayor Schewel for Mr. Harro and consensus to re-advertise an RDU Airport Authority seat, Council unanimously voted 7-0 to settle the upcoming regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Year-End Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel called the special Tuesday work session to order at 1:00 p.m., and the clerk confirmed all seven council members were present virtually. Council Member Charlie Reece noted this was the final council meeting of 2020, and members exchanged holiday remarks while noting upcoming January Joint City-County and workforce meeting conflicts.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items (Outdoor Dining Extension, White Flag Shelter, Streets, and Citizen's Matter)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager requested suspending the rules to vote on Item 5 (extending the July 1, 2020 temporary outdoor dining ordinance until the COVID-19 state of emergency ends) and Item 7 (Open Table Ministry Inc. White Flag cold-weather emergency shelter contract set to expire December 31). She also noted attachment updates for Item 14 (Contract ST-286 Petition Streets 2021), Item 19 (COVID-19 update scheduled at 1:15 p.m.), and Item 27 (Stella Adams Citizen's Matter). Council voted unanimously 7-0 to support the manager's priority items.

agenda_items.title: Administrative Consent Items and Pulled Items Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel reviewed the administrative consent slate, noting Items 5 and 7 were set aside for rule suspension and same-day action, Item 27 would be heard immediately as a Citizen's Matter, and Items 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, and 16 were pulled for discussion. Presentations and public hearings for the upcoming cycle (including FY21-22 Annual Action Plan needs and economic development incentives) were also previewed.

agenda_items.title: Citizens' Matters — Stella Adams on Small Local Business Enterprise (SLBE) Procurement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Stella Adams addressed Council regarding the November bid report, asserting that nearly all listed contracts fell outside the Small Local Business Enterprise (SLBE) program in violation of City Code Section 18-86. She urged Durham to strengthen supplier diversity, support local Black-owned and minority/women-owned enterprises, and partner with trusted financial institutions to leverage transit, CDBG, HOME, and affordable housing bond dollars.

agenda_items.title: Presentation — City Contractor Workforce Diversity and RFP Scoring
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance, Equity and Inclusion, and City Attorney staff briefed Council on distinguishing business-ownership disparity goals under the EBOP/UBE/MWBE ordinance from contractor workforce diversity and EEO-4/E104 reporting. Staff proposed a mandatory workforce diversity questionnaire for RFPs allowing non-responsive bids to be rejected and enabling workforce diversity to be scored in RFPs for the first time. Council Member DeDreana Freeman argued the city should press statutory authority and examine all construction, repair, and purchase contracts for equity and inclusion, Mark-Anthony Middleton urged connecting the effort to the Shared Economic Prosperity Plan and Built to Last, and Mayor Steve Schewel commended staff for operationalizing workforce diversity in RFP scoring.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Appointments Tie-Break and Settling the Regular Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported a tie on a board appointment, which Mayor Schewel broke in favor of Mr. Harro, and noted council consensus to re-advertise the Raleigh-Durham Airport Authority seat. The City Manager then presented the settled Consent Agenda (Items 1-4, 6, and 8-18) and General Business public hearings (Items 22-26), which Council approved unanimously 7-0 before wishing everyone happy holidays.

votes.item_title: Support City Manager's Priority Items (Items 5, 7, 14, 19, and 27)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Jillian Johnson seconded supporting the City Manager's priority items, including the request to suspend rules for same-day votes on temporary outdoor dining (Item 5) and White Flag cold-weather shelter (Item 7). The clerk called the roll and the motion passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Settle Upcoming Regular Meeting Agenda (Consent Items 1-4, 6, 8-18; GBA Public Hearings Items 22-26)
votes.discussion_detail: Following the City Manager's recommendation placing Items 1-4, 6, and 8-18 on Consent and Items 22-26 on the General Business public hearing agenda, Pierce Freelon moved and Charlie Reece seconded approving the agenda. All seven members voted Aye on roll call.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Work Session Dec 22, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Scope and Legal Caution in City Contractor Workforce Diversity Procurement Policy
disagreements.summary: During the Finance and City Attorney presentation on contractor workforce diversity, Council members diverged over whether Durham should focus on legally defensible RFP scoring questionnaires or aggressively test statutory limits across all purchase, construction, and repair contracts to advance equity and inclusion.
disagreements.side_a_position: Push beyond narrow diversity snapshots and legal risk avoidance by questioning all contractors—including construction, repair, and purchase bidders—and tying procurement to broader equity initiatives.
side_a_arguments: Focusing only on diversity rather than equity and inclusion perpetuates historical inequities in city spending.
The city should investigate hiring practices across all contract categories and push statutory authority rather than smoothing over issues to avoid lawsuits.
Workforce diversity efforts should be integrated with the Shared Economic Prosperity Plan and Built to Last rather than run on a separate finance track.
disagreements.side_b_position: Advance a legally defensible workforce diversity questionnaire usable as an RFP scoring criterion without losing sight of existing legal constraints.
side_b_arguments: Systematizing workforce diversity as an actual scoring factor in RFPs is a historic first for Durham within state legal constraints.
Progress made through the EBOP ordinance and legally defensible RFP scoring should not be lost while pursuing broader goals.
disagreements.resolution: Informational work session briefing; no formal vote was taken on the procurement policy.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Dec 21, 2020 (full meeting)
meetings.executive_summary: Convening virtually on December 21, 2020 with all seven members present, the Durham City Council opened with reflections on the pandemic and federal COVID-19 relief legislation before unanimously passing the Consent Agenda 7-0 (excluding Item 1, which Mayor Steve Schewel pulled). The Consent Agenda approved GoTriangle commuter rail technical service reimbursements, water facility and paving contracts, police and automated refuse vehicles, a Blue Benevolence grant, a DOJ Sexual Assault Kit Initiative (SAKI) grant, and a Duke University fiber-optic network agreement for Durham Housing Authority campuses. Following a closed-captioner break and public hearing on Item 22, Council unanimously voted 7-0 across four roll-call motions to annex 4115 Angier Avenue, enter a utility extension agreement, amend the Future Land Use Map to Low-Medium Density Residential, adopt a consistency statement, and amend the UDO. At the close of the meeting, Council agreed by unanimous consent to refer pulled Item 1 (a mayoral appointment to the RDU Airport Authority) back to Mayor Schewel.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, W.H. Auden Reading, Moment of Silence, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel read an excerpt from W.H. Auden's 'September 1, 1939' before leading a moment of silence, Charlie Reece led the Pledge of Allegiance, and all seven members answered roll call. Council announcements addressed COVID-19 vaccine equity (declining to jump the line ahead of service and frontline workers), the pending federal COVID-19 relief package including transit, rental aid, and Save Our Stages funds, and local restaurants offering outdoor/to-go cocktail service under the governor's order.

agenda_items.title: City Manager, City Attorney, and City Clerk Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager reported attachment and motion updates for Item 5 (water facility expansion design services with Stantec Architecture), Item 6 (Williams Water Treatment Plant paving award), and four consolidated annexations: Item 19 (Carrington Woods 2), Item 20 (924 Old Oxford Road), Item 21 (551 Olive Branch Road), and Item 22 (4115 Angier Avenue). The City Attorney had no priority items, and the City Clerk confirmed the social media livestream was operating.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Excluding Pulled Item 1)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel pulled Item 1 (Raleigh-Durham Airport Authority mayoral reappointment) and read the remaining consent items covering Safety and Wellness Task Force appointments, the Workers' Bill of Rights discussion, GoTriangle commuter rail technical services reimbursement, water management design and paving contracts, refuse and police patrol vehicles, pest and elevator contracts, employment and training grants, the 2020 Blue Benevolence and DOJ SAKI grants, and a Duke University fiber-optic network agreement for DHA campuses. Council approved the Consent Agenda unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — Consolidated Annexation, FLUM Amendment, and Rezoning for 4115 Angier Avenue
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After a brief pause to give closed captioners a break, Council resumed the public hearing for 4115 Angier Avenue and heard from four speakers (Nate Bueller, Bob Mishler, Patrick Byker, and Jamal Levonne). Council Member Charlie Reece noted the applicant's engagement with Planning Commission concerns and contrasted the site favorably against the environmental concerns at Olive Branch, while DeDreana Freeman noted traffic and pedestrian safety concerns. Council approved annexation/utility extension, Future Land Use Map amendment to Low-Medium Density Residential, consistency statement, and UDO amendment across four unanimous 7-0 roll-call votes.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Item 1 — Raleigh-Durham Airport Authority Mayoral Appointment Referral
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel consulted the City Attorney on procedural handling of pulled Item 1, a mayoral appointment to the RDU Airport Authority requiring council concurrence. On the City Attorney's parliamentary guidance, Council agreed by unanimous consent (thumbs up without a formal roll-call vote) to refer Item 1 back to the Mayor.

votes.item_title: Item 22 — Adopt Ordinance Annexing 4115 Angier Avenue and Authorizing Utility Extension Agreement
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Charlie Reece seconded adopting the ordinance annexing 4115 Angier Avenue into the city and authorizing the City Manager to enter into a utility extension agreement. The clerk called the roll and recorded 7 Ayes.

votes.item_title: Item 22 — Adopt Resolution Amending Future Land Use Map to Low-Medium Density Residential (4115 Angier Avenue)
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Mark-Anthony Middleton seconded adopting a resolution amending the Future Land Use Map for 4115 Angier Avenue to Low-Medium Density Residential. The motion passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 22 — Adopt Consistency Statement for 4115 Angier Avenue
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Jillian Johnson seconded adopting the statutory consistency statement for the 4115 Angier Avenue rezoning. All seven council members voted Aye.

votes.item_title: Item 22 — Adopt Ordinance Amending Unified Development Ordinance for 4115 Angier Avenue
votes.discussion_detail: Charlie Reece moved and Jillian Johnson seconded adopting the ordinance amending the Unified Development Ordinance for 4115 Angier Avenue. The motion passed unanimously 7-0.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Work Session Dec 10, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At its December 10, 2020 virtual work session with all seven members present, the Durham City Council opened with COVID-19 holiday stay-at-home guidance from Javiera Caballero, gun violence condolences and concern over shootings at the 900 East Main Street apartments from DeDreana Freeman, and consensus to bring forward a CROWN Act anti-hair-discrimination resolution. Council voted unanimously 7-0 to accept the City Manager's priority item, then voted 7-0 to suspend the rules and 7-0 to approve an interlocal agreement receiving $250,000 in additional Durham County CARES Act funds for the Durham CARES Small Business Grant Program before the December 31 deadline. Members also heard public comment opposing Walltown displacement around the Northgate Mall sale, reviewed the Durham County Transit Plan update (including commuter rail vs. bus tradeoffs and cost-sharing), and questioned City Manager Wanda Page on one-time emergency funding options for violence interruption ahead of a January 7 staff report before settling the regular agenda 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Council Announcements (COVID-19 Order, Gun Violence, CROWN Act)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: All seven council members answered roll call. Javiera Caballero urged virtual holiday celebrations under the governor's 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. stay-at-home order amid surging COVID-19 rates, another member mourned a recent shooting homicide and promoted the Durham Arts Council auction, and DeDreana Freeman highlighted five to six recent shootings near 900 East Main Street while gaining council consensus to draft a local CROWN Act resolution banning natural hair discrimination.

agenda_items.title: Supplemental Item 24 — Durham County Interlocal Agreement for CARES Small Business Grant Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager presented Supplemental Item 24, an interlocal agreement to accept $250,000 in Durham County CARES Act funding for the Durham CARES Small Business Grant Program prior to the December 31 federal spending deadline. Council voted 7-0 to accept the priority item, 7-0 to suspend the rules for same-day action, and 7-0 to authorize execution of the interlocal agreement.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Pulled Items and Public Comment on Northgate Mall / Walltown
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Items 3 (Workers' Bill of Rights), 6 (Williams Water Treatment Plant paving), 7 (Synagro Central biosolids contract), and 16 (Duke University/Durham Housing Authority fiber-optic agreement), while praising Item 15 (DOJ SAKI grant). A Walltown community organizer addressed the sale of Northgate Mall to Northwood Investors and its potential tax and rent displacement impacts on Black working-class families.

agenda_items.title: Presentation — Durham County Transit Plan Update and Regional Commuter Rail Cost-Sharing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City-County Planning and transit staff updated Council on socially distanced community engagement, integration with the Comprehensive Plan, and prioritization under the Durham County Transit Plan. Council members reflected on balancing regional commuter rail commitments with local bus service needs, referencing the $160 million spent on the prior light-rail effort and noting that county commissioners would negotiate commuter rail cost-sharing with Raleigh.

agenda_items.title: Violence Interruption Funding Options and Settling the Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Acting City Manager Wanda Page confirmed staff would return January 7 with funding and geographic options for expanding violence interruption, and explained to Mark-Anthony Middleton that one-time fund balance and pro-rated 1/12 monthly county ILA payments could support mid-year action outside the regular budget cycle. Council then voted 7-0 to settle the regular Consent Agenda (Items 1-16, including Item 3 with an updated motion) and General Business public hearings (Items 19-22).

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Item (Supplemental Item 24)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder not explicitly named in audio transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the City Manager's presentation of Supplemental Item 24 (CARES Small Business Grant ILA with Durham County), Council moved, seconded, and approved accepting the priority item 7-0 by roll call.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules to Vote on Supplemental Item 24 at Work Session
votes.discussion_detail: Because CARES Act funds had to be obligated before December 31, Pierce Freelon moved and DeDreana Freeman seconded suspending the rules to vote immediately on Item 24. Passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 24 — Authorize City Manager to Execute City-County Interlocal Agreement for Durham CARES Small Business Grant Program
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton moved and Pierce Freelon seconded authorizing the City Manager to execute the interlocal agreement accepting $250,000 from Durham County for small business CARES grants. Passed unanimously 7-0, with Mayor Schewel thanking Mr. Pettigrew's department for administering the grants in-house.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Mtg. with Durham Delegation Dec 9, 2020
meetings.executive_summary: In a virtual joint legislative consultation on December 9, 2020, members of the Durham City Council and legislative staff (including Carmisha Wallace) presented the city's 30-item 2021 Long Session Legislative Agenda and 10-item advocacy agenda to members of the Durham General Assembly delegation, including Senator Mike Woodard, Senator Natalie Murdock, Representative Vernetta Alston, and Representative Marcia Morey. Discussions covered statewide housing and tax proposals such as expanding the circuit breaker property tax exemption, inclusionary zoning and impact fees, and using county land near old Lowe's Grove School, alongside enterprise-fund utility rate flexibility, driver's licenses for undocumented residents, repealing the controlled-substance excise tax, Ban the Box expansion, Extreme Risk Protection Orders, and ending non-DWI license suspensions. Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton and delegation members also examined two proposed local charter amendments—adding election flexibility for filling council vacancies and expanding grant-making flexibility for COVID-style relief—before Senator Woodard outlined next steps ahead of legislative bill filing. Because this was a consultative intergovernmental briefing, no formal council votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Welcome and Framing of the 2021 Legislative Committee Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members, city staff, and Durham state legislators gathered virtually in place of the traditional legislative breakfast. Mayor Steve Schewel turned table-setting over to Legislative Committee Chair Charlie Reece, Vice Chair Mark-Anthony Middleton, and staff coordinator Carmisha Wallace to walk through the 2021 legislative items.

agenda_items.title: Circuit Breaker Tax Exemption, Inclusionary Zoning, and Utility Enterprise Funds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Delegation members and city leaders distinguished state bills requiring broader municipal coalitions (such as removing age/disability limits on the circuit breaker property tax exemption and inclusionary zoning/impact fees) from local bills. Senator Mike Woodard noted prior Senate opposition to affordable housing land-use bills (such as a county parcel near old Lowe's Grove School) and flagged Local Government Commission scrutiny over utility enterprise fund rate changes.

agenda_items.title: Undocumented Driver's Licenses, Ban the Box, Gun Violence Prevention, and License Suspensions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Participants reviewed items carried over from 2019 and justice-reform priorities, including issuing driver's licenses to undocumented immigrants, repealing the controlled-substance excise tax, expanding Fair Chance Hiring (Ban the Box) to state contractors and private employers, supporting gun violence prevention and Extreme Risk Protection Orders (ERPOs), and eliminating permanent driver's license suspensions for non-DWI offenses.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Charter Amendments on Council Vacancy Filling and Grant-Making Flexibility
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and Mark-Anthony Middleton explained two proposed local charter amendments requested after the 2020 council vacancy process and CARES Act grant distribution: allowing the option of an election alongside appointment when filling a vacant seat, and granting Raleigh-style local grant flexibility subject to state constitutional public-purpose constraints. Legislators asked clarifying questions about the breadth of flexibility under the vacancy proposal.

agenda_items.title: Advocacy Agenda Review and Pre-Session Delegation Follow-Up
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Ms. Wallace noted the finalized package comprised 30 legislative items plus 10 advocacy items (including Environmental Affairs Board energy-efficiency priorities). Senator Mike Woodard commended the early December outreach ahead of January bill filing and stated legislators would review items with council staff before Mayor Steve Schewel adjourned the meeting at 4:39 p.m.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Dec 7, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting virtually on December 7, 2020 with all seven members present, the Durham City Council established a new two-hour closed-captioner break custom and unanimously approved the Consent Agenda 7-0, covering the FY21-22 budget schedule, Safety and Wellness Task Force bylaws, police impound storage leasing, NCCU police jurisdiction, street/sidewalk contracts, and a WIOA workforce contract amendment. On Item 8 (2021 Long Session Legislative Agenda), Council debated whether to include two local charter amendments—on council vacancy election flexibility and grant-making authority—with Charlie Reece voicing caution about drawing state legislative scrutiny to Durham's charter while Mark-Anthony Middleton and colleagues argued for presenting them to the Durham delegation for vetting; Council ultimately passed the full agenda 7-0 after removing staff drafting notes. On Item 25, following a public hearing on the CARES Act First Substantial Amendment to the FY2020-21 Annual Action Plan and 2020-25 Consolidated Plan covering $5,449,225 in HUD CDBG-CV, ESG-CV, and HOPWA-CV funds, Council passed five unanimous 7-0 roll-call motions before adjourning at 8:57 p.m.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Closed-Captioner Break Policy, Condolences, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel opened the meeting with a moment of silence for residents affected by COVID-19 and gun violence, instituted a five-minute break every two hours for closed captioners, and extended condolences to DeDreana Freeman and Beverly Thompson on family losses. Council announcements congratulated newly sworn-in Durham County Commissioners and discussed gun violence and policing ahead of upcoming work session updates.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Clerk Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted added attachments for Item 8 (2021 Long Session Legislative Agenda) and Item 24 (UDO Omnibus Changes 15, TC2000002). agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval (Budget Schedule, Task Force Bylaws, Street/Water Contracts, Police Impound, WIOA)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Schewel read the Consent Agenda including Durham Housing Authority and Planning Commission appointments, the FY21-22 Budget Development Schedule, revised Safety and Wellness Task Force bylaws, the Stagecoach Road lift station condemnation, a police impound storage lease, NCCU Police extended jurisdiction, paving and sidewalk repair contracts, Lakewood Avenue/NC 54 utility work, and a PY2020 WIOA contract amendment. Council approved the Consent Agenda unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: 2021 Long Session Legislative Agenda (Including Proposed Local Charter Amendments)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carmisha Wallace and Senior Assistant City Attorney Krista Kukarot presented research on two unresolved legislative proposals requested by Mark-Anthony Middleton: charter amendments for council vacancy election flexibility and Raleigh-style grant-making authority (noting state constitutional public-purpose limits). Charlie Reece expressed concern over inviting General Assembly intervention into Durham's charter, while Middleton, Mayor Schewel, and Javiera Caballero favored forwarding the proposals for the Durham delegation to vet; after confirming removal of extraneous staff notes flagged by DeDreana Freeman, Council approved the agenda 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing — CARES Act First Substantial Amendment (FY2020-21 Annual Action Plan & 2020-25 Consolidated Plan)

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Dec 7, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Including Local Charter Amendments in the 2021 Long Session Legislative Agenda
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to formally include two proposed local charter amendments—council vacancy filling flexibility and Raleigh-style grant-making flexibility—in the 2021 Legislative Agenda presented to the General Assembly.
disagreements.side_a_position: Questioned taking charter amendments to the current state legislature due to risk of inviting General Assembly interference with Durham's charter and doubts over whether the grant amendment overcomes constitutional hurdles.
side_a_arguments: Opening Durham's charter before the current composition of the North Carolina General Assembly could invite unwanted modifications.
The grant charter language may still be constrained by the state constitution's exclusive emoluments and public-purpose clauses.
disagreements.side_b_position: Include both charter amendments in the agenda so the Durham delegation can vet their viability during the December 9 consultation.
side_b_arguments: Constituents and civic groups asked for expanded democratic options on council vacancies and municipal agility to distribute COVID-style relief grants.
Durham's charter is already a creature of the state and the city routinely takes principled positions without self-censoring.
Placing the items on the agenda allows candid feedback from the Durham delegation before any bill is filed.
disagreements.resolution: Accepting that the December 9 delegation meeting would vet what was legislatively movable, Charlie Reece joined Mark-Anthony Middleton in moving/seconding the full agenda, which passed unanimously 7-0.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Nov 19, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting virtually on November 19, 2020 with five members present (DeDreana Freeman previously excused and Charlie Reece absent due to illness), the Durham City Council voted 5-0 to grant an excused absence to Charlie Reece and 5-0 to approve the City Manager's priority items. Council agreed by unanimous thumbs-up consensus to schedule the Workers' Rights Commission's Workers' Bill of Rights on the December 10 work session agenda, and heard a Citizen's Matter from William Powell regarding street hazards from ATVs and dirt bikes. Staff then delivered two major presentations: Water Management reported on non-payment disconnection suspensions, virtual hold improvements, ESL outreach, and roughly $70,000-$75,000 remaining in utility assistance funds with fewer than 20 accounts disconnected, while Police Chief C.J. Davis presented the 2020 Third Quarter Crime Report covering gun violence task forces, pandemic-depressed clearance rates, and sexual assault kit processing. Council concluded by voting 5-0 to settle the upcoming regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absence for Charlie Reece, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With DeDreana Freeman on a previously approved excused absence, Council voted 5-0 to grant an excused absence to Charlie Reece, who was under the weather. In announcements, Javiera Caballero urged Thanksgiving COVID-19 testing and gathering limits, and Jillian Johnson secured unanimous thumbs-up consensus to place the Workers' Rights Commission's Workers' Bill of Rights on the December 10 work session agenda.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Clerk Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager presented added attachments for Item 8 (2021 Legislative Agenda), Item 20 (water disconnections), Item 21 (Q3 crime report), Item 26 (William Powell Citizen's Matter), and Supplemental Item 27 (Eckerd Alternatives PY2020 WIOA contract amendment). Council approved the manager's priority items 5-0, and the City Clerk introduced new staff member Paula Roland.

agenda_items.title: Administrative Consent Review and Citizens' Matters — William Powell on ATVs and Dirt Bikes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Item 5 (FY21-22 budget development schedule) and Item 6 ('We Are the Ones' COVID-19 response) while Mayor Schewel noted public infrastructure contracts sustain employment during the recession. Resident William Powell (Item 26) raised concerns about dirt bikes and ATVs on city streets, noting police pursuit constraints and discussing temporary dedicated riding spaces as a stopgap measure.

agenda_items.title: Presentation — Water Disconnections for Non-Payment Suspension and Resumption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Water Management staff briefed Council on customer billing call-center virtual hold options, leak/high-bill challenges for residents working or schooling from home, and utility assistance utilization—noting roughly $155,000 spent through October and $70,000-$75,000 remaining from the second allocation ahead of a mid-year funding check-in. Members commended staff's multilingual outreach and noted fewer than 20 accounts were currently without water service.

agenda_items.title: Presentation — 2020 Third Quarter Crime Report (Durham Police Department)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief C.J. Davis presented the Q3 Crime Report, detailing violent crime reduction strategies (Centralized Violent Crime Task Force, All Hands on Deck, anti-gun violence videos, and federal coordination), state crime lab processing of sexual assault kits, lower Q2/Q3 clearance rates linked to reduced COVID-19 in-person contact, and a virtual Citizens Police Academy pilot. Mark-Anthony Middleton questioned whether a small group still drove most shootings and commended DPD's handling of racial justice demonstrations.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager recommended placing Items 1-5, 7, 9-18, and 27 on the Consent Agenda and Item 8 (2021 Legislative Agenda) plus public hearings Items 22-25 on the General Business Agenda. Council approved the settled agenda 5-0 and adjourned at 5:26 p.m.

disagreements.meeting_title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Nov 16, 2020 (Live Stream)
disagreements.issue: Doc Nichols Road Townhome Annexation: Montague Street Stub Traffic vs. Housing Supply and Predictable Rules
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-2 over whether to approve a townhome annexation and rezoning connecting to Montague Street in Fennel Farms or reject it to compel the developer to fund off-site NCDOT/traffic mitigations.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the Doc Nichols Road townhome annexation and rezoning because street stubs are intended to connect, the project supplies relatively attainable townhomes, and by-right development would lack proffers.
side_a_arguments: Existing street stubs in newly built subdivisions like Fennel Farms are explicitly designed to be extended into adjacent developments.
The townhomes offer more attainable pricing than surrounding single-family homes and generate modest additional trips compared to by-right development.
Refusing projects under existing rules risks capricious decision-making driven by neighborhood opposition while traffic calming can still be explored.
disagreements.side_b_position: Vote no to send the developer back to the drawing board to finance an alternative NCDOT connection or pursue a one-way traffic hardship solution for Montague Street.
side_b_arguments: Neighbors on Montague Street raised serious pedestrian and senior safety concerns from cut-through traffic.
The developer had not priced or engineered an alternative NCDOT road connection or one-way street arrangement, which only a no vote would force them to pursue.
disagreements.resolution: All three motions (annexation and utility extension, consistency statement, and UDO amendment) passed 4-2, with DeDreana Freeman excused absent.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Nov 5, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At its November 5, 2020 virtual work session with all seven council members present, the Durham City Council opened with Charlie Reece advising mail-in and provisional voters on checking ballot status at dcovotes.com before November 12, then voted unanimously 7-0 to approve the City Manager's priority items (setting the FY2020 CAFR as a presentation and postponing Item 5, 'We Are the Ones,' by two weeks). Council reviewed departmental items—pulling deputy finance officer appointments, the virtual city auction, and Street Smart LLC software, and asking for floodplain vehicle relocation plans at the Public Works Operations Center—before hearing two key staff briefings. The Equity and Inclusion Department reported on department-level data disaggregation, a 25-member frontline racial equity team, and survey confusion between diversity and equity as council members pushed for structural funding shifts, while Transportation staff reviewed 4,000K LED streetlight conversions, shielding/removal procedures, and the 40% city cost share to replace fixtures. Council closed by voting 7-0 to settle the regular meeting agenda and adjourned at 3:48 p.m.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Election Ballot Cure Announcements, and City Manager's Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: All seven council members answered roll call. Charlie Reece urged absentee voters to verify and cure mail-in ballots via dcovotes.com by November 12 and explained provisional ballot verification; another member explained requesting postponement of Item 5 ('We Are the Ones'). Council voted 7-0 to approve the City Manager's priority items placing the FY2020 CAFR as a presentation and referring Item 5 to the next work session.

agenda_items.title: Departmental Items Review and Pulled Items 8, 9, and 14
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed departmental items including the October 2020 employee evaluation audit, NC Justice Center Welcome Home grant, Participatory Budgeting bylaws, Farrington/Fayetteville Road apartments loan, Wheels Fun Park land acquisition, remote learning center grants, and Balfour Beatty's Public Works Operations Center CMAR amendment (with Mayor Schewel requesting an email on floodplain vehicle relocation plans). Council discussed pulled Item 8 (signature controls for deputy finance/tax collector appointments) and pulled Item 9 (potential revenue impacts of a virtual city vehicle/equipment auction).

agenda_items.title: Presentation — Equity and Inclusion Department Racial Equity Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Equity and Inclusion staff reported on expanding racial equity teams (including 25 self-nominated employees and frontline workers), tracking departmental data disaggregation capabilities, and addressing Racial Equity Viewpoint Survey findings showing confusion among diversity, inclusion, and equity. Council members pressed staff and Acting City Manager Wanda Page on moving beyond symbolic steps toward structural resource reallocation, reparations/UBI/grant possibilities, and state/federal advocacy.

agenda_items.title: Presentation — LED Street Lighting Conversion Program Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation staff (Mr. Judge) presented on the Duke Energy LED streetlight conversion, detailing limited data on lower-Kelvin alternatives compared to 4,000K fixtures, alignment verification and shield installations for glare complaints, majority-block polling for streetlight removals, and the city's 40% cost share if fixtures were swapped out. Javiera Caballero and Mayor Schewel agreed that spending millions on a mass swap was infeasible under current budget constraints while urging careful standards going forward.

agenda_items.title: Settling the Upcoming Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager recommended placing Items 1-4 and 6-14 on the Consent Agenda and General Business public hearings Items 18-21 (1432 Ellis Road, Cortez Drive, Doc Nichols Road, and 851 Slater Road). Council approved the settled agenda unanimously 7-0 and adjourned at 3:48 p.m.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Items (Item 1 CAFR Presentation & Item 5 Referral)
votes.discussion_detail: DeDreana Freeman moved and Pierce Freelon seconded approving the City Manager's priority items setting Item 1 (CAFR) as a presentation and referring Item 5 ('We Are the Ones' COVID-19 response) to the next work session. All seven members voted Aye on roll call.

votes.item_title: Settle Upcoming Regular Meeting Agenda (Consent Items 1-4, 6-14; GBA Public Hearings Items 18-21)
votes.discussion_detail: Javiera Caballero moved and Charlie Reece seconded approving the City Manager's settled agenda placing Items 1-4 and 6-14 on Consent and Items 18-21 on the General Business public hearing agenda. The clerk recorded the motion passing 7-0.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Meeting Nov 2, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting virtually on November 2, 2020, all seven Durham City Council members opened with a proclamation honoring the late Honorable Mary Ann E. Black (with remarks from her son Jonathan Black), election-eve transit updates recognizing GoDurham for distributing roughly 100,000 masks, and council comments calling for measurable short-term and long-term outcomes on violence interruption initiatives. City Manager Wanda Page presented priority updates covering the Eno-Haw Regional Hazard Mitigation Plan, Multifamily Production and Preservation RFP awards, a Coronavirus Relief Fund plan amendment, and the ordering of Chesterfield Avenue street closing after 1700 Hillandale Road. Council unanimously approved 7-0 a multifamily housing revenue bond authorization not to exceed $12 million and, following a public hearing featuring Durham CAN and resident concerns over Durham Housing Authority (DHA) transparency and maintenance standards, unanimously passed 7-0 up to $15.4 million in multifamily housing revenue bonds for J.J. Henderson Towers.

agenda_items.title: Proclamation Honoring the Life and Legacy of the Honorable Mary Ann E. Black
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Steve Schewel read a proclamation honoring former Durham County Commissioner, Duke University Health Systems leader, and N.C. House District 29 Representative Mary Ann E. Black for her public service in health care, aging, and education. Her son, Jonathan Black, thanked the Council and reflected on his mother's devotion to helping people across Durham.

agenda_items.title: Election Day Transit Access, GoDurham Pandemic Service, and Gun Violence Interventions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council shared Election Day transportation resources including GoDurham routes and DurhamRides.com, while praising GoDurham bus operators as pandemic MVPs who maintained essential-worker service and distributed approximately 100,000 face masks. Members also addressed recent gun violence and ongoing work-session deliberations on violence interruption, stressing the need for clear timelines and measurable policy metrics during the emergency.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Updates and Consent Agenda Introduction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page reported updated attachments for Item 7 (2020 Eno-Haw Regional Hazard Mitigation Plan), Item 19 (2020-2021 Multifamily Production and Preservation RFP recommendations), and Item 27 (Durham City Coronavirus Relief Fund plan amendment), and requested Item 21 (Z180013 Chesterfield Avenue Street Closing) be heard after Item 22 (Z180032 1700 Hillandale Road). Mayor Schewel then introduced the Consent Agenda.

agenda_items.title: Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds Authorization (Not to Exceed $12 Million)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered an authorization for multifamily housing revenue bonds in an aggregate amount not to exceed $12 million. DeDreana Freeman moved and Pierce Freelon seconded approval of the financing.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Bond Authorization — J.J. Henderson Towers Multifamily Housing Facility ($15.4 Million)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a staff report by Mr. Johnson, Council held a public hearing in which speakers A.J. Williams/Willy and Heather Ladd (Durham CAN) criticized Durham Housing Authority (DHA) property management staffing, unresolved mold/maintenance issues, and unposted public hearings, urging Council to tie future affordable housing bond funding to transparency and quality-of-life benchmarks. DHA staff acknowledged failing to post the September hearing online as an oversight, and Council members debated minimum housing code enforcement and incremental use of the $95 million housing bond toward DHA's $544 million capital needs before voting unanimously to authorize up to $15.4 million in bonds.

meetings.title: Virtual Durham City Council Work Session Oct 22, 2020 (Live Stream)
meetings.executive_summary: At its October 22, 2020 work session, all seven Durham City Council members recognized retiring Assistant City Clerk Laverne Brooks and unanimously approved 7-0 priority items from the City Manager, City Attorney (closed session on Darryl Howard v. City of Durham), and City Clerk (supplemental Workforce Development Board appointments, after DeDreana Freeman requested clearer vetting transparency).
